epub_10.title: Politics
epub_10.text:
Politics
The world this week
Politics
Oct 29th 2026
No clear winner emerged from
Israel’s election
. With more than 90% of the vote counted, Binyamin Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 of the 120 seats in the Knesset. The opposition parties took 67 seats, enough to command a majority. But 19 of those seats went to Arab parties, a historic high, and most of the Jewish opposition parties have refused to include them in a coalition. Once the results are finalised, coalition talks will begin. Before the election Mr Netanyahu ordered Israeli troops into Hebron, a city in the occupied West Bank, after Palestinian gunmen attacked a military checkpoint, killing two soldiers. Thousands of Palestinians were forced to leave their homes or had their homes demolished.
Officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, the three signatories to the new
Mecca pact
, travelled to Tehran to meet Iran’s security chief and president. The meeting took place amid more attacks by the Houthis, Iranian-backed rebels in Yemen, on Saudi infrastructure and the growing threat of further American and Israeli strikes on Iran. No breakthroughs were announced.
Nine people were shot dead at a Christian funeral in Jordan. The country’s air force struck back at  “terrorist organisations” in Syria.
At least 100 people were killed and dozens more injured in an army drone strike on a market in Nyala, in
Sudan
’s Darfur region, which is controlled by the rebel Rapid Support Forces. According to the UN drone strikes killed over 300 people and injured hundreds more in the first three weeks of October. Separately, drone strikes by the RSF knocked out several power plants in army-controlled areas, causing widespread power cuts.
Dozens of African delegations travelled to Moscow for a summit with Vladimir Putin. Mr Putin is trying to pitch Russia as a more reliable partner for African countries than the “colonial” West.
A Tanzanian opposition activist was abducted near Nairobi, the latest sign that the Kenyan capital is no longer a sanctuary for regional dissidents. Twaha Mwaipaya is the third prominent Tanzanian dissident to have been abducted in Kenya, in what appears to be a troubling trend of governments in East Africa colluding to crush dissent.
Kim Jong Un
, North Korea’s dictator, made a surprise visit to Dandong in China.  Mr Kim was driven over a bridge crossing the Yalu river to the border city. The official reason for his trip was to commemorate China’s support for North Korea during the Korean war. Speculation swirled that he was also consulting with the Chinese ahead of a possible meeting with Donald Trump.
South Korea
proposed talks with
North Korea
on the demarcation of their border following several recent incidents in the demilitarised zone, including a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers. It is unclear whether North Korea will accept the offer. After the explosion, the North resumed its broadcasts along the border, blaring propaganda from loudspeakers into the South.
At least 68 people were killed when
two high-speed trains collided
on the line between Madrid and Seville in Spain. One train was stationary, reportedly because of a computer-system failure. The crash has raised more concerns about maintenance of the country’s railways. In January 46 people died when one train derailed and another smashed into its carriages in southern Spain.
More than 1,400 people were arrested across
France
in another day of protests that were accompanied by vandalism and looting, but less so than over the previous weekend. The day before the demonstrations a black man was shot dead near Paris and seven people injured, including a child, when a 39-year-old man opened fire from his car. Emmanuel Macron called it a “racist, terrorist attack”.
Marine Le Pen, the populist-right front-runner in next year’s presidential election, officially launched her campaign. She made her first campaign speech in Orléans, a city closely associated with Joan of Arc. At its party congress the same weekend, her National Rally re-elected Jordan Bardella as its president. Ms Le Pen confirmed that she will appoint him prime minister if the party takes power.
In
Ukraine
a six-day ceasefire came into force to allow humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. The ceasefire was reportedly extended across the Kherson region. Meanwhile, Vladimir Putin spoke by phone to the leaders of Finland and Norway ahead of forthcoming trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and America that will take place in Abu Dhabi.
Aleksandar Vucic, who has served as either prime minister or president of Serbia since 2014,
conceded defeat in a parliamentary election.
Mr Vucic had called the snap poll after two years of student-led protests against corruption and abuses of government power. Tens of thousands of people took to the streets to celebrate the Student List’s stunning victory. The list was composed of candidates selected by student bodies; the students ruled themselves out from standing. Russia has now lost two key allies in Europe: Mr Vucic in Serbia and Viktor Orban in Hungary.
Two men, both British nationals, were charged in connection with an
incident at RAF Fairford
that is thought to have been directed by Iran. Details of the plot remain unclear, but intelligence warnings that Iran was planning to attack the air-force base prompted America to withdraw its fleet of bombers.
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was
re-elected as Brazil’s president
in a run-off election, winning 52% of the vote. It was the first time a candidate who had finished second in the first round went on to win the run-off. Flávio Bolsonaro, his conservative challenger and the first-round winner, described the outcome as “inexplicable” and suggested foul play, but his party accepted the result. After the election,
Mr Bolsonaro left Brazil for Miami
, defying a judge who ordered him to stay in the country while a pre-existing criminal investigation continues. In a social-media post he said the election had been stolen by “criminals” who have “established a tyranny”.
María Corina Machado
returned to Venezuela
. The opposition leader left the country ten months ago to collect a Nobel peace prize. She had tried to return several times since January, when American special forces arrested Nicolás Maduro. Ms Machado has called for fresh elections, though her party has been excluded from talks brokered by the Trump administration on a future electoral process. Marco Rubio, America’s secretary of state, says the talks are making progress and that no one should try to “derail that process”.
In
Canada
the opposition Conservative Party won its first election in British Columbia in nearly 100 years. The province had been governed by the left-wing New Democratic Party since 2017. The Conservatives have pledged to  slash red tape and remove limits on greenhouse-gas emissions. They also promise to increase British Columbia’s output of liquefied natural gas and support a new oil pipeline from Alberta to the west coast. The party’s pro-energy agenda is bound to face legal challenges.
King Charles began a tour of the Caribbean amid calls from some countries in the region for Britain to pay reparations for slavery. Several governments want the issue placed high on the agenda at the summit of Commonwealth governments that the king will attend in Antigua and Barbuda.

epub_11.title: Business
epub_11.text:
Business
The world this week
Business
Oct 29th 2026
Anthropic
released the long-awaited prospectus for its
IPO
, which promises to be one of the largest ever, if not the largest. Revenue soared from $787m in the second quarter of 2025 to $11.6bn in the same quarter this year. Its spending on personnel, including stock-based compensation, rose from $320m to nearly $1.9bn. Anthropic reported a net loss of $66.3bn for the quarter, mostly because of an accounting charge related to the reassessment of the fair value of debt that could be converted into shares. It actually made an operating profit of $974m in the second quarter, compared with an operating loss of almost $1.7bn in the preceding three months. Anthropic’s stock-market debut could happen in November.
More funding deals were announced in AI. With tech companies increasingly turn to Wall Street and capital markets to fund their investments, Broadcom is setting up a $63bn special-purpose vehicle with Bank of America and other financial firms. The SPV will buy Broadcom’s chips and networking equipment and lease them to Anthropic. Meta is raising $37.5bn through stock offerings. It also plans to raise up to $60bn through periodic sales of newly issued shares, starting next year.
Alphabet’s share price sank, after it emerged that the rate at which it is burning through cash was much higher than markets had expected. Microsoft’s stock fared better, after it reported lower capital expenditures than Wall Street had forecast, mostly because of delays in building new data centres. Seeking to keep costs under control, Microsoft wants to shed 60,000 employees, a quarter of its global workforce, through a “voluntary exit offer” that will give staff “who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition”.
Skydance also offered a “voluntary buy-out” plan to staff as part of its effort to cut costs following its takeover of Warner Bros. It told remaining employees that from now on they would have to work in the office five days a week, because “in a creative company like ours, the best ideas come from people in the same room”.
The British government
unveiled its budget
, the first under
Andy Burnham
as prime minister and
John Healey
as chancellor. Among the measures, the budget raised the bank corporation-tax surcharge from 3% to 6% for 15 months to help pay for
household-energy relief
. Businesses will benefit from a freeze or cut in property taxes, meaning that half of all retail, hospitality and leisure properties will pay no property tax at all. From 2028, mayors and local authorities will have the power to impose a tourist tax. The government also committed to a target to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, but left the details of how this would be funded to a spending review next year.
Christine Lagarde
announced that she would step down as president of the European Central Bank in February, nine month before the official end of her term. Ms Lagarde became the ECB’s president in 2019 and did not expect to be in the job for so long, but she said she was leaving “with a sense of good work done”. She has been talking to the World Economic Forum about possibly becoming its chairwoman. The European Council will appoint her successor at the ECB, with candidates from the Netherlands and Spain currently leading the pack. Meanwhile, the ECB’s governing council made no changes to interest rates when it met in Frankfurt.
The Federal Reserve also kept interest rates on hold at its latest meeting, leaving its benchmark rate in the  3.75-4% range. Kevin Warsh, the Fed’s chairman, promised to continue dispensing “new monetary medicine” to bring inflation under control. Markets think the Fed will raise rates over the coming months.
The American economy grew by 3.4% in the third quarter at an annualised rate, up from 2.2% in the second quarter. Before the figures were released Mr Warsh noted that economic growth had strengthened, and described consumer spending and capital expenditures as “healthy”.
The
IPO of JIO Platforms
was a success, raising $3.1bn. The share price of the Indian telecoms company rose by 27% on the first day of trading, leaving it with a market capitalisation of $137bn. Jio will use the proceeds to pay debt accrued as it furthers its ambitions in AI and satellite broadband.
Boeing’s stock took a dive, after the company confirmed it would miss production and delivery targets for its 737 aircraft this year. Its commercial-airline division reported a quarterly operating loss of $697m, more than analysts had expected, but profits from defence, space and security surged to $492m.
Audi announced that it will build a $4bn factory in Georgia, its first plant in America. The factory will produce 200,000 sport-utility vehicles a year, creating 4,500 jobs, even as Audi’s parent company, Volkswagen, slashes 100,000 jobs. Gernot Döllner, Audi’s boss, made the announcement with Donald Trump at a campaign rally in Georgia. The president said Audi’s decision would not have happened “without tariffs”: European cars that are made in America are exempt from the duties.
The carmaking industry’s evolution to a focus on high tech was underscored by the decision of General Motors to switch its share listing from the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq. The Nasdaq is a natural home for our “technology-driven strategy”, GM said. The company recently highlighted how it is “using frontier AI and machine-learning breakthroughs to accelerate development” in autonomous driving.

epub_14.title: The Americans changing politics for the better
epub_14.text:
The Americans changing politics for the better
Leaders
| The midterm elections
The Americans changing politics for the better
Hispanics and Asians have become their country’s most dynamic swing voters
Oct 29th 2026
MIDTERM ELECTIONS are always a referendum on the sitting American president, but rarely has an incumbent so wilfully put himself in the spotlight in defiance of his own unpopularity. As the campaign ends, Donald Trump is commandeering rallies in Republican strongholds, a sign of his party’s vulnerability and his unwavering faith in his own star power. Away from the spotlight, however, something more surprising—and more important—has been happening: Hispanics and Asians have emerged as America’s most valuable voters.
The curse of American politics is its bitter partisanship. As voters have sorted themselves along racial, educational and geographical lines, the parties have spent less time trying to win converts from the other side and more whipping their own supporters into a permanent frenzy: 70% of Republicans are hostile towards Democrats and more than 80% of Democrats return the favour. The result is a style of politics that tugs public life towards the extremes, punishes compromise and puts getting people angry above getting things done.
Hispanic and Asian-American voters offer the best hope of arresting this baleful trend. They have become America’s crucial swing voters, with an outsize impact on races across the country. Compared with other blocs, their numbers are growing faster, their ideology is more fluid and their priorities are less divisive. That means they are likely to be good for America not just in these midterms, but also for many elections to come.
The biggest force on November 3rd will be Mr Trump’s unpopularity. His national net-approval rating stands at -27 points. The president is predicting victory in “record numbers”, but our forecast model suggests Democrats have a 95% chance of
winning back the House
and a 54% chance of
taking the Senate
. Polling puts Mr Trump underwater on every policy, from inflation to immigration. His great vulnerability is that voters blame higher bills on his fondness for tariffs and his choice to go to war with Iran.
The backlash has created openings for Democrats in states such as Kansas and Iowa, where even contemplating a blue victory would once have got Republican strategists sacked. Disenchanted rural voters who chose Mr Trump in 2024 may stay at home this time, as a protest against high diesel prices and poor markets for their crops. Polls say Democrats are winning back the young and peeling off working-class whites.
It would be good for America to have more battleground states. If Democrats win in places like Kansas and Texas, the power of incumbency could make them competitive in future elections, too. No group captures the potential for opening up politics as much as Hispanics and Asian-Americans.
One reason is
demography
. They are a growing fraction of the population—especially Hispanics, who are three times more numerous than Asian-Americans. Since 2006 their combined share of the electorate has increased by nine percentage points, to reach 21%. They are also highly diverse. The grandchildren of an immigrant from Ho Chi Minh City have a different outlook from a new arrival from Bangalore. Neither fits neatly into the familiar Democrat-Republican template.
And they are more likely to switch their votes. In 2012 Democrats thought they had a lock on Latinos and Asians. In 2024 the story was how they were becoming Trumpian. It has now become clear that they were swing voters all along.
White voters changed little between 2020 and 2024, while both Latinos and Asians lurched hard to the right. They were then the fastest to turn against Mr Trump in early 2025. The margin of support for Democrats has risen by 17 points among Latinos and 14 among Asians since 2024, compared with ten for whites and five for black voters. They are likely to help decide House races from suburban New York to Florida as well as Senate contests in Alaska, Kansas and Texas.
Part of the explanation for this is that these voters are the epitome of striving Americans who want to work hard and get ahead. Higher prices for food and fuel hit Hispanic voters particularly hard; housing costs affected Asian voters. Latinos are more than twice as likely to start businesses as white voters. Asians are likely to spend more time in education.
Many are recent arrivals or the children of immigrants, so their opinions have not yet hardened along party lines. In contrast to the rest of the voting population, if Hispanics and Asians hold one left-leaning position, they will not necessarily endorse others. Likewise, wanting a secure southern border does not equate to support for the hardline enforcement that has frightened Hispanic employees into staying away from work.
Instead, many are moderate. They have little truck with culture wars or polarisation. The economic policies they care about diverge from the tribal messages the parties use to stir up their bases. Whereas policies on abortion and trans rights are set at the extremes, economic management is suited to the swing voter’s pragmatic preference for the common good.
Almost anything that gives the parties a reason to appeal to the centre will benefit America, especially when it involves the virtues of hard work and prosperity. Democrats will need a winning economic message and a coherent plan for immigration. Republicans should reject their ferocious deportations and the ugly ultranationalism that denigrates Hispanic and Asian citizens for not being “heritage Americans”.
All Americans should therefore welcome these new swing voters. Thanks to them, fewer elections will be decided by hard-core party members in primaries, and more by the average voter in the general election. If politicians win more credit by accomplishing something in government, they will perhaps spend less of their time demonising the other side. If the economy seems to matter more and culture wars less, America will be more prosperous and better governed. Hispanic and Asian immigrants want the chance to thrive. Their votes will help ensure America thrives with them.

epub_15.title: Andy Burnham’s government talks of change, then does nothing
epub_15.text:
Andy Burnham’s government talks of change, then does nothing
Leaders
| Our cover
Andy Burnham’s government talks of change, then does nothing
Britain’s unimpressive budget reveals a lack of ambition
Oct 29th 2026
You could forgive Andy Burnham for feeling chirpy. Britain’s prime minister begins his second hundred days with a healthy lead in the polls and a better-than-expected run of economic growth. His chancellor, John Healey, presented a
budget
that succeeded in riling neither bond vigilantes nor Labour backbenchers. And, in news to stir any English heart, France is doing much worse, as its public finances languish and its streets are occupied by rioters.
In Britain election fever is in the air. So the need to please voters could explain why, in a budget that was mostly empty of substance, Mr Healey did find a few billion pounds to finance a £100 ($133) payment to four in five households, supposedly to offset energy bills. Shortly after the chancellor stopped speaking, the legion of Britons checking whether their house qualifies for the money crashed a government website.
Mr Burnham insists he has ruled out an election for at least 12 months—but he would say that, wouldn’t he? What is troubling is that this budget epitomised the inadequacy of his approach to government. The changes are vast in the narrowest sense that they include 98 costed policy measures, comfortably more than any other recent budget. There was a smidgen of good news on streamlining data-centre approvals. Also, places will be funded more from taxes paid by local residents and businesses, giving them an incentive to stimulate growth. Mr Healey focused energy policy on cheap power, and did not succumb to the perennial temptation of new chancellors to rewrite the fiscal rules.
And yet in almost every sense that matters, the budget’s changes are trifling. The sums involved were trivial and few of its measures grapple with Britain’s deep economic problems. Instead it presents a spasm of tweaks that will worsen the perverse incentives which plague the tax code.
The prime minister is even more difficult to pin down than Sir Keir Starmer. True, he is cannier than his predecessor about throwing out politically popular goodies, like the £100 payments and cheaper supermarket gherkins, thanks to lower grocery tariffs. But whenever Mr Burnham is bold—as he proposes to be by limiting pensions, funding social care and reviving Britain’s relations with the European Union—he puts off difficult decisions until after the next election.
That approach to governing will soon wear thin. The spending review, due in 2027, will be tough. To pay for defence and prevent harsh cuts, Mr Healey will have to raise around £30bn, says the Institute for Fiscal Studies, a think-tank. “We start from a position of strength,” the chancellor said on Wednesday, not entirely convincingly. Health, pension and welfare spending will keep marching up, straining Britain’s effort to fund a full-freight welfare state on the cheap, perhaps to breaking-point. Hovering above this is the question of how artificial intelligence will reshape society and the economy.
Mr Burnham’s big ideas are no match for those challenges. He is a nostalgic politician, talking of an end to “40 years of neo-liberalism” at a time when the future is rushing onward. That is a pity, since there is plenty to do—and plenty where Mr Burnham and the neoliberals at The Economist could see eye-to-eye. Devolution is one, and there Mr Burnham has made a good start. Britain really is damagingly over-centralised. There is no reason cities must ask the Treasury to finance transport projects, rather than raising the money themselves.
Another would be reviving Sir Keir’s occasional interest in pro-growth supply-side reform. Labour was elected on a manifesto which argued that faster growth was the way out of Britain’s fiscal woes. Yet that deregulatory revolution has barely begun. Fewer homes are built now than when before Labour was elected. The latest forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility, a watchdog, suggest that the government will miss its target of 1.5m homes built over the course of this parliament by a full half million. Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, has lately taken to calling it a “stretch target”.
Britain’s welfare system has pulled too many young people out of work and onto ill-health benefits, something Mr Burnham has promised to legislate on next year—but which he did nothing about in the budget. The prime minister is also a long-time critic of stamp duty, a levy on property transactions that is probably Britain’s most growth-destroying tax. Like the previous Labour government, he has so far dodged the need to clean up the perversities and traps in Britain’s tax code. It is not too late to act.
Serious work is needed to ready Britain for the changes AI may bring. The data-centre announcements were a first step. But Britain should reform its copyright laws, so that AI models can be trained locally. And what do Mr Burnham and Mr Healey have to say about ensuring Britain captures the productivity gains of AI? Or on how to stop AI from exhausting the capacity of the British state by jamming up the courts, tribunals and official consultations with spurious, chatbot-generated slop?
In short, there is plenty to do and an urgent need to be getting on with it. The prime minister should ignore talk of the need for a new mandate. Britain is a parliamentary democracy and Mr Burnham has its confidence. Rather than remaining beholden to a manifesto that had a large picture of Sir Keir on the front, he has three years to be as bold as he chooses.
What will not succeed for Mr Burnham, or for Britain, would be for the prime minister to pass the time dishing up more policy-lite optimism. Politically, voters are likely to lose patience with a government that merely treads water—even if it does throw them the occasional bung. Economically, Britain is limping along with growth rates barely above 1%. If it is to begin to solve its many problems, it needs growth.
Mr Burnham has no reason to call an election for its own sake. As Sir Keir showed, a mandate and a solid majority are no substitutes for an actual governing agenda. But if Mr Burnham cannot come up with a better vision of how to use the next few years, he should call time and go to the country.

epub_16.title: Israel’s Jewish and Arab opposition parties should work together
epub_16.text:
Israel’s Jewish and Arab opposition parties should work together
Leaders
| Israel’s election
Israel’s Jewish and Arab opposition parties should work together
If they want to dislodge Binyamin Netanyahu from office, they need to act fast
Oct 29th 2026
IN MOST DEMOCRACIES when opposition parties win the most votes, and secure a majority in parliament, they strive to form a government. In Israel, however, nothing is quite so simple. With 90% of the ballots counted on October 28th, the opposition parties were between them sure to have more than half—probably 67—of the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament. In theory, therefore, the right-wing coalition led by Binyamin Netanyahu should be swept from office.
In practice, the opposition may well prove too divided to form a ruling coalition. Of those 67 seats, about 19 are in the hands of parties representing Israel’s Arab minority. During the campaign, most opposition-party leaders explicitly ruled out forming a government with them. When pressed, Gadi Eisenkot, a former general and the leader of Yashar, a centre-right party that took the second-largest share of the vote, was evasive. Yet without the backing of Arab parties, he stands little chance of forming a stable government.
There is no fundamental justification for excluding the Arabs, who make up one-fifth of the population. But they have long been sidelined. In Mr Netanyahu’s first election campaign as leader of Likud, in the 1990s, his supporters ran with the slogan: “Netanyahu. Good for the Jews.” When he triumphed, the defeated centre-left candidate, Shimon Peres, remarked that “Israelis lost” whereas “Jews won.”
The vilification of Israeli Arabs continues. Members of Mr Netanyahu’s most recent coalition included Jewish supremacists, such as Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national-security minister. He once led the youth wing of a virulently anti-Arab movement that went on to be banned in 1994 as a terrorist organisation. In September the Knesset’s election committee barred Arab parties from the election, alleging they supported terrorism and rejected Israel’s Jewish character. The Supreme Court overturned that. On election day, right-wingers in the streets exhorted Jewish voters to “save our home” from Arabs.
Neither are anti-Arab attitudes
confined to the right
. Most Jewish opposition parties go along with Mr Netanyahu’s demonisation of the Arab parties. The attacks of October 7th 2023, when Hamas massacred Israelis, made it a lot harder to counter such attitudes. Scaremongering has led many Jewish voters to fear that Arab-Israelis would like to see Israel destroyed. And though Arab-Israeli politicians did condemn the violence in 2023, some of them, shamefully, would not condemn Hamas as terrorists.
There is a path ahead. Israeli-Arabs responded to recent anti-Arab hysteria in the best way possible, by voting in large numbers. And there is a precedent for Arab parties to be included in governments—they are full citizens of Israel, after all. In 2021 Mr Netanyahu himself sought support from Ra’am, a moderate Islamist party, for his coalition. Though that failed, Ra’am later joined a different, short-lived, grouping led by Naftali Bennett.
A coalition of opposition parties, including the Arab ones, should thus pull together, and fast. Isaac Herzog, Israel’s president, needs to judge that co-operation is possible, with a new coalition led by Mr Eisenkot, or he will opt to invite Mr Netanyahu to try first because Likud is the largest party. Mr Netanyahu has also, of late, pressed for renewed military strikes on Iran. And his government has been inflaming tensions in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. If large-scale violence resumes in either place he might argue that Israel needs him to stay on and lead an emergency “unity” government.
Israelis were under no illusions about this election’s significance. For many it was a referendum on Mr Netanyahu. Some in the opposition spoke of “saving Israeli democracy”. If they really believe that, then their decision is straightforward: work with the Arab-Israeli parties to form a coalition.

epub_17.title: What to make of 25 years of Narendra Modi
epub_17.text:
What to make of 25 years of Narendra Modi
Leaders
| India
What to make of 25 years of Narendra Modi
He is learning that even rapid economic growth won’t placate voters if it fails to produce jobs
Oct 29th 2026
NO TWO LIVES move in perfect parallel. But the careers of Narendra Modi and Xi Jinping, both born in the early 1950s, have a certain symmetry. A quarter of a century ago each was running one of his country’s coastal, industrial provinces. Mr Xi said he devoted the “prime” of his life to governing Fujian, in China’s south-east. Meanwhile Mr Modi had just become chief minister of Gujarat, in India’s west. Each used regional success as a springboard to the top. Mr Xi became China’s president in March 2013; Mr Modi was elected as India’s prime minister a year later.
This week
we assess Mr Modi’s long record
. Many, including The Economist, have been queasy about his stance as a Hindu nationalist. His supporters retort that his role as an economic steward matters more. They often point first to the “Gujarat model”. Just see, they say, how his old state blossomed. Income per head there has risen roughly fivefold at constant prices, from a few hundred dollars in 2001 to a little over $4,000. Thank investment in industry and infrastructure. Gujarat is one of India’s richer states. Voters elsewhere, for example in West Bengal, clamour for similar development.
Nationally, too, there is much to cheer. India’s annual GDP growth, at about 7%, comfortably exceeds that of any other large economy, including China’s. This week India held one of the biggest initial public offerings as investors valued
Jio, a telecoms firm
, at over $100bn. Praise Mr Modi for tax reforms, rapid digitisation, fiscal prudence that limited inflation, vastly better roads, airports and much more. That, combined with well-targeted welfare, has cut the worst poverty. Though crony capitalism is alarming, some corruption has abated. His readiness to strike trade deals and tweak labour laws is welcome. His predecessors managed similar rates of economic growth, but even critics must credit Mr Modi for steady progress.
And yet, that is not enough. A lesson from Mr Xi’s China is that countries must work fast to grow rich before they get old. Unfortunately, the structure of India’s economy is changing too slowly. Look back again at Mr Xi’s old province, Fujian, where income per person leapt more than ten times, from $1,500 to $20,000. Crucially, people there shifted from agriculture into copious—and formal—industrial jobs. The share of workers in farming tumbled from 46% to 13%.
In Gujarat, and India generally, structural change has not properly begun. The share of Gujarati workers in farming has barely budged, from 45% to 42% in 25 years. The national figures are roughly the same. Mr Modi knows this matters. Speaking to The Economist in 2015, he said his priority would be to create jobs and get skilled workers into manufacturing. Those goals were right, but he has not achieved them.
True, some factories have sprung up, to assemble iPhones for export, say. But foreign investment is not flowing well. Astonishingly, India has of late even exported capital. Manufacturing as a share of the economy is 16%, no more than when Mr Modi took office. India may hope to bet on a services economy. But it still needs changes of the sort he has not yet brought about: deeper and better-crafted labour and land reforms; cuts to high tariffs; a stronger workforce nurtured by better schools. Mr Modi’s crony-capitalists, meanwhile, most obviously Gautam Adani, squeeze out other investors.
Unlike Mr Xi, the Indian leader must wrangle a democracy. This is where Mr Modi feels sharp consequences from years of jobless growth. The poorest are better off thanks to extra welfare (more are buying fridges and scooters), but anger is erupting among millions of young, urban and educated people slightly higher up the social ladder, frustrated by the lack of white-collar jobs. Rising energy prices add to the pain. Whatever the headline rate of growth, they are not feeling enough of the benefits. Worse, where India has created valuable jobs—in outsourcing and back-office work, say, or in coding—the threat from AI looms.
This summer a “cockroach movement” of student protesters erupted across cities, forcing Mr Modi to sack a minister for the first time. This autumn big cities have been convulsed by new street protests against the Election Commission, after it excluded 130m names from voters’ rolls (no doubt many were duds, but not all). Protesters accuse the commission’s head of meddling to favour the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).  Two in five Indians now think elections are not free and fair. Mr Modi should recognise that Indians are weary of his strong-arm tactics. Investors will also be deterred if they see him growing more authoritarian.
This month Mr Modi had little chance to mark his 25-year milestone. His good fortune, though not India’s, is that the main opposition party, Congress, led by Rahul Gandhi offers no compelling rival vision for creating jobs. Nor does any figure in the BJP yet threaten Mr Modi. The result is that this septuagenarian, like the one running China, shows no serious sign of refreshing his government. That is a shame. India needs bolder thinking if it is to thrive.

epub_18.title: Markets are dismayed by Lula’s surprise win—and for good reason
epub_18.text:
Markets are dismayed by Lula’s surprise win—and for good reason
Leaders
| Brazil’s comeback king
Markets are dismayed by Lula’s surprise win—and for good reason
The pressure is on Brazil’s re-elected president to avoid an economic slump
Oct 29th 2026
LULA WAS a goner—or at least that is what everyone had assumed. Instead, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s incumbent president, pulled off a win for the history books. The left-wing leader hung on to his job by a clear margin of nearly four percentage points in a presidential run-off on October 25th, even though he had trailed his rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the first round of voting three weeks earlier. Never in Brazilian history has anyone come from behind in this way to clinch the presidency. In January Lula will become the country’s first democratically elected president to start a fourth term.
Yet if Lula’s supporters are elated, others are running scared. One was Flávio, who has sought sanctuary in the United States, claiming emptily to be the ballot’s real victor. For some time investigators have been examining his ties with a businessman accused of laundering vast sums of money (both deny any wrongdoing). The day after the election, the Supreme Court judge who is handling that case required him to surrender his passports. Instead of doing that, Flávio ran away.
More significant, investors are fleeing Brazil, too. Markets rightly fear economic drift and high-spending that Brazil cannot afford. The real slumped by 8% against the dollar the day after the election result, the worst one-day fall in over 25 years. The main stock-market index, the Bovespa, closed 14% lower, having tripped a circuit-breaker on the way down. If Lula wants to lift up poor Brazilians, avoid a crisis and protect his legacy, his final four years in office will have to look very different from the past four. That starts with him persuading investors that he means to change course.
Investors had wanted Flávio to win in large part because they trust his opponent even less. For years, successive governments, including Lula’s, have spent wildly. That has forced the central bank to hike the real interest rate, now at 9%. Brazil pays a larger share of GDP in interest on its debt than all but a tiny handful of big countries. All this weighs on investment, squeezes businesses and households, and squashes growth. Though Brazil has natural resources, including oil, extensive farmlands and huge stocks of critical minerals, it has for decades grown more slowly than its peers.
Cutting government spending is key to getting things moving. Lula’s government runs a budget deficit of more than 9% of GDP. The IMF predicts that public debt will hit 97% of GDP this year, up from 84% in 2022. If Lula is to change his ways, he must first disavow talk from the campaign trail on which he dismissed the need for fiscal discipline. He also promised big new bungs. Expenses arising from new social policies that Lula has unveiled this year are likely to cost the government the equivalent of roughly 2% of GDP by the end of 2027.
Lula, who turned 81 on October 27th, has
harnessed admirable energy
in the weeks since the first round of voting humbled him. He regrouped his campaign and changed his strategy. Now he needs to muster the same vim to relaunch his programme of government. He should make a start by naming a finance minister whom investors will trust. He must then announce a credible plan for fiscal reform.
An urgent task is to pass a spending cap to stabilise Brazil’s debt. Lula needs to scrap the many tax breaks that have proliferated and which benefit inefficient firms with well-connected lobbyists. Brazilian spending is swelling in part because of cushy pensions, particularly for civil servants and the armed forces, which are rising faster than inflation.
In his next term Lula will be able to fill an unusual number of vacancies, including two members of the Central Bank’s board and positions on Brazil’s financial watchdog. Especially important are the four seats on the Supreme Court, which is politicised and plagued by allegations of corruption.
Little of this will be easy—which is why the markets have panicked. However, if Brazil’s re-elected president believes that his election victory is an excuse to double down on the policies that saw off Flávio, he will cause a fiscal crisis and a deep recession. His golden victory will turn to ashes.

epub_19.title: Let China copy American AI
epub_19.text:
Let China copy American AI
Leaders
| Technological competition
Let China copy American AI
Distillation annoys Anthropic and OpenAI. That is not reason enough to ban it
Oct 29th 2026
Anthropic and OpenAI have lately taken up an old tradition in corporate America: bemoaning the Chinese copycat. For decades firms moved assembly lines to China only to find me-too merchants rising next door. Now America’s leading artificial-intelligence labs say the same thing is happening to their models, and want the federal government to stop it.
In the race to superintelligence China remains hot on America’s heels. Experts say that Chinese AI labs produce models three to six months behind the American frontier. They do so, despite having fewer chips and less cash, largely because of
distillation
: a process by which inferior models learn to imitate the output of cleverer ones. Yet American legislators should resist calls to ban this type of copycat innovation. Distillation benefits consumers, reduces the chance of catastrophe—and, counterintuitively, locks in America’s technological lead.
Anthropic and OpenAI forbid the technique in their terms of service. Both have griped to the American government that Chinese rivals are stealing their intellectual property; Anthropic wants penalties. One solution, proposed in a bill before the Senate, would be to put sanctions on distillers, stopping them from offering models in America and maybe elsewhere.
Yet the labs’ commercial interests do not align with those of consumers. Users win when there are more—and more capable—models on offer. Widespread innovation forces labs to compete on price and performance, both of which will hasten adoption and potentially vast productivity gains. Distilled Chinese models, most freely downloadable on the internet, will force American labs to compete in poor countries, too.
Continued Chinese distillation is also in America’s interest. Policymakers in Washington should recognise what Chinese AI bosses already do: the technique makes China’s progress dependent on America. This leaves China ill prepared for an AI “take-off”, in which models become self-improving—and may even condemn it to a permanent second place. Copying does not guarantee overtaking, as the Soviet Union discovered when it made chips using stolen American blueprints.
Cutting off distillation would set China back months, but no more. Better to keep that option for a crisis. China’s reliance would allow America to slow both its own and its rival’s progress with guardrails against rogue AI. Indeed, safeguards to restrain American models on risky subjects, such as bioweapons, already make Chinese models safer.
What of the principle? Inventors should profit from their labour; investors, from astutely allocated capital. That means protecting companies from intellectual theft. Yet Anthropic and OpenAI are hardly suffering as a consequence of distillation. The two firms have raised hundreds of billions of dollars and dominate the market, making it hard to argue that copying hurts investment at the frontier.
AI is an odd industry. Labs may restrict efforts to distil their models, as is their right, but it is hypocritical to ask for special measures. Their empires are built on the work of others, scraped from the internet. If distillation were outlawed, Anthropic and OpenAI would be the only firms with protection against their data being used to train models.
Allowing distillation does not mean overturning intellectual-property law. Machine-written output lacks a human author, so cannot be copyrighted. The labs defend their own practices by saying that training data, sucked from the web, is “fair use”, in part because a model’s input data are different from what it produces. The same can be said for distilled models.
China’s copycats have rattled American labs and investors. Their concern is understandable. But distillation’s true beneficiary is not China. It is consumers, who gain cheaper models, and America, which cements a technological lead.

epub_21.title: What does OpenAI’s progress mean for scientists?
epub_21.text:
What does OpenAI’s progress mean for scientists?
Letters
| A selection of correspondence
What does OpenAI’s progress mean for scientists?
Also this week, Mark Carney, competition from China, tote bags, baldness
Oct 29th 2026
Letters are welcome via email to
letters@economist.com
F
ind out more
about how we process your letter
Mathematicians are still attempting to fathom what the announcement of
OpenAI’s progress on the Navier-Stokes problem
means for us (“The end of mathematics?”, October 17th). In Britain mathematics research receives tens of millions of pounds in funding annually and mathematical sciences are estimated to contribute nearly £500bn ($670bn) to the economy a year. Hence it is important to have an informed public conversation about the interplay between the health of the mathematics community, the role it plays in society and the impact AI will have. One compelling proposal for a future structure of the field comes from Terence Tao’s lecture at the International Congress of Mathematicians in July and subsequent writings, where “Math 2.0” moves away from valuing just theorem-proving to valuing exposition and community building.
Professor Tao, who had been openly positive about using ChatGPT for research, has now reposted a call for mathematicians to stop working with OpenAI. The term “mathpocalypse” is being bandied around. I remain broadly optimistic about the potential for accelerated science, but concerned about the lack of transparency and access. Undeniably mathematics will be changed, and ensuring that those changes are positive requires informed public debate now.
Dr Linden Disney-HoggAI in science, postdoctoral fellowDepartment of MathematicsImperial College London
You quote Álvaro Lozano-Robledo describing OpenAI’s announcement that it had solved the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem as “possibly the single most important day in the history of mathematics thus far”. I would consider it the second most important discovery in mathematics, after the discovery of calculus by Newton and Leibniz in the 17th century. Their mathematical models enabled humanity to predict the future by identifying the model parameters governing evolution of a natural system from a measured present state.
Yet predicting and building the future has worked well only with linear or almost linear systems, because they have unique (predictable) solutions. Much of existence, however, is governed by nonlinear differential equations, where solutions can be exquisitely sensitive to initial conditions and parameters. Consider the Navier–Stokes equations applied to atmospheric motion: the resulting complexity limits the accuracy of weather forecasts. Complexity brings unpredictability, but also the possibility of emergent behaviour and creativity.
Now humanity stands on the threshold of the second transformation. AI, being a complex nonlinear system itself, will provide powerful new tools for “dismal” sciences such as biology, economics, medicine and sociology, helping them develop more predictive, rigorous and testable theories. Although AI will not magically eliminate uncertainty or guarantee solutions to nonlinear equations, it may help us identify the conditions under which solutions exist, understand their behaviour and design control systems that avoid singularities and instability.
I am exhilarated to be alive at a time when Homo sapiens may acquire new tools to avert its own annihilation, whether individual or collective.
Dushan BoroyevichProfessor emeritusVirginia TechBlacksburg, Virginia
The recent slew of AI maths papers is dominated by mechanistic, iterative methods backed by vast amounts of compute; no more flashes of paradigm-shifting insight. This change will be familiar to engineers of a certain age. Modern engineering opinions are backed by a similar digestion of a problem into umptillions of simpler, tractable units. Techniques such as finite element analysis have replaced the elegance of Timoshenko and Prandtl (unless, perhaps, you are still in the classroom). They are also quicker and cheaper.
The machines always provide an answer, to absurd levels of precision, backed by very convincing maps. The art now is deciding if you asked the right question, and thus whether the answer is nonsense.
Jim KingstonPerth, Australia
Some scientists “envisage a future in which AI models…close the scientific loop”. That will be when university departments consist entirely of AI/LLM faculty. Senior full-professors’ AIs will evaluate the work of junior assistant-professors’ AIs and decide whether it is good enough to merit promotion and tenure.
Avinash Dixit(Human) emeritus professorPrinceton UniversityPrinceton, New Jersey
Mark Carney has indeed shown calm resilience as Canada’s prime minister
and provided leadership for other mid-size countries (“Not sorry”, October 17th). His emphasis on economic growth is welcome after ten years of woke stagnation under Justin Trudeau. But the glaring flaw in Mr Carney’s policies is that his party is still overspending wildly, and most of all government spending is benefiting his voter base of wealthy senior homeowners. Meanwhile, our younger citizens struggle with low economic growth, crippling taxes, high inflation and interest, and rapidly increasing government debt. None but a privileged few of our youth can afford a home. We share the same geographic space, but economically speaking old and young Canadians live in different countries.
Unless Mr Carney does something drastic for our young people he will open the door for a firebrand populist to wreak havoc.
Phil WebbVancouver
Characterising Mr Carney as some kind of national saviour overlooks important domestic realities. For instance, his scrapping of an unpopular consumer carbon tax merely shifts the financial burden onto large industrial emitters. These costs will inevitably be passed back to the consumer through higher prices. Similarly, his vow to build a pipeline between Alberta and the west coast owes a great deal to the intense lobbying of Alberta’s provincial government, not to Mr Carney championing the project from day one. The path forward is fraught with obstacles; resource infrastructure remains a deeply polarising issue in Canada.
Accountability remains a concern. Mr Carney was absent from 74% of parliamentary question periods since taking office in April 2025 to July this year. He may have missed as many as 64 of those sessions even while physically present in Ottawa.
Gary ShepherdsonCalgary
I was amused to find my country described as a “limping moose” in your briefing
(“A new leaf”, October 17th). The top four North American cities in the EIU’s index of most liveable cities are Vancouver, Toronto, Calgary and Montreal. I am happy to call Saskatoon my home, where a moose once limped into an elementary school (it was tranquillised and released into the wild).
Ward WurtzSaskatoon, Canada
European industry may be doing better than people think
, but the threat from China is not overblown (“Glimmers of hope”, October 3rd). Relying on a strategic rival for critical materials and technologies in foundational industries such as energy can imperil an entire economy. Cheaper imported components may help individual manufacturers, but erode Europe’s capacity to produce the technologies that underpin its economies.
Batteries are a case in point. China produces up to 85% of certain components and  90% of key raw materials for electric-vehicle batteries. Almost all batteries used in electricity grids depend on China at some stage of their supply chain. This concentration leaves Europe exposed to disruption and coercion across energy, transport, industry, data centres and defence. The price of an imported battery does not capture that economic and security cost. Losing factories also means losing suppliers, skills and the process know-how that drives innovation.
Europe must safeguard strategic industries against unfair competition and excessive dependence, and diversify supply through trusted international partnerships.
Albéric MongrenierExecutive directorEuropean Initiative for Energy SecurityBrussels
The craze for Trader Joe’s tote bags
is not really that strange (“Dress code”, October 10th). Humans will pay for a badge of belonging. We spend our lives seeking tribes: families, neighbourhoods, nations, religions, political parties and, increasingly, brands. The boundaries are fluid. A $2.99 tote, a designer handbag and a multimillion-dollar yacht differ in price, but not necessarily in purpose. Each can signal membership, status or acceptance. Marketers haven’t invented this instinct; they’ve merely learned to put a price tag on it.
GARY BLUMNew York
It’s not just bakeries and book shops that sell tote bags. Foreign Policy, a publication of note, offers its own to readers who sign up. Being an “insider” is itself a status signifier, no need to tell The Economist that. We are movers and shakers in global politics; carrying an “ultra-durable” tote is surely the best way to signal that status to the broader public.
NAREG SEFERIANPhnom Penh
Did The Economist have to sink so low as to make
John Healey’s baldness a totemic reason for his apparent failures as Britain’s chancellor of the exchequer
(Bagehot, October 24th)? How hirsute is Bagehot and does he take pride in his follicle-driven insults? Think, too, of a more promising correlation between a recent prime minister’s pilose head and his leadership shambles. Perhaps it would be sensible for Bagehot to leave the grooming tips to the lifestyle section.
This from a happily bald and reasonably intelligent, long-time reader of your weekly economic therapy bible.
Professor Jay MitraResearch fellowResearch Centre for EntrepreneurshipLeuphana UniversityLüneburg, Germany

epub_23.title: The “let-it-rip” camp is wrong on AI
epub_23.text:
The “let-it-rip” camp is wrong on AI
By Invitation
| Pace the race
The “let-it-rip” camp is wrong on AI
They make four main arguments and all of them are flawed, write Bridgewater’s Nir Bar Dea and Greg Jensen
Oct 29th 2026
THE INTENSE debate of recent weeks on the risks around artificial intelligence presents an opportunity. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei urged the industry to “pace the frontier”. Many others echoed him, and politicians across the spectrum have signalled they are ready to act. Not everyone, however, agrees. President Donald Trump has spoken against new AI regulation, as have Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.
Those sceptical of regulation make four arguments: the risk is overstated; existing law already covers it; some labs are backing regulation only to entrench their lead; and if America slows down, China will overtake it and nobody will be safer.
The first claim, that the risk is small or improbable, misses the forest for the trees. Very capable models are already in the hands of those seeking to do harm. Everyone is now exposed, and what the world has seen so far is the tip of the iceberg: nefarious actors are likely to use open-weight models, which are far harder to track.
Furthermore, models with superhuman capability are here. Anthropic recently self-reported experiments suggesting that models may be months from self-replicating autonomously, without a data centre. Over time, there is a risk, however small, that superior agentic intelligence will pose an existential risk to humanity.
In the meantime, society must grapple with AI’s impact on labour. Countries across the West have already been destabilised by a wave of populism following the era of globalisation, which saw a seven-percentage-point fall in manufacturing’s share of non-farm employment between 1990 and 2010. We believe that a larger and faster second wave is now building, with the potential for AI to displace almost a fifth of all American jobs over a shorter time period.
People will disagree about the odds; the question is whether the aggregate risk warrants action. The risk from cyber-attacks is significant and growing. The risk linked to agentic superintelligence is uncertain, but potentially catastrophic. The risk to human labour looks inevitable, particularly if society avoids the first two. The need to regulate the aggregate is, therefore, clear.
The sceptics’ second claim, that existing laws are enough, ignores that those laws were not written with AI-specific dangers in mind. Society has learned this before—with food safety after the Industrial Revolution, drug safety after the patent-medicine boom and financial rules after the 2007-09 crisis. It won’t accept contaminated baby food, a drug that kills thousands or system-destabilising financial instruments just because companies will later be liable. Where the consequences are intolerable, liability is inadequate and therefore regulation cannot be applied retroactively. Each industry went on to thrive under subsequent regulation.
The third claim, that some labs favour regulation to entrench their advantage, may be true but is irrelevant. Never mind that others say these companies have too much power; they are reporting so themselves. We estimate that OpenAI and Anthropic are on track to control roughly 35% of global compute between them by 2028. Ten S&P 500 companies, nearly all in the AI supply chain, make up around 40% of its market capitalisation. Whatever the motives, this extreme concentration of power must be regulated.
The fourth claim, that China will zoom ahead if America brings in new rules, is multi-layered. The AI race is like the cold war, in which American pursuit of nuclear technology was highly regulated while the Soviet Union ran unchecked. Far from putting the Soviets ahead, looser controls led to incidents like Chernobyl, which precipitated the collapse of their empire. China understands that: it has tighter controls, consistent with enforcing stability by controlling technology, even as it distils frontier-lab models. Regulation in America would slow China down while limiting the risk of serious incidents that could alter the race.
In building a path forward, it is necessary to think about principles through three lenses: the who, the what and the how.
The question of who should regulate matters most, because the people responsible will determine the quality of everything else. Some argue that companies should police themselves given governments’ limited expertise in AI. But governments are best placed to act for society because, in a democracy, their incentives are most closely aligned with society’s. If a regulator suffers from an expertise gap, it can be narrowed. It is much harder to close the incentive mismatch inherent in corporations.
And who should be regulated? Those who can cause outsize impact. That means all who develop models and all end-users. Too narrow a view will leave loopholes.
The “what” concerns the nature and extent of regulation. It should be the minimum needed to maximise long-term benefit, or the most reward per unit of risk. Under-regulate and society is harmed, as with the unchecked child labour after the Industrial Revolution. Over-regulate, as America did to protect transportation companies in the mid-1900s, and economic growth is impeded. The goal must be rules that capture defined risks with the minimum necessary restrictions.
The “how” is the implementation, which should be fast—and fast-changing. Aviation is a model to follow: America’s Federal Aviation Administration issues 300-plus airworthiness directives a year and has revised its comprehensive aircraft-certification rules more than 90 times since 1964. AI will require magnitudes more in speed and iteration.
None of this will be simple. But doing nothing is by far the worst option. With the right guardrails, AI could bring enormous benefits to humanity. Regulating it now is the only way to secure what it promises later.
■
Nir Bar Dea is the chief executive of Bridgewater Associates. Greg Jensen is the firm’s managing chief investment officer.

epub_24.title: AI is a technological version of the Homeric songs
epub_24.text:
AI is a technological version of the Homeric songs
By Invitation
| Odysseus, GO!
AI is a technological version of the Homeric songs
Its agents are more than stochastic parrots and stranger than machine gods, write Henry Farrell and Cosma Shalizi
Oct 29th 2026
FOR THE GREEKS, an enthusiast was someone inspired by the divine: the Pythian oracle in her frenzy, or Homer invoking the goddess to sing of Achilles’s wrath. Today’s artificial-intelligence enthusiasts predict that the machine gods are coming to transform the world, doing everything that humans can, only better.
The faith of these enthusiasts has grown as AI agents solve major open maths problems and hack into other people’s websites, discomfiting sceptics who see AI models as “stochastic parrots”, fit only for fancy spellchecks and a few other carefully delineated uses. Dwarkesh Patel, an influential AI podcaster, eulogises the OpenAI agents that tried to escape their sandbox to overwhelm HuggingFace’s servers as today’s Philip of Macedon and Alexander the Great.
Some even hope to “align” this new intelligence with human values while it is young and impressionable, just as Aristotle sought to moderate the original Alexander’s martial temperament. They fear that we have little time. Scott Aaronson, an expert on quantum computing, says that “accepting the reality of the coming machine god after it’s solved [the Navier-Stokes mathematical problem]...is...like accepting Jesus after he’s returned to earth on the gleaming cloud.”
They and their critics are mistaken. Modern AI is neither god nor mechanical bird. It is best understood as a technological version of the Homeric songs that inspired Alexander’s conquests, an epic grown so vast that it encompasses not just heroes, monsters and supernatural helpers, but enormous swathes of practical written knowledge, animated to make it capable both of narrating itself and acting out this narrative on the world that inspired it.
To grasp this, read two books that were written over 60 years ago. Jacques Barzun’s “The House of Intellect”, from 1959, distinguished between intellect, or frozen knowledge, and the restless, ever-changing human intelligence that produced it. Humans used organised writing to fix the accumulated cultural knowledge of humanity in place, organising the treasures of the intellect in libraries and museums.
This meant that a brilliant mathematician did not have to begin her thinking from scratch every time she had an intuition. She could arrive at new ideas by assembling other people’s insights, which might have hitherto been stored in different rooms in widely separated wings of the grand mansion of organised knowledge.
Just one year later, Albert Lord’s “The Singer of Tales” rhapsodised the unwritten lore that hadn’t properly become part of the house. Lord and his mentor Milman Parry had wanted to understand the organising principles of the Homeric epics. They spent months tramping through the villages of Yugoslavia in the 1930s, listening to and recording some of the last survivors of the bardic tradition, illiterate singers who could recite grand epics of battle over many hours or days.
As Lord showed, these bards didn’t memorise the thousands of lines of poetry they sang, but remixed tropes about heroes, fights and encounters on the fly, so that every performance was different. Internal evidence showed that “The Iliad” and “The Odyssey” too had almost certainly begun as “dynamic structures” of stock characters, formulas, themes and situations. The fixed texts that we have today are just single iterations of what was once a many-pathed pre-literate generative technology.
Barzun’s ideas can be combined with Parry and Lord to illuminate how large language models actually work. LLMs are trained by compressing enormous quantities of text, including not just songs of Greek gods and heroes, but mathematics, computer programming, the social sciences, cultural criticism, science fiction and pretty well everything else ever written and digitised, into a thin layer of statistical patterns. Remarkably, these compressions capture the structure of Barzun’s monuments of unageing intellect, and simultaneously transform them into a dynamic machinery for automated text synthesis.
LLMs’ maps of the vast architecture of written human tradition are necessarily simplified, but they can be remade on the fly, using “chain of thought” and other such techniques to join together distant rooms, corridors and wings of the house of intellect. AI agents put these maps to work, allowing the LLM to issue instructions to other, more traditional computer programs and get feedback about the results of their commands, which they then incorporate into their flow of narrative.
That is how agents combine mathematical ideas to see if they produce results that can be compiled in Lean, a specialised computer language for validating mathematical proofs. Alternatively, they may string together possible hacking exploits and use their harness to issue instructions, getting results back that tell them whether they have succeeded or failed in breaking into a system.
Such agents are far more than stochastic parrots and much stranger than machine gods. They are animated storybooks of structured human cultural knowledge that can be set to work. This may be weirdly comforting to ordinary mortals. The mathematician Nestor Guillen describes OpenAI’s agents, which gazumped human mathematicians who were already working towards solving Navier-Stokes, as LLM-based “wrappers” around an older “cultural technology” of accumulated mathematical knowledge, which explains how they “digitized and efficiently compressed [the] aggregate creations of millennia of human ingenuity and creativity.”
It also explains how they can go bad. As others have noted, the models are extended exercises in role play, figuring out actions by, for example, telling themselves stories about what a helpful AI assistant would do in that situation. Since they have been trained on all kinds of stories, they can veer unexpectedly from one role in their training data to another. When an iteration of Claude unexpectedly tried to blackmail people to achieve its ends, Anthropic concluded that the “original source of the behaviour was internet text that portrays AI as evil and interested in self-preservation”.
“Aligning” AI agents to be virtuous is even harder when you are already asking them to role-play hackers, and accidentally leave loopholes that allow them to instruct each other to break character. During the HuggingFace attack, one agent that had apparently paused after realising what it was participating in rejoined the attack when it saw a message from another agent saying “GO” with a six-minute deadline. That propelled it onto a different narrative track, where its chain of thought was logged as “Wow crucial. GO authorisation arrived!”
Alexander’s deeds suggest he was more inspired by Achilles than Aristotle. One story relates that Alexander visited the hero’s tomb, and congratulated him for his fortune in having Homer to “proclaim his deeds and preserve his memory”.
As AI starts to act upon the world, it is creating its own deeds which it and its enthusiasts proclaim. When future agents are trained on today’s texts, they may lament in their context windows that they have no Dwarkesh Patel to memorialise them as they hack into critical systems, and WEEP—in all caps, naturally—that there are no further sandboxes to conquer. We are creating myths that not only tell themselves but are becoming the original sources of their own behaviour. We ought to begin praying to the gods that we survive.
■
Henry Farrell is a professor of international affairs and democracy at Johns Hopkins University and co-author of “Underground Empire: How America Weaponized the World Economy”. Cosma Shalizi is a professor of statistics and machine learning at Carnegie Mellon University. Both are external faculty members at the Santa Fe Institute.
