epub_26.title: Narendra Modi and the battle for India
epub_26.text:
Narendra Modi and the battle for India
Briefing
| 25 years of Modi
Narendra Modi and the battle for India
India’s strongman has changed the country for good and ill. Now he is facing one of his sternest tests yet
Oct 29th 2026
IN EARLY OCTOBER India’s cabinet issued 11 pages of gushing praise to mark their leader’s quarter of a century in public office. As chief minister of Gujarat, a rich western state, then as prime minister, Narendra Modi had transformed “the lives of every citizen”, earning “unwavering support”. His dedication and honesty showed “the strength of India’s democracy”.
A month of celebrations was organised to mark Mr Modi’s silver jubilee, including exhibitions, tree-planting and grassroots events. It has not gone quite to plan.
Throughout October India has been gripped by protest, as unrest over the leak of an exam erupted into a broader anti-Modi movement. Gen Z activists, student groups and opposition parties accuse Mr Modi and his ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of rigging elections, and are agitating for education reform and jobs.
The 76-year-old strongman has appeared unsure how to respond. At times he has tried to mollify activists, notably by sacrificing his education minister in July. Now he is cracking down on them. In Delhi the authorities cut off the mobile internet, cancelled trains and blocked roads while police detained thousands of protesters, beating them with sticks. All of it has been streamed around the world.
Mr Modi still has strong support, particularly among older voters. His ideology remains potent. Though opposition parties are now more unified, they lack organisational muscle and are yet to offer a coherent alternative. Still, the unrest on the streets is a striking challenge to Mr Modi’s rule—both to a governing model that is no longer meeting many Indians’ aspirations, and to strong-arm methods that have closed down other avenues for opposition.
That makes it a good moment to reflect on Mr Modi’s 25 years in office. What kind of India has emerged under him? And what does his record suggest he will do next?
Mr Modi’s arrival on the political stage was heralded by an earthquake, which in January 2001 tore through Kutch in his native Gujarat, killing more than 20,000. The BJP’s ailing chief minister responded haplessly. His party installed a trusted apparatchik—a bearded, bespectacled 51-year-old who had never before stood for public office, let alone built a mass following. Few expected him to last long.
He almost did not, as a result of horrific religious violence that took place in Gujarat the next year. After a group of Hindu pilgrims was burned to death on a train, vigilante mobs went on the rampage; more than 1,000 people died, most of them Muslims. Mr Modi never accepted responsibility or apologised for the bloodshed on his watch—instead, at an election later that year, he inflamed tensions with communal speeches. The BJP won a landslide. He has since won five elections in a row, two more in Gujarat and three nationally.
One confidant from the early days attributes Mr Modi’s remarkable ascent to his long training touring villages as a foot-soldier in the RSS, a Hindu-volunteer group. “His advantage has always been his grasp of the average Indian’s psyche, their hopes and fears,” he says. Steeped in Hindu-revivalist ideology, Mr Modi was particularly attuned to the victimhood many Hindus felt over policies that they believed had unfairly prioritised Muslims.
In Gujarat he established a governing model. Styling himself as a Hindu hardliner and a “development man”, he aggressively courted foreign investment and forged close links with industrialists. He offered businesses land, tax breaks and subsidies. He kept the police, the courts and party cadres under tight control. All the while he projected an image of himself as uniquely incorruptible: ascetic, celibate and without a family to enrich.
As prime minister, Mr Modi applied this model to India. A country of 1.45bn is, in effect, ruled by a few dozen people in the prime minister’s office and around Amit Shah, the home minister and Mr Modi’s longtime enforcer and strategist. Many in Delhi say that Mr Modi is rarely challenged, and cabinet ministers take direction. So do BJP chief ministers.
Only twice before has India had such a dominant leader. The first was Jawaharlal Nehru, who over 17 years as prime minister forged a newly independent India as a secular democracy inspired by socialist economic thinking. The second was his daughter, Indira Gandhi, who took India leftward during her 16 years in office, often ruling as a populist authoritarian.
Mr Modi, born into poverty, defined himself against these figures. By promoting a mixture of Hindu-nationalism, pro-business reform and welfarism, he reduced their once-mighty party, Congress, to a husk. Like Gandhi, though, he took a firm grip over his party, the media and institutions, and built a personality cult. “Even Indira never had this level of control,” says Neelanjan Sircar, a political scientist.
The BJP’s formidable political machine was on show in May when the party unseated Mamata Banerjee, the chief minister of West Bengal, a populous eastern state. More than 70% of Indians now live in a state run by the BJP (see chart 1). Yet five months on, Mr Modi is facing the most difficult test of his premiership. “The BJP is in its strongest and its weakest position simultaneously,” says Rahul Verma of Shiv Nadar University, Chennai. It has never ruled more of the country, nor has it faced such fatigue and open discontent.
To see what kind of country Mr Modi has made, consider his impact in three areas: the economy, society and democracy. On the first he has been a moderniser, though not the reformer many had hoped for. In 2014 he inherited plans for a national digital-identity and -payment system and a goods-and-services tax, to replace 17 state-level taxes. Weaker, coalition governments—long the norm before Mr Modi—had struggled to implement such changes. Mr Modi used top-down power to force them through, a massive achievement.
The result has been to knit India together with a stronger internal market, in which almost all Indians can access services and make payments online. The national highway network is 60% longer than it was when Mr Modi took power and rural households enjoy 22.6 hours of electricity a day, up from 12.5. Voters have been given free grain, electricity connections and cooking gas. Direct cash transfers have cut graft and reduced poverty, forging a direct link between Mr Modi and the poor.
Pro-business more than pro-market, Mr Modi has tilted India towards a model of national capitalism. Since Gujarat his rise has been bound up with that of Gautam Adani, who has built an empire spanning ports, airports, energy and defence. Tycoons like Mr Adani have, like Mr Modi, got hard things done and helped the economy grow—by around 6% a year (similar to before Mr Modi came to power). The Reserve Bank of India has largely kept inflation in check, too, avoiding the gyrations that undid previous prime ministers. Mr Modi has been unusually fiscally prudent.
But the rewards have been top-heavy. The tycoons have done as well as ever. Mr Adani’s wealth has risen from $7bn in 2014 to more than $100bn. Rural workers have not. Their real wages, which typically grew by 6% a year between 2006 and 2014, have since grown by 1%. Salaried workers have done worse still: adjusting for inflation, average pay for this group, accounting for around a quarter of the Indian workforce, has fallen by 5% since 2017 (see chart 2).
Mr Modi’s failure was that he abandoned deeper land and agriculture reforms when they triggered mass protests. Ironically, giving in to that discontent has helped lead to the discontent now. Despite steady growth, Mr Modi has not achieved the economic transformation he desired (and of which his cabinet boasts). The share of workers in agriculture has remained stubbornly at two-fifths; the share in manufacturing has grown only a little. Though India has been covered in shiny roads, informal labour remains ubiquitous. A huge expansion in higher education has not been matched by growth in salaried jobs, suppressing wages and creating a large cohort of frustrated youngsters.
“What we are seeing is Modi reaching the limits of his governing model,” says Pratap Bhanu Mehta, a former vice-chancellor of Ashoka University near Delhi. He has been able to push through big changes that require raw executive power. But he has failed in areas that require consensus-building or systemic reform.
The change to Indian society, the second area, has been more dramatic. Under Mr Modi India has become more brash, nationalistic and Hindu, and, bluntly, a more forbidding place for the country’s 200m Muslims (just under a seventh of the population). This is the most controversial part of his legacy. It is also where opposition to Mr Modi has been least effective.
The most visible change is that Mr Modi has fused religious nationalism with politics. As prime minister he has regularly taken part in ceremonies and rituals—above all the consecration of the Ram Temple on the site of a former mosque in Ayodhya, fulfilling a decades-long campaign. The BJP has pushed through citizenship laws and begun to overhaul Muslim family law. Although the word “secular” remains in the constitution, Mr Modi has damaged the principle that India is a republic that treats all religions equally.
This is unlikely to be reversed. “Hindutva [Hindu-ness] is still a powerful magnet for the middle class,” says Rajdeep Sardesai, a TV anchor and political analyst. BJP chief ministers have emulated Mr Modi—and taken his ideology to new extremes. Opposition politicians have joined in “temple hopping” and “soft Hindutva”. The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), the youth movement at the centre of the protests, has notably steered clear of religious issues.
Since his fateful first year as chief minister in Gujarat, Mr Modi has fostered a culture of permissiveness around anti-Muslim bigotry and violence. BJP politicians call Muslims “infiltrators” and “encroachers” and issue threats against them. Communal violence has continued to fall from its peak in the 1980s, a period marred by regular bloody riots. But there has been a rise in targeted attacks on Muslims by vigilante groups, which often meet with impunity. This will be the most damaging part of Mr Modi’s legacy—and it, too, will be difficult to reverse.
With his blend of modernisation and religious nationalism, Mr Modi has been remarkably successful at unifying the Hindu vote. But how long can that go on if voters fret about the economy? In the national election in 2024, voters angry about jobs turned away from the BJP, forcing Mr Modi to govern in coalition (see chart 3). Praveen Chakravarty, an MP who leads polling for Congress, claims that age is now the main electoral dividing line, with under 30s—who make up almost 30% of eligible voters—turning against Mr Modi.
The focus of those on the street is the third area: Mr Modi’s handling of elections and institutions. Protesters accuse him of “stealing democracy” through a voter-verification process called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), under which more than 130m names were removed from draft voter rolls. On October 14th Abhijeet Dipke, leader of the CJP, sardonically compared the circumstances with “the Emergency”, a period when Gandhi cancelled elections, locked up political opponents and clamped down on the press: “Declare Emergency officially,” he said.
The last revision of electoral rolls took place more than two decades ago, so one was overdue. The number of removals this time was much higher than before, at least some of which might be explained by higher internal migration or voters dying. Mr Modi’s defenders argue that only a small fraction of the 130m were eligible voters.
The problem is the way the process has been carried out, which has been rushed, opaque and—true to form—centralised. Millions who were wrongly removed were not given a proper chance to appeal, leaving them disenfranchised when appeals were completed, the vast majority were successful). Whereas previous exercises have been run by state and local operators, this one was run centrally from Delhi, using software that allowed little transparency about who had been removed and why.
To some, this is proof that Mr Modi is a would-be dictator who will break Indian democracy to cling to power. That is going too far. The SIR process has been murky, but there is no evidence that it has swung elections. The argument that Mr Modi holds power because he steals votes skims over the way the opposition has struggled to offer a more compelling alternative.
SIR is better seen as an extreme example of Mr Modi’s strong-arm tactics. His government has extended control over Supreme Court appointments, weakening the independence of the judiciary, and has cowed the once-combative Indian media with a combination of takeovers and hostile investigations. It has similarly used the state to tie political opponents in legal knots. In all, Mr Modi has abused his powers more ruthlessly and over a longer period than any other Indian leader (though Indira Gandhi did suspend democracy, after 21 months she pulled back from the brink, called elections, and was voted out.)
And yet, Indian democracy is more resilient than many make out. The country is vast, diverse and noisy; competitive elections, while flawed, are ingrained. The scandal over SIR has shown that Indians remain deeply attached to their vote, and that the media are still capable of holding the government to account. They have put pressure on the Supreme Court and the Electoral Commission of India to improve the appeals process for excluded voters.
This is a pattern in other democracies, says Milan Vaishnav of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, a think-tank. “When you have a very strong leader, they can bend institutions to their will,” he says. “But when their popularity begins to fade, institutions tend to bounce back.”
Mr Modi has never faced stronger headwinds. At 76 he is—whisper many in Delhi—showing signs of ageing. Still, he is unlikely to back down or change his approach. Instead, he will continue to try to divide and weaken the opposition. In private, officials say ministers have been rattled by the way a handful of kids with smartphones have seized the agenda. They will aim to stop the youth protests gathering steam by keeping leaders in custody or tied up in the courts, and channel discontent into opposition parties, which they are more comfortable fighting.
It is not clear such tactics will work. So far protesters have turned crackdowns into viral clips. Attempts to brand the CJP—who wrap themselves in the Indian flag and talk of constitutional rights—as “anti-nationals” have failed. Mr Modi cannot easily take the sting out of the movement, as he did in 2021 by dropping the reforms that had angered farmers; many in his party regard more concessions as a slippery slope. But stifling legitimate dissent will also cause pressure to build.
The prime minister may look to shift the political debate onto more comfortable terrain. He could dial up the Hindu-nationalist rhetoric. Or suddenly table a controversial bill, say on delimitation, a thorny issue involving the allocation of parliamentary seats between states. The BJP will try to paint Rahul Gandhi, the grandson of Indira and leader of the Congress party who heads the opposition alliance, as a street agitator who wants “regime change” without winning elections.
The underlying sources of discontent—education, jobs, wages—will fester. But the opposition will need to show that it has better answers. Mr Gandhi often speaks as if the mood had already turned decisively (and he had not lost three elections in a row). “We are going to destroy them,” he said of Mr Modi and Mr Shah at a rally on October 6th. So far, Mr Modi’s approval ratings have only dipped. Some voters dislike the BJP’s authoritarianism, but also worry about how an unwieldy coalition led by Congress, which has moved to the left under Mr Gandhi, would govern.
The next big test will come in the spring with elections in several states, including the largest, BJP-run Uttar Pradesh. That one looks to be tight. If the BJP wins, it will claim that Mr Modi’s enduring popularity has been proved and the opposition are sore losers. If it loses, it will be the surest sign that Mr Modi’s appeal is waning.
For Mr Modi the risk now would be to believe what his outriders say—that the protests are just a small group of anarchists and anti-nationals who do not reflect Indians’ real grievances. For the opposition it is the reverse: to believe that a few months of street action mean that Mr Modi is in terminal decline. Over 25 years he has proved remarkably resilient. He is not going to go down without a fight.

epub_28.title: Russia has seized a Japanese journalist
epub_28.text:
Russia has seized a Japanese journalist
Asia
| A nasty story
Russia has seized a Japanese journalist
Vladimir Putin may be preparing for a prisoner exchange. Pressuring Japan also pleases China
Oct 29th 2026
Imai yuki spent years learning to read Russian literature in the original. On a student-exchange programme in St Petersburg in 2014-15, the lanky young Japanese man impressed Russian friends with his knowledge of their city and its literary luminaries, such as Fyodor Dostoyevsky. Mr Imai parlayed his language skills into a job covering Russia for the Hokkaido Shimbun, a regional newspaper from Japan’s northernmost big island. On October 13th operatives from the Federal Security Service (FSB) burst into his hotel room on Sakhalin, off Russia’s far-eastern coast, and handcuffed him. “You are suspected of espionage,” a masked Russian officer says in a video released by the FSB. “V smysle?” a befuddled Mr Imai answers in Russian. “What do you mean?”
Mr Imai is being held at Lefortovo (pictured), a notorious prison in Moscow. The meaning of his arrest is far bigger than a local news story. His case ensures a freeze in relations between Japan and Russia will only get icier. Mr Imai may also end up embroiled in global hostage diplomacy, much like Evan Gershkovich, an American journalist who was arrested on baseless espionage charges in 2023 and was freed 16 months later in
the largest prisoner swap between Russia and the West since the cold war
.
Arresting a journalist for being a spy “probably means Russia is trying to get somebody home”, reckons Mr Gershkovich, the author of
“This Cursed Beautiful Land”
, a book about his experience and Russia’s hostage diplomacy. In Russian, such detainees are referred to as aktivy (assets) in the country’s obmenny fond (exchange fund). Officials speak openly about its status: “It may be time to fill up our exchange fund with European and American idiots in order to get our guys out,” Dmitry Medvedev, a former president turned attack dog, wrote days before Mr Imai’s arrest.  While Mr Imai may be familiar with such terminology, the Japanese government has little first-hand experience with the practices. Another Japanese journalist was detained on spying charges in Russia in 2019, but deported within three days.
What exchange might Russia want? The Kremlin may hope that Japan—or its ally, America—can help bring a multinational deal to fruition. The exchange that freed Mr Gershkovich centred around Vadim Krasikov, a Russian operative convicted of murder and jailed in Germany; it also included two men associated with hacking and cyber-crime groups who were held in American jails.
One particular figure of interest now may be a Russian hacker from Qilin, a cyber-crime group linked to
big ransomware attacks
, who was nabbed on holiday in Japan and extradited to Germany less than two weeks before Mr Imai’s arrest. “Instead of sushi, he’s now getting cheese sandwiches in a German prison,” a German official crowed. Russia could also have targets in mind elsewhere in Asia. Over the past two years Australia has arrested and charged at least three individuals with working for Russian intelligence.
Russia may see Japanese citizens as fungible aktivy. There are recent precedents. American negotiators freed two Japanese nationals from jail in Belarus as part of prisoner exchanges last year. Talk of swaps has increased as Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump explore a possible meeting at next month’s Asia-Pacific summit in China: at Mr Trump’s request, Mr Putin last week released an elderly American held in Russian prison for four years.
At any rate, Mr Imai’s arrest comes at a low point in the complex and consequential relationship between Japan and Russia. In the waning days of the second world war, Russia took back control of Sakhalin (where Mr Imai’s grandfather grew up), as well as the nearby Kuril Islands. The two have yet to sign an official peace treaty ending that war; Japan still claims sovereignty over the four southernmost Kurils, which it calls the Northern Territories. Talks to resolve that territorial dispute have been frozen, along with the overall relationship, since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which Japan vehemently opposed.
The freeze got even colder in the months leading up to Mr Imai’s arrest. In August Mr Putin observed naval exercises on Sakhalin, his first visit in more than a decade. He also made his first-ever trip to the Northern Territories. In September Russia installed a monument in its far east depicting a soldier destroying a chrysanthemum emblem, the symbol of Japan’s imperial family. Japan condemned the visit and the monument; in early October Japan imposed fresh sanctions on ships linked to Russia’s shadow fleet of oil tankers.
Several factors may explain Russia’s recent frostiness. Japan’s continuing
efforts to strengthen its armed forces
, while focused on countering China, also have implications for Russia, which uses the Sea of Okhotsk as a bastion for nuclear submarines. And Takaichi Sanae, the prime minister, is seeking to
build up Japan’s intelligence services
. For Russian spooks, Japan has long been an important posting, says Andrei Soldatov, an expert on Russian intelligence: “You can’t really approach Americans in America, but you can try to recruit Americans there.”
The most telling factor may be China’s bitter feud with Japan over Ms Takaichi’s support for Taiwan. Russian pressure on Japan “allows Russia to show the Chinese that we’re on the same side”, says Alexander Gabuev of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre, an American think-tank. Russia has echoed China’s rhetoric about Japan’s “new militarism”; the two now speak of the second world war as a shared battle against Japan. As Mr Imai’s newspaper noted in an article about Russia’s new monument, “This appears to be an attempt to convey a willingness to co-operate with China—which is at odds with Japan over the Taiwan issue—on matters such as historical interpretation.”
Mr Imai’s imprisonment has only chilled relations further. For now, his pre-trial detention is scheduled to last until December 12th. (Ms Takaichi has denied that he is a spy.) On October 23rd Japanese diplomats managed to pass him a parcel with supplies in Lefortovo; three days later they were finally granted consular access. One thing Mr Imai will not lack there is reading material: thanks in part to a long history of well-read prisoners (including Mr Gershkovich), Lefortovo is equipped with a library of around 9,000 books. Mr Imai, sadly, may have plenty of time to brush up on his Russian classics.

epub_29.title: A tiny Pacific country rolls out universal basic income
epub_29.text:
A tiny Pacific country rolls out universal basic income
Asia
| Marshall plan
A tiny Pacific country rolls out universal basic income
The Marshall Islands uses an American windfall to pay every citizen
Oct 29th 2026
SOON AFTER the second world war, America went looking for a place to test its fast-expanding nuclear arsenal. It settled on the Marshall Islands, then an American-administered collection of atolls scattered across a vast stretch of the Pacific. Over 12 years the Americans carried out 67 nuclear tests. The resulting radiation did lasting damage to the health of the Marshallese, but it also shaped the islands’ relationship with America.
These days the country of 42,000 people is independent, but gets aid from America under a “compact of free association” in exchange for allowing it military access. Some of that money is now financing a different sort of experiment. For nearly a year every citizen in the Marshall Islands, including children, has been getting a quarterly payment of about $200. The precise amount varies, because the government shares a fixed pot equally among all those enrolled.
The programme, Enra Jen Lale Rara (sharing plates to care for those around us), is believed to be the world’s first national universal basic income (UBI) scheme, a term that describes unconditional government payment given to all citizens as a supplement to or replacement for wages. (Other UBI experiments have covered small groups of people, or individual cities, provinces or groups of villages.)
David Paul, the finance minister and the programme’s architect, has said it will give Marshallese “peace of mind” amid concerns over the cost of living. He also hopes it will hand them a reason to stay on the islands. Under the country’s compact with America, Marshallese citizens can live and work there freely (around 44,000 already do so).
Officials insist that the payment is not intended to replace work; it is not nearly big enough to do that. At around $800 a year, it amounts to only about a tenth of the Marshall Islands’ income per person. Still, in American terms, that would be equivalent to an annual payment of roughly $9,000, a not inconsiderable sum. Unsurprisingly, the transfers are popular: almost everyone has enrolled. It is however too early to draw conclusions about the impact on labour supply, says Stefania Pozzi, an economist working with the country’s finance ministry.
More certain, though, are the impacts on consumption. On payment days offices empty in Majuro, the capital, which employs the bulk of the labour force, as workers queue to collect cheques; soon afterwards shops and restaurants fill up as they spend the money. “Families have found it hugely beneficial,” says Giff Johnson, editor of the Marshall Islands Journal. Much of the spending has been on food, but people have also used the cash for bigger purchases, like air-conditioners and lawnmowers, he says. Inflation, another common concern with cash transfers, has risen, but officials attribute that largely to the economic shock from the war in Iran rather than specifically to the UBI. The scheme is reaching people on the country’s more remote islands, many of which lack banks, ATMs or reliable internet.
The Marshall Islands’ compact with America has helped it overcome the biggest obstacle to UBI. The cost of it amounts to a whopping 8% or so of GDP, but is paid from an American trust fund, now worth around $1.8bn. Still, the IMF worries that the payments are already taking the place of more useful long-term spending on infrastructure and climate adaptation. Even before the first payment in November 2025, it recommended replacing the UBI with a targeted scheme at the “first available and feasible opportunity”. The Marshallese government argues that deciding who should qualify would be costly and cumbersome.
No evaluation of the scheme has yet been published, but plenty of countries are watching the experiment closely. All the economies of island-states in the Pacific are to some extent dependent on remittances and are vulnerable to economic shocks. But conventional social-protection efforts are often very difficult to implement in populations that are scattered across the ocean’s islands.
Bigger countries should be interested too. The emergence of artificial intelligence and its potential for  job displacement have revived talk of UBI everywhere. AI-induced concern is one reason the Opportunity Party, a newish centrist group in
New Zealand
, is campaigning on a “citizen’s income” ahead of elections next month. The Marshall Islands’ UBI may be tiny, but its lessons could travel far beyond its shores.

epub_30.title: India has stabilised its currency. But at what cost?
epub_30.text:
India has stabilised its currency. But at what cost?
Asia
| Ashoka
India has stabilised its currency. But at what cost?
The central bank is using ever harsher measures to keep the rupee below 100 to the dollar
Oct 29th 2026
THE RUPEE is back, baby! And all it took was some gentle management by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Over the past few months the central bank has, among other things, wooed dollar deposits from overseas Indians with juicy interest rates and currency guarantees; spent tens of billions of dollars to buy rupees in the open market; severely limited the ability of investors to speculate on the currency; and, on October 10th, imposed punitive costs on businesses that legitimately need to hedge their own foreign-currency exposure. As a result, the rupee recovered for a while from just under 97 to the dollar to just under 95. Break out the party hats.
Or perhaps not. “Just under 95”, as a close-of-day price, is the level the rupee hit in late March. So unacceptable was the idea that India’s beloved currency might cross that threshold that the RBI imposed a set of measures described by one analyst as rolling back a decade of market liberalisation in just a few days. The intervention brought some relief. But the currency crossed 95 within weeks, marching ever onwards towards the big “100” flashing like a neon sign in front of traders’ eyes. Ajay Shah, an economist, describes this dynamic as “the recurring round-number skirmish”. Few numbers are rounder than a century.
Ever since independence and even more so since a balance-of-payments crisis in 1991, any steep fall in the value of the rupee has been
seen as a national humiliation
. In 2013 Narendra Modi, then chief minister of the state of Gujarat, cannily used its sharp depreciation to paint the Congress-led government of the day as corrupt and incompetent. For Mr Modi to preside over the rupee’s slide into triple digits now would be rather embarrassing. It would also provide the opposition with a delicious attack line just months before elections in Uttar Pradesh, a bellwether state of 240m people. The words “hoist” and “petard” come to mind.
The RBI is, of course, an independent, inflation-targeting central bank. It aims for no specific exchange rate, it says. Its measures are designed only “to ensure orderly functioning of the foreign-exchange market”, it stresses. Yet its actions argue otherwise. The problem is that “a failed defence is worse than no defence”, as Duvvuri Subbarao, a former governor of the bank, has noted. If the bank folds easily, markets may start to believe they can push it around and pile yet more pressure on the rupee.
And…so what? A currency is worth whatever people are willing to pay for it. That is determined by forces outside the central bank’s control. In recent years global capital has been lured away because of AI investments abroad, rising interest rates in America and overvalued markets in India, lowering demand for the rupee. It has not helped that energy prices have shot up since March after someone started another needless war in the Middle East, boosting India’s demand for dollars. As long as these conditions persist, the rupee will weaken.
The costs of the RBI’s defence are escalating. India’s foreign-exchange reserves fell by some $50bn in September alone as the central bank sold dollars to buy rupees. And bets on the currency are moving from financial markets into the real economy. Exporters anticipating further depreciation will delay bringing cash back to India. Importers will fill their warehouses.
Members of India’s diaspora
, who sent home $144bn or about 3% of GDP last financial year, may delay remittances. Resident Indians will buy even more gold than they usually do.
Another cost is that limiting hedging—along with unpredictable policymaking followed by clarifications and reversals—could discourage the capital inflows that would help bolster the rupee. The biggest cost, though, is to the credibility of the RBI, which risks looking as if it is fighting a political battle. Traders now believe 97 is its red line to prevent a collapse to 100. But there is no good reason to defend that number.
The RBI has, for now, arrested the currency’s decline. The rupee appreciated by 1% on the first trading day after the latest announcements and has since remained stable. It even enjoyed a little boost thanks to foreign demand for shares in India’s
biggest-ever IPO
on October 21st. And, who knows, India may get lucky. A devastating defeat for the Republicans in America’s midterms could weaken the dollar. The AI bubble could burst. The Iran war could end and the Strait of Hormuz could reopen. All sorts of things could happen. Until they do, the costs of defending a round number will mount ever higher.

epub_31.title: Meet the millennial centrist shaking up New Zealand’s election
epub_31.text:
Meet the millennial centrist shaking up New Zealand’s election
Asia
| A new kingmaker?
Meet the millennial centrist shaking up New Zealand’s election
The Opportunity Party claims to be taking on the rich world’s biggest problems
Oct 29th 2026
FOR A SMALL party in a small country, New Zealand’s Opportunity Party has some big ideas about how to solve the rich world’s biggest problems. Campaigning ahead of the November 7th general election, Qiulae Wong, its polished 38-year-old leader, is pitching a universal basic income of NZ$370 ($210) per week. The handout, she says, would replace most other welfare payments and offer a cushion for middle-class workers hit by layoffs because of artificial intelligence. To fund the scheme, the Opportunity Party would introduce a tax on urban land at a rate of 1.75% of its value per year.
On the campaign trail a 40-minute ferry ride from downtown Auckland, Ms Wong (rather bravely) tells a room crammed mostly with rich property owners that the new tax would help to slow rising housing costs by discouraging property speculation. It would also, she says, put capital now sunk into land to more productive use. As pensioners on the lawn outside play croquet, Ms Wong fields questions about what the plan would mean. The tax might need to be phased in, she admits.
Opportunity is polling at just above the 5% threshold needed to break into parliament. If it does so, analysts say that Ms Wong may well end up as the kingmaker between two competing minority coalitions. Both of the two biggest parties, National on the right and Labour on the left, have seen their polling numbers shrink under the weight of unpopular leaders. Christopher Luxon, the incumbent prime minister and National leader, has presided over a stagnant economy and stubborn inflation. Chris Hipkins, the Labour leader, succeeded Jacinda Ardern in 2023 but lacks her star power.
That has left many New Zealanders thinking that the real question in this election is which minor parties will help National or Labour to form a government. Mr Hipkins can call upon the Greens and the Maori Party to his left, but their culture-war style of politics makes some centre-left voters grimace. Mr Luxon’s current coalition partners do much the same on the right. ACT, which started life as a libertarian party, has become more of an anti-woke protest movement. And New Zealand First, another small party, has a long record of divisive populism.
Ms Wong cannily says that she could work with either bloc, and is careful to avoid betraying her ideological biases as voters quiz her about her preferences. That has allowed Opportunity to attract voters from across the political spectrum. Rich Green voters, for instance, see in her a more business-friendly approach to setting emissions targets; libertarians are drawn to the idea of shrinking the state by getting rid of the bureaucrats who hand out means-tested benefits.
Opportunity has its critics. Helen Clark, a Labour leader who was prime minister from 1999 to 2008, has taken to calling it the “Opportunistic” party, arguing that its self-described centrism makes it an empty vessel. Politicians on both sides bitterly accuse it of just being a stalking horse for their opponents. But its most extreme critic has been Winston Peters, the foreign minister and leader of New Zealand First.
Mr Peters, who has a long record of making racist taunts at Asian New Zealanders despite his own part-Maori heritage, seemed distinctly uncomfortable on a debate stage earlier this month with Ms Wong, who immigrated to New Zealand from Fiji as an infant. And yet his discomfort may have less to do with her ethnic-Chinese father than her political strategy. Despite his populist rhetoric, Mr Peters has long positioned himself as New Zealand’s kingmaker, supporting governments led by both Labour and National on two occasions each. No other minor party leader has threatened to rival him in that role—until now.

epub_32.title: The North Aral Sea is expanding after decades of shrinkage
epub_32.text:
The North Aral Sea is expanding after decades of shrinkage
Asia
| Bank form the brink
The North Aral Sea is expanding after decades of shrinkage
The southern remnant is probably still doomed, however
Oct 29th 2026
THE ARAL SEA has long been a byword for ecological disaster. Once the world’s fourth-largest lake, it has been steadily drying up since the 1960s, when the Soviet Union diverted rivers flowing into it to boost cotton production. The lake’s exposed bed became a desert lined with the toxic remnants of fertilisers and industrial waste. Strong winds blow poisonous dust from the sands onto nearby communities.
But the Aral is not gone yet. Two much smaller bodies of water still straddle the edges of the new desert. The southern remnant lies in a trench in the lake’s bed. It survives with inflows from nearby aquifers. It may last a bit longer though little can be done to enlarge it.
The North Aral is a different story, though. It is bordered by higher ground, which cuts it off from the desert except for the tiny Kokaral Strait. Kazakhstan dammed that gap in 2005, but for many years struggled to refill the rump lake.
Finally, however, a recovery is beginning. Early results are promising. Since 2022 its volume has risen by a quarter. Kazakhstan’s government says it has reclaimed 870 square kilometres of desert and lowered the lake’s salinity by 75%. Fish, which had vanished, have been reintroduced: locals caught 8,000 tonnes last year. After planned upgrades to the Kokaral Dam, Kazakhstan hopes to fill the lake to its highest level since the North Aral split off in 1987.
Kazakhstan’s success is thanks to several factors. Canal and dam upgrades along the Syr Darya river coupled with unexpectedly high seasonal inflows account for most of the gains since 2022. In 2025 the country negotiated a new water-sharing agreement with its upriver neighbours, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, selling the former electricity in exchange for more water.
But problems persist. Roughly 60% of the water on Kazakhstan’s side is soaked up by agriculture, but less than a quarter of the country’s farmers use water-saving technologies like sprinklers or drip-fed irrigation. Existing infrastructure is in disrepair. The Syr Darya is at risk, too. The glaciers that feed it are slowly melting. Inflows have already fallen below peak summer demand. All the same, the North Aral Sea has begun to defy doomsayers predicting its ultimate extinction.

epub_34.title: China’s investment in transport infrastructure has peaked
epub_34.text:
China’s investment in transport infrastructure has peaked
China
| Turning-point
China’s investment in transport infrastructure has peaked
Has it built too many expressways and high-speed rail lines?
Oct 29th 2026
In the south-western province of Guizhou, the Huajiang bridge straddles a yawning valley hemmed in by steep mountains. It is a mind-boggling feat of engineering. With a 1,400-metre steel deck suspended 625 metres above a river, the bridge is the world’s highest: two Eiffel Towers could almost be stacked beneath it. Opened in September last year, officials boast that it cuts journey times across the canyon from two hours to two minutes.
Fewer such marvels are likely to be built. China’s years-long splurge on bridges, tunnels, expressways, high-speed rail and airports is beginning to tail off. Questions are likely to grow, however, about whether it was worthwhile. The Huajiang bridge carries a motorway (or expressway, as China calls its high-speed multi-lane roads). But the area is remote and impoverished; heavy traffic is unlikely. The local government talks up the bridge-builders’ technical achievement; far less so the likelihood that the 2.2bn yuan ($330m) cost will ever be recouped, despite road tolls and the tourists it has attracted.
In 2015 Bert Hofman, who was then the head of the World Bank’s office in China, said that having invested so much in new transport infrastructure, the country should turn its attention to keeping it in good shape. Yet China did not apply the brakes. It was not until 2023 that investment peaked in transport-related fixed assets—3.9trn yuan was spent that year (see chart 1). The authorities finally seem to agree with Mr Hofman. In July this year a senior transport official said China’s main transport network was “91% complete”, and the country would pivot from expanding to upgrading existing infrastructure. Mr Hofman jokes that he had not realised he was “so far-sighted”.
To be sure, plenty more will be built. China’s annual investment in transport infrastructure is 2.6% of GDP. That is a far lower share than after the global financial crisis of 2007-09, when it reached 9% as the country unleashed a massive stimulus package. But it remains strikingly high compared with, say, America, where the outlay was just 0.6% of GDP in 2024.
By the end of last year, China had built more than 50,000km of high-speed rail, about 70% of the global total. It plans to build another 20,000km by 2035—roughly 1.5 times the length of such tracks in operation in Europe. And China will also spend money on other types of infrastructure beyond transport. It has earmarked 25trn yuan over the next five years for electric grids, data centres, mobile-phone networks, logistics, canals and pipelines (the “six networks”, as it calls such stuff).
But in the building of transport infrastructure, China’s most conspicuous needs have been met. Long gone are the days when officials would pleadingly intone that “if you want to get rich, first build roads” (it’s a rhyming couplet in Chinese). Since opening its first expressway in 1990, China has built about 200,000km of such whizzy roads (see map)—about twice the length of motorways in America. There are now about 270 commercial airports, three times as many as in 1990. America has twice the number, but the gap is narrowing—China is adding half a dozen entirely new airports a year; America rarely builds any at all.
The humanitarian cost has been enormous: millions have been turfed off their land to make way for roads, railways, airports and other such projects—often without their consent and sometimes with little compensation. The country, however, has grown richer, and praise for the transport network, at home and abroad, is often effusive. Westerners gush about China’s fast, comfortable trains, often contrasting them with the dilapidated state of their own rail networks. The Huajiang bridge is among numerous awe-inspiring record-setters, from the world’s fastest train (430km per hour, between Shanghai and its airport) to its longest motorway tunnel (22.1km, in the far-western region of Xinjiang).
Weighing up the benefits of transport infrastructure is difficult in any country. Railways rarely pay back capital or yield a commercial profit: historical railway-building manias have ruined investors but left behind tracks that boosted economic growth for decades afterwards. China’s rail and expressway networks cannot be judged in isolation. In some places they free up capacity on older lines and roads. They can cut journey times and costs for freight. Chinese people now move around much more easily. Their mobility expands labour markets and makes manufacturing more efficient, letting firms draw on workers and suppliers across a much larger area.
Some Chinese experts, however, argue that the country has invested far more than necessary. Lu Dadao of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has called high-speed rail a “great leap forward”. That is not a compliment—it refers to Mao’s effort in the late 1950s to make China “surpass Britain and catch up with America”. That led to mass famine.
Mr Lu is not suggesting there will be such a disaster this time, but in an essay last year he argued that transport infrastructure had “significantly outpaced actual demand”. He said its achievements had “come at a significant cost”. Another critic is Li Xunlei, an economist at Zhongtai Securities, a state-controlled brokerage. In August Mr Li wrote that China had “overlooked excess capacity” in its building of transport infrastructure. In a country where criticism of the government is heavily muted, these are strong words.
Mr Li’s analysis notes a mismatch between the wealthier coastal regions that most need fast roads—such as Shanghai and Zhejiang—and those where they are being built the fastest, such as the poorer south-western regions of Yunnan and Guangxi. “The areas with the most expressways built saw the least increase in freight demand,” Mr Li wrote of the years between 2014 and 2024. In 2023 China had just under 1,800 vehicles for each kilometre of motorway, far lower than the ratio in most rich countries (see chart 2).
A lot of China’s new infrastructure is underused. Fast rail services in poorer inland regions have more empty seats than, say, the highly profitable line from Beijing to Shanghai. “On many lines…revenue can cover the operation of services but is insufficient to maintain the infrastructure,” said a World Bank review in 2019. Commercial airports have a similar problem. Between 2019 and 2025, 43% of them saw a drop in traveller numbers (not counting airports newly opened since 2019), according to data from the Civil Aviation Administration of China (see chart 4). Declines were concentrated in airports outside major hubs.
Even less economic rationale exists for the proliferation of lavish buildings linked to the new rail lines and airports. In small poorer cities, rail stations and airport terminals are often colossal—built in extravagant ultra-modern style to awe visitors. Take Yantai, a medium-sized coastal city in northern China. The glazed dome and sleek curves of its international airport, opened in 2015, won the title of “world’s most beautiful airport” at the Prix Versailles last year.  Such vanity projects impress slack-jawed Westerners online. Type “China infrastructure” into YouTube and feast your eyes on the results. This surely pleases leaders in Beijing.
Top officials are, however, less happy about the debts that have piled up alongside. Local authorities have borne much of the cost of building expressways and local sections of rail. Local-government debt held in off-balance-sheet vehicles may amount to 72trn yuan, or 51% of GDP. Poorer regions have relied most on such methods—Guizhou, for one. In the end, the central government will probably have to pick up the tab for the Huajiang bridge. Managing the burden will mean less money for health care and social security: both badly in need of funding, not least to encourage consumers to spend.
If the government is betting that demand will eventually catch up with the enormous expansion of transport infrastructure, it should ponder a looming problem. China’s population is ageing rapidly, and the old do not travel as much as the young. By 2050 it will shrink by 150m, according to UN projections. There will thus be fewer passengers on the network. And fewer to admire the breathtaking views from the Huajiang bridge.
■

epub_35.title: Kim Jong Un’s curious visit to China
epub_35.text:
Kim Jong Un’s curious visit to China
China
| Comrades in arms
Kim Jong Un’s curious visit to China
North Korea’s dictator rebuilds ties with an old friend
Oct 29th 2026
Kim Jong Un, North Korea’s leader, rarely travels abroad. So his surprise visit on October 24th to Dandong, a Chinese city that borders on
North Korea
, deserves attention. Mr Kim is rebuilding ties with China after four years of cosying up to Russia (by sending it troops and supplies for the war in Ukraine). He may also be preparing for new diplomacy with America, and possibly a meeting with President Donald Trump in November.
The official purpose of Mr Kim’s latest visit was to commemorate China’s entry into the Korean war in 1950 to support the communist North. China and North Korea are playing up their wartime solidarity. This year is the 65th anniversary of their “friendship” treaty, a mutual-defence pact. Still, it is rare for Mr Kim to acknowledge China’s war effort so prominently on Chinese soil. He was also strikingly effusive about the relationship, hailing bilateral ties “forged in blood”.
It was unusual, too, for Mr Kim to show up in China without seeing its leader, Xi Jinping. The pair met in Pyongyang, the North Korean capital, in June when Mr Xi
visited
for the first time in seven years. That followed a summit between them in Beijing in 2025. This time, however, Mr Xi was busy preparing for a long-scheduled meeting of the Communist Party’s Central Committee in Beijing, which started on October 26th. He sent Wang Huning, who ranks fourth in China’s leadership, instead. On each of Mr Kim’s five previous visits to China since taking power, he spoke with Mr Xi in person.
Mr Kim normally crosses the border on his personal armoured train, which can also run on Chinese tracks. This time, he was driven in a Mercedes Maybach limousine across a bridge over the Yalu river, which separates the countries. The bridge was completed in 2014 as part of an earlier Chinese push to expand cross-border transport links. But its opening was repeatedly delayed after Mr Kim executed an uncle who had pioneered the project and was later accused of planning a coup (and was considered too close to China). It opened, at last, on October 15th.
Mr Kim’s visit and the bridge’s opening both seem to be designed to ease Chinese concerns about Russia’s growing influence over North Korea. China accounts for more than 90% of the country’s official global trade. But Mr Kim and Vladimir Putin, Russia’s leader, have drawn closer of late. In exchange for troops and weapons, Russia has supplied Mr Kim with fuel, food and military technology. The two countries signed a mutual-defence treaty in 2024. They have expanded their own cross-border infrastructure, including a road bridge that opened in September.
In response, Mr Xi has publicly played down his concerns about North Korea’s nuclear ambitions. At the same time, China has been upgrading transport links with North Korea and relaxing restrictions on cross-border trade. In the first nine months of the year, official bilateral trade reached $2.3bn, up from $1.9bn during the same period last year. Mr Wang said the new bridge would help to “expand personnel exchanges and trade co-operation”.
Most intriguingly, Mr Kim’s visit may have been intended to co-ordinate his diplomacy with America. Mr Trump met Mr Kim three times in his first term, hoping to strike a deal to end North Korea’s nuclear programme. Before two of those meetings, Mr Kim had travelled to China a few weeks previously, to talk to Mr Xi. America’s president has said that he would like to meet Mr Kim again, possibly during a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen in mid-November.
American officials have since sought to squash the idea, saying a meeting is unlikely. But some Chinese government advisers say Mr Xi is keen on one. He hopes to reassert his influence and ensure that China has a say in any potential deal between Messrs Trump and Kim. By pitting rival powers against each other, Mr Kim is once again playing a weak hand well.

epub_36.title: China loves to rank its cities. The government wants it to stop
epub_36.text:
China loves to rank its cities. The government wants it to stop
China
| Closing ranks
China loves to rank its cities. The government wants it to stop
Annual city scorecards of all sorts are being torn up
Oct 29th 2026
A scandal is turning over tables in China. Each year apparatchiks in cities and counties across the country battle one another for coveted municipal rankings. The league tables, which are published by media and consulting firms, declare winners and losers in the race for development and attractiveness of living. The rise and fall of many county-level cadres can be traced to a “100 strong counties” list published for the past decade, until this year.
The central government wants to end such competition. New rules have banned organisations from creating data-based rankings or awarding special titles to cities and towns without permission.
Blame officials in Haicheng, a city in the rust-belt north-east, who in 2025 appeared to be so good at their jobs that they leapt from well outside the 100 strongest counties to 91st on the list. It was revealed this year that they had in fact paid CCID, the consulting firm behind the tables, around 5m yuan ($750,000) for the boost. The disclosure caused uproar among ambitious bureaucrats. One frustrated statistician in Hubei province called the incident China’s newest form of corruption.
Municipal pecking orders have long been a useful, if unofficial, way of understanding a country with around 700 cities and close to 3,000 counties. Since the late 1990s most have received an informal “tier” status. The first tier—Beijing, Guangzhou, Shanghai and Shenzhen—has always been clear. Things grow murky at the fifth and sixth. Property developers have used these rankings to gauge real-estate values. The central government has never officially recognised them, although it does refer to city tiers in some property-market data.
Consulting firms have made a business out of rankings. A city-research unit at Yicai, a media group, began evaluating and scoring hundreds of cities in 2016. The same year CCID started issuing its top-counties list. Others have published scorecards focused on specific industries or administrative geographies. One online media outfit publishes a list of city districts with the strongest economies. State-backed groups also participate. The China National Institute of Standardisation (CNIS), for example, issues a report that ranks cities on natural beauty and culture, among other things.
The most closely watched list has been Yicai’s, which tracks 337 cities. It has used metrics such as economic competitiveness, intercity mobility, industrial strength, consumer spending and even nightlife to devise scores for each city. Among these is the “new-first-tier” ranking, a list of China’s 15 most promising second-tier cities. Officials often cite such rankings as a mark of success. Those in Haicheng made sure to highlight their incredible achievements in the county’s annual work report for 2025.
The crackdown on rankings might make it more difficult to figure out who is up and who is down. CCID appears to have stopped posting its “100 strong counties” list after the Haicheng debacle. CNIS posts its ranking in October; it had not released one at the time of reporting. Yicai has continued to publish a wide range of information on Chinese cities this year but has stopped assigning them clear rankings. These are still easy to create with the data Yicai provides, wonks point out.
Perhaps it is a good time to phase out city rankings. Ma Liang, a professor at Renmin University in Beijing, has observed that city officials have started experiencing “ranking anxiety”. With economic growth slowing considerably since scoring began, a property crisis sapping local finances and a perpetual anti-corruption campaign upending careers, it is one less thing for them to fret over.

epub_37.title: China’s most successful Astroturf operation: grassroots football
epub_37.text:
China’s most successful Astroturf operation: grassroots football
China
| Chaguan
China’s most successful Astroturf operation: grassroots football
Provincial leagues spur spending and a hometown renaissance
Oct 29th 2026
ON A COOL autumn night, a man dressed as Guan Yu, a legendary general from 1,800 years ago, mounted his black steed and charged around a stadium. From the stands 26,000 fans erupted in cheers—and then thunderous chants for their football team: “Yiyang must win!” Nearly two hours later Yiyang had lost, 1-0, to their stronger opponents from Changsha, the capital of Hunan province. Yiyang’s players, their bright orange jerseys muddy and socks torn from the hard-fought match, could not hold back tears.
Welcome to the spectacle, and the emotion, of the grassroots provincial football leagues sweeping across China. “Xiangchao (the Hunan league) is better than the World Cup,” goes one local joke. The skills are—put politely—uneven, with lots of missed passes, fluffed shots and, in the Yiyang match, a goal review that took 11 excruciating minutes. But the passion is real, more so than that surrounding China’s perennially inept national team.
The city-versus-city amateur competitions began only in spring 2025, starting in Jiangsu, and have inspired copycats in about 20 other provinces. Officials see the leagues chiefly as economic catalysts. Their most striking impact, though, has been social. Against the backdrop of a sluggish economy, they have given people something to cheer, and with all the devotion and irrationality of sports fans anywhere. “It’s been a morale booster for us,” says a sponsor of the Yiyang team.
A few hours before kick-off, the plaza outside the Yiyang stadium had a carnival atmosphere. Stalls sold spicy soup, stinky tofu, a mashed tea drink and other local delights. The biggest queues were for giveaways, including jars of Hunanese chilli relish. Superfans gathered early to bang on drums, wave oversize flags and belt out their chants. They were a good-natured bunch, joking with fans of the opposing side and wrapping Chaguan in a team scarf. Cheerleaders warmed up for their half-time performance; in keeping with the family atmosphere of the whole event, they were clad in ankle-length Chinese opera-style robes.
In the streets around the stadium, the penumbra of China’s property downturn is visible in closed restaurants, half-finished buildings and unoccupied flats. A business partner of the Hunan league says it was created in part to revive economic activity. Officials had tried several things, from night markets to concerts. Nothing worked as well as football, he says. It drew spectators, young and old, as well as out-of-towners. With domestic tourism bemoaned as homogeneous and predictable—cities offer similar pedestrian streets, similar trinkets, similar virtual-reality experiences—there is something to be said for the drama and uncertainty of sport. The inaugural season of the Hunan league brought a Cinderella story when Yongzhou, much poorer than Changsha, clawed its way to the championship.
The matches also tap into a vein of local pride. Decades of migration for work have torn many Chinese from their home towns. Now that they are richer, people are searching for new forms of meaning. Football is one way to reconnect with and express their local identity. “It’s your own family out there,” says Mr Zhang, a convenience-store clerk. Though he worked in Changsha for many years, he could never bring himself to support the capital. “Speaking frankly, Changsha is like a landlord. They have far too many advantages.” In her social-media videos, Zhou Meimei, an influencer from Yiyang, emphasises the value of friendly exchanges between Hunan’s cities. Yiyang, often overlooked by other Hunanese, can show off its hospitable culture to visiting fans, she says. Yet she is competitive, too. “We all want to win because as locals we want our hometown to earn honour,” she says.
The provincial leagues may help football’s image in China. At the professional level, the China Super League is seen as hopelessly corrupt, marred by match-fixing scandals. The provincial leagues have a purity about them. “There’s no money in these games, just people struggling to win,” says one fan at the Yiyang match. Some hope the triumph of these leagues will radiate upwards to the national team, which has not reached a World Cup since 2002. But the provincial leagues come far too late in players’ development to feed into the national programme. Nevertheless, rekindled enthusiasm may entice more young people to play.
Rules are in place to keep the provincial leagues resolutely amateur and local. In Hunan, for example, each team must have at least three high-school students on the pitch at all times. All players must have ties to their city, such as a hukou (household registration). Governments also keep ticket prices down. In Yiyang, seats were just 9.9 yuan ($1.50); nearly 90,000 people had entered the ticket lottery. When scalpers muscled in, authorities introduced facial-recognition turnstiles, ensuring that original ticket recipients could not sell their seats.
For all their grassroots feel, the leagues are mostly run from the top down: bureaucrats organise the matches, vet the entertainment and manage the commercial deals. Their charm depends on that hand staying light. Much as Chinese cities compete to attract investments, they may also start treating league standings as a performance metric. Languishing at the bottom of the table could reflect poorly on a city’s organisational abilities, so the pressure to lure better players or spend more on training is likely to grow.
Money is starting to wend its way into the local leagues. In Jiangsu, sponsors now include Heineken, Coca-Cola and Adidas. In Yiyang, by contrast, one of the main sponsors was a hometown producer of packets of little dried fish seasoned with a fiery sauce. Fans queued for samples of the spicy minnows and for photos with the CEO, a local success story. For now, the small fry are thriving. But the big fish are circling.

epub_39.title: America’s decisive voters are its most recent arrivals
epub_39.text:
America’s decisive voters are its most recent arrivals
United States
| In full swing
America’s decisive voters are its most recent arrivals
Hispanic- and Asian-Americans will shape this year’s midterm elections and more
Oct 29th 2026
THE DEATH knell for Kamala Harris’s presidential campaign first sounded in Loudoun County, Virginia. Home to affluent voters, one-quarter of whom are of Asian descent, the county had plumped decisively for Joe Biden in 2020. When it was reported, early on election night in 2024, that Ms Harris had won by 16 points compared with Mr Biden’s 25, pundits wondered if there had been a glitch.
The county may now move left once more. At an early-voting centre, volunteers recently handed out sample ballots in Hindi. Arjun, a man in his 50s, described a case of “buyer’s remorse” after backing Donald Trump two years ago. “Everything he said was a lie,” he explained. Outside Patel Brothers, a bustling supermarket, one woman said she will vote for Democrats because Mr Trump’s cuts have gutted care for her disabled child. Other former Trump supporters said they were repelled by the Iran war, high prices, cuts to visas, cruel deportations and reductions in the federal workforce. “A lot of my friends lost their jobs,” said Mohammed, an architect.
Mr Trump’s declining popularity in Loudoun in some ways mirrors trends across the country: nationally, his net approval rating is -27. But these swings, towards Mr Trump two years ago and away from him since then, are not distributed evenly across America. Instead, they have been concentrated in states and districts that are geographically disparate but share a striking demographic similarity: they have large shares of Asian or Latino voters.
Democrats and Republicans alike have too often conflated demography with destiny. For the left, the growing ranks of non-white voters seemed to ease the need to win over culturally conservative whites, while Republicans have feared that immigrants would secure lasting Democratic power. Indeed, the share of eligible voters who are Latino has risen from 9% to 16% in the past 20 years, while the share of Asian-Americans has risen from 3% to 5%. But both sides were wrong. America’s fastest-growing ethnicities are also its most politically open-minded. That gives the country’s newest Americans disproportionate sway in determining its direction.
In this country of immigrants, recent arrivals have shaped party politics throughout its history. The latest wave began after 1965, when immigration quotas were lifted and people began arriving once more, mainly from Latin America and Asia. They did not become rigid partisans. Exit polls showed that Ronald Reagan won 37% of Hispanics in 1980 (he described them as Republicans who “don’t know it yet”), and George W. Bush won a robust 44% in 2004. In the 1990s the Republican Party fared even better with Asians, winning them outright in 1992 and 1996.
It was not until 2012, when exit polls found Barack Obama winning 73% of Asian-Americans and 71% of Latinos, that strategists started seeing these groups as reliable Democrats. “With New Support Base, Obama Doesn’t Need Right-Leaning Whites Anymore”, read one headline in the Atlantic in 2013. Mr Trump’s victory in 2016 seemed to vindicate the idea that Republicans should run up their numbers with white voters, rather than reach out to ethnic minorities.
Yet despite Mr Trump’s often racist rhetoric, his share of the Hispanic and Asian vote inched up in 2020, a trend that accelerated in 2024, when he won 40% of Asian voters and 46% of Hispanic ones (see chart 1). In that election, according to the Co-operative Election Study (CES) at Harvard University, Asians and Latinos made up 14% of voters, but comprised 24% of those who voted for a presidential candidate from one party in 2020 and a different party four years later. That does not make them the biggest bloc of swing voters in absolute terms: non-Hispanic white voters still outnumbered them in 2024, comprising 59% of switchers. But their rejection of strict partisanship, growing numbers and reasons for changing parties are what gives them particular clout.
Even in 2012, when Mr Obama won more than 70% of Asians and Latinos, only 13% and 27% of them identified as “strong” Democrats, according to polling for The Economist by YouGov. Hispanic voters, as well as Asians, stand out for their heterodox positions, agreeing with Democrats on some topics and Republicans on others. Analysing a series of policy questions in the CES, The Economist found that around 34% of Latinos and 30% of Asians hold views which are either moderate or combine left- and right-leaning positions, compared with only 20% of white voters. Latino and Asian respondents’ views on any single issue are less likely to predict how they will respond on another subject. For example, Asians are unusually supportive of both regulating pollution and work requirements for government benefits. Hispanics are more likely than other Americans to back a ban on abortion as well as cancelling student debt.
In part, these combinations of views are a product of diverse cultural traditions between these groups and within them, as well as a range of income levels (see chart 2). They are also a reminder that newcomers do not fit neatly in pre-existing categories. Naturalised citizens are overwhelmingly Hispanic or Asian. Just 9% of Asians and one-third of Hispanics have two native-born parents (compared with 90% of whites and 77% of blacks), making them less likely to inherit a partisan identity.
For these voters the culture wars, which bind a large and growing share of white voters to a particular party, are less important. Economic issues are paramount. In polling for The Economist by YouGov in September and October, the share of respondents listing consumer prices or “jobs and the economy” as their most important issue was 57% for both Asian-Americans and Latinos, compared with 50% for black respondents and 45% for white ones.
That reflects the broader priorities of Latino and Asian-American voters. They spend more time working than the average American. Latinos are more than twice as likely as whites to start a business; Asian-Americans spend more time in school. “Even if you’re not yourself an immigrant, but you’re descended from them, you’re in this country to work hard and get ahead, and that means that economic considerations come ahead of so much else,” says Carlos Odio, a researcher who specialises in surveying Latinos. As Ruben Gallego, a Democratic senator, put it last year, “every Latino man wants a big-ass truck”, often described affectionately as la troquita.
All this set up Latino and Asian-American voters as the perfect swing group in 2024, when prices were the dominant issue. Latinos were particularly exposed to the spike in petrol prices in 2022 owing to their higher-than-average spending on cars, trucks and fuel. Later, in 2023 and 2024, the effect of inflation shifted to housing costs; that disproportionately affected Asian-Americans, who spend more on housing than other groups. This year it is Mr Trump’s turn to feel their wrath.
According to a series of large-sample polls of likely voters conducted for the Argument, a digital news company, Democrats’ margin over Republicans has risen by 17 percentage points among Hispanics and 14 among Asians since 2024, compared with ten for white voters and five for black ones. And although poll cross-tabs can be prone to errors, statewide elections since Mr Trump’s inauguration show the same trend. In gubernatorial elections in New Jersey and Virginia last year and California’s all-party House primaries in June, Democrats’ biggest gains relative to the presidential vote of 2024 were in precincts or districts with their states’ highest concentrations of Asians and Latinos.
Their discontent will play a crucial role in the midterms. Republicans in Texas pushed through a gerrymander that could net the party up to five seats in the House—if only Mr Trump could hold on to his gains in largely Hispanic south Texas. Instead, our forecasting model favours Democrats in three of these districts, and makes Republicans only narrow favourites in two more. In total, Latinos and Asian-Americans represent a larger than average share of voters in 28 battleground House races (see map).
Latinos and Asian-Americans will bring their political heft to high-profile statewide races, too. Combined, they make up 36% of the electorate in Texas and 24% in Florida, the two largest Trump-voting states. Democrats trail by just a few points in both states’ gubernatorial contests, thanks largely to leads among Hispanics of 12 points in Florida and 27 points in Texas. For the Senate, an upset in Florida is unlikely. But James Talarico is up by two points overall and 33 points among Latinos in his bid to become the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas since 1988.
“I’ve spent most of my career telling white, well-intentioned political consultants and candidates that Latinos aren’t a monolith,” says Chuck Rocha, a Democratic political consultant. He now says the opposite: “they’re all monolithically pissed.” Democrats are hammering the president for turbocharging consumer prices by imposing tariffs and beginning a war.
In California’s dusty, agricultural Central Valley, Randy Villegas, a Democrat, is running to unseat David Valadao, a moderate Republican in a district whose voters are two-thirds Hispanic. “I want you to raise your hand”, Mr Villegas said at a rally in Bakersfield, “if you or someone you love drives across the border to Tijuana to get cheaper prescription drugs, cheaper dental care, cheaper health care.” Hands shot up all around the room.
In addition to the economy, this year immigration looms large. Voters in both groups, who by definition have already become citizens, generally support border enforcement and take a moderate view on immigration. But they see the president’s tactics as going too far. In Florida María Elvira Salazar, a Miami-area Republican incumbent facing a tough Democratic challenger, ran an ad in September addressed to Mr Trump in which she said that “the same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”
In early 2025 Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents targeted California’s agricultural heartland. They are once again roaming the area ahead of the midterms. In Delano, a farm town that swung towards Mr Trump by 15 points in 2024, shop signs are mostly in Spanish and residents often greet each other with a friendly “buenos días”. Now the streets are quiet and many stores remain shuttered. “I just don’t love what’s happening with immigration,” says Griselda Aguilar, a 34-year-old mother who backed Mr Trump two years ago but attended Mr Villegas’s rally. “The way it’s been handled is inhumane.”
In the waning days of the campaign, the White House—far from easing its rhetoric on immigrants—is playing it up. J.D. Vance, the vice-president, has touted Mr Trump’s deportation campaign and wants a radical overhaul of visas for skilled workers. In Montana on October 26th, he offered adulation for Americans who “homesteaded this land” and “buried their own kin” in the state’s “beautiful soil”. Mr Trump has repeatedly warned, without evidence, that illegal voting by non-citizens will threaten the elections’ integrity.
This obsession is hardly welcoming to Asian or Latino voters, nor does it address their main concern: the economy. If they help secure victory for Democrats, the party may assume that supporters are “coming home”. The lesson of recent years, however, is that neither party should take these voters for granted. Even as more Asians and Latinos swing left, fewer identify themselves as Democrats than in 2024.
“The fact that we view it as so peculiar that Latinos are moving by 20 points is the sign of what’s wrong,” says Mike Madrid, author of “The Latino Century”. Among other constituencies, “nobody moves despite pandemic and war and recession and depression,” he says. “If people do a bad job, you fire them. Latinos are the only group doing that.”
