epub_40.text:
Our forecast of the midterms’ outcome
United States
| How the dominoes might fall
Our forecast of the midterms’ outcome
The auguries are good for Democrats
Oct 29th 2026
WHEN AN UNSTOPPABLE force meets an immovable object, one or the other has to give. For most of Donald Trump’s second term, pundits have assumed that the object, Republicans’ seemingly impregnable Senate map, had the edge over the force, Democrats’ lead in national polls. Last year Sabato’s Crystal Ball, a leading forecasting outfit, called Republicans “strong favourites” to hold their Senate majority, and classified Alaska, Iowa and Kansas as “safe” red seats. As late as this June, the group still found enough races at least “leaning” towards Republicans for the party to control the chamber.
Now, with midterm elections less than a week away, conventional wisdom holds that the force has claimed the upper hand. Crystal Ball’s latest update says Democrats “have a slight advantage in the battle for the Senate”, while betting markets make the party a 67% favourite to flip the chamber. Nate Silver, America’s most prominent quantitative election forecaster, gives Democrats a 76% chance. But
The Economist’s own prediction model
is more cautious, putting the probability of the Senate changing hands at just 54%.
The main source of this disagreement is our model’s intentional breach of a common forecasting maxim: thou shalt not attempt to predict the direction of polling errors. Although “generic-ballot” surveys, which ask respondents which party they plan to support for Congress, have an impressive record of accuracy, they also have a marked tendency to overshoot: wave elections usually prove less towering than advertised. On the eve of the 2006 midterms, for example, Democrats led these surveys by 13 percentage points on average, while their final margin in the national House vote was a mere seven. And when national polls misfire, that error usually appears in state-specific surveys as well.
This year’s Democratic advantage, at around 8.5 points on the generic ballot, is less extreme than that of 2006. Nonetheless, based on history, our model projects that polls across the country will overestimate the party’s margin by around a point. This gap is smaller in historically Democratic states, but larger in Republican ones—and to control the Senate, Democrats need to win at least two states that Mr Trump won by double digits in 2024.
Another potential factor is fundraising. Overall, Democratic Senate candidates have received far more in contributions from individual donors (which are capped at $3,500) in their states than their opponents have. Many forecasts weight this heavily. However, Democratic Senate nominees as a group have also out-raised Republicans in this category in every other election since Mr Trump’s first inauguration. This has not translated into poll-beating electoral performances. As a result, our model compares each candidate’s fundraising to their own party’s average. This helps Republicans’ prospects in states like Iowa, where we reward their nominee for eking out a narrow financial advantage.
Relative to the consensus, our model is most pessimistic about Democratic hopes in Alaska. Betting markets make Mary Peltola a 69% favourite over Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, whereas we show a 51-49 race favouring Mr Sullivan. And Ms Peltola may yet suffer from allegations that her team planted spoiler candidates on the ballot, a controversy that is likely to dominate the final week of campaigning.
Nonetheless, our model still clearly favours Democrats in enough states—including Maine, Michigan, North Carolina and Ohio—to win 50 Senate seats. It gives them even odds in two more (Alaska and Texas) that could be the majority-making 51st seat. Importantly, our model gives Democrats a 95% chance of gaining control of the House of Representatives, which would allow them to reject Mr Trump’s agenda and to launch investigations of his administration. Winning the Senate would enable them to block his judicial nominees as well.
The makeup of the Senate, where terms are six years, will also strongly influence whether Mr Trump’s successor, who will be elected in two, can implement a partisan agenda. Looking beyond 2028, Democrats’ 52nd seat could matter just as much as their 51st. And they currently have a plausible path to winning considerably more than 52 seats. Their candidates are neck-and-neck in polls of Kansas, Iowa and even South Carolina, where Lindsey Graham, a longtime Republican incumbent, died in July and was replaced by his sister Darline, a political novice. On October 28th the New York Times and Siena College, America’s most prominent team of pollsters, reported a tied race in South Carolina, where Mr Trump won by 18 points two years ago.
Democrats are modest underdogs in all these states. However, if even one of these dominoes falls, they may well have benefited from a nationwide polling error, raising the odds that the others fall too. Should Dan Osborn, a Nebraska independent who vowed not to caucus with either party if elected, join Democrats instead, we give the party a 15% chance of holding at least 55 seats. Even in 2006, when the generic ballot vastly overstated the Democratic advantage, the party still managed to flip six Senate seats and secure a majority.

epub_41.title: The midterms could reshape American politics far beyond Congress
epub_41.text:
The midterms could reshape American politics far beyond Congress
United States
| Downballot blues
The midterms could reshape American politics far beyond Congress
Democrats may take control of several state governments
Oct 29th 2026
On a recent Saturday morning in Greendale, Wisconsin, 50 people gathered outside a modest ranch house to knock on doors for the Democratic Party. Addressing the group, Ben Wikler, the former chairman of the state party, stressed the importance of their task. Democrats have a chance to undo 16 years of Republican dominance in the state.
Wisconsin is not the only state Democrats have their eye on. Though the battle for Congress gets most of the attention nationwide, Democrats also have a chance to wrest control of several state governments. Republicans have “trifectas” in 23 states—meaning they control both chambers of the state legislature and the governorship. Democrats have 16. With a big enough blue wave, Democrats could create six new trifectas, including in Wisconsin, and break several Republican ones.
The consequences of such a shift would be far-reaching. State governments wield enormous power over matters like abortion, education, health care, taxation and labour laws. They also help determine the rules governing elections and the boundaries of congressional districts, shaping the balance of power in Washington. With a trifecta, a party can enact its agenda with relative ease. Wisconsin is a case in point.
Though Tony Evers, a Democrat, became governor in 2019, Wisconsin retains a raft of conservative laws enacted by his Republican predecessor, Scott Walker, who governed with a trifecta. Mr Walker weakened unions by allowing private-sector employees to benefit from collective bargaining without paying for it. He also sharply curtailed collective-bargaining rights for public-sector workers. His administration resisted attempts to increase the minimum wage, which is a paltry $7.25 an hour, and refused to expand Medicaid under Obamacare. Before leaving office Mr Walker signed legislation weakening his successor’s executive powers, making it harder for Mr Evers to reverse course.
With a trifecta, Democrats could undo Mr Walker’s “legacy of destruction”, says Devin Remiker, the state’s party chairman. They might also legalise marijuana, enshrine abortion rights in state law and end the state’s school-voucher system. Their prospects improved after a judicial election in 2023 delivered a liberal majority on the state Supreme Court. It struck down Wisconsin’s electoral maps, prompting Republican legislators to approve new ones drawn by Mr Evers rather than risk even less favourable versions being imposed by the court. Under the new maps, Democrats made big gains in 2024. They now need to flip just five seats in the state’s lower house and two in the upper house.
Elsewhere, the path to a Democratic trifecta varies. In Arizona, as in Wisconsin, Democrats would need to flip both legislative chambers to create the party’s first trifecta in over 60 years. In Michigan, Minnesota and Pennsylvania just one chamber would need to change hands. In Nevada the critical contest is a tight governor’s race. All six also happen to be presidential battlegrounds states. If the presidential election in 2028 is as closely fought as the previous two, control of their statehouses may matter.

epub_42.title: The winners and losers of Trumponomics
epub_42.text:
The winners and losers of Trumponomics
United States
| MAGA transfer
The winners and losers of Trumponomics
The president promised to help ordinary Americans. He achieved something rather different
Oct 29th 2026
ALL POPULISTS promise much to the working man, but Donald Trump predicted a golden age. Just before the election in 2024, he told voters they were days away from “the best jobs, the biggest paycheques and the brightest economic future the world has ever seen”.  His unorthodox blend of tariffs, tax cuts and deportations, he claimed, would bring down living costs,
revive America’s industrial heartland
and restore middle-class prosperity.
Has the president delivered? On October 22nd the White House claimed his economic policies were driving up wages and fuelling a “blue-collar BOOM”. America’s economy is indeed growing briskly, with output on course to expand at an annualised rate of around 3% in the third quarter. But many of those Mr Trump claimed he would help have lost out, while richer Americans have gained.
The most politically toxic policies are those that have raised daily costs. The
president’s sweeping tariffs
have pushed up the cost of consumer goods by roughly 2%, according to the New York Fed. The Budget Lab at Yale estimates they will cost the average household $1,100 this year. The war in Iran has also sent oil prices soaring, and is set to add another $1,000 to the average household’s costs by year’s end.
Pushing in the other direction, Mr Trump’s flagship tax-and-spending law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, has boosted tax refunds by around $340 on average. The law also created “
Trump accounts
”, an effort to broaden ownership in the stock market, with eligible newborns entitled to $1,000 to invest in shares. But the biggest gains went to richer Americans through lower taxes, even as the act tightened access to food stamps—with more than 5m Americans losing benefits so far—and to Medicaid, the government health-care programme for the poor.
To tally the net effects of these gains and losses, The Economist combined estimates of the impact of tariffs, higher petrol prices and Mr Trump’s tax-and-spending law across income groups in 2026. We estimate that Mr Trump’s policies will cost the poorest tenth of American households, with average income after taxes and transfers of around $37,000, almost 3% of their income. The richest tenth, with average after-tax incomes of nearly $500,000, will gain nearly 3% (see chart 1). Households in the middle, with average income of roughly $100,000, lose more than $400. That does not account for the effect of a decision, taken by congressional Republicans last year and endorsed by Mr Trump, to let enhanced Obamacare subsidies expire. That has raised average premiums for individual insurance purchased on exchanges by nearly $800 a year, according to KFF, a health-policy research group.
Housing costs pose another problem for the president. Mortgage rates, pushed up in part by the inflationary effects of his war in Iran, have climbed above 7%, prompting existing owners to stay put. Adding new supply has become more costly. Last year builders estimated that tariffs on materials would add nearly $11,000 to the cost of a typical new home. His immigration crackdown is fuelling labour shortages, too; in September a survey from the National Association of Home Builders reported that labour costs were up by 4.2% from a year earlier. It is lower-income and middle-class voters, again, who are most pinched. In May sales of starter homes fell by 5.4% from a year earlier, even as luxury-home sales rose by 6.2%, according to Zillow, an online property firm.
When it comes to jobs, health care and social assistance have accounted for almost all private-sector gains since January 2025, to meet demand from America’s ageing population. The AI boom has been another bright spot, with data-centre investment creating roughly 180,000 new jobs in industries related to the build-out. In other sectors, though, private employment has barely budged. Annual wage growth across the private sector has slowed from 4% to 3%; rising inflation means that workers’ hourly pay is 0.7% lower in real terms than a year ago. Labour’s share of non-farm business output has fallen to its lowest level since records began in 1947 (changes to how business owners’ earnings are classified explain only some of the decline).
A renaissance in manufacturing jobs has been particularly elusive. Though manufacturing output has risen, manufacturing employment has fallen by some 20,000 since January 2025, while factory workers’ wages have failed to keep pace with inflation over the past year. In North Carolina, which Mr Trump won in 2024 and which now looks set to elect a Democrat to the Senate, nearly 9,000 factory jobs have disappeared over the past year.
Americans invested in the stock market have more to celebrate, as the AI bonanza has driven up the value of the S&P 500. But the impact is, once again, lopsided. Of the $17trn increase in Americans’ equity and mutual-fund wealth since the end of 2024, nearly 90% accrued to the richest tenth of households, compared with just 0.6% for the poorer half, according to data from the Federal Reserve (see chart 2).
These phenomena have not gone unnoticed. Nearly two-thirds of Americans think that Mr Trump’s economic policies have made conditions worse, according to a recent survey by the Pew Research Centre; the same is true of 35% of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents, nearly twice the share in January. Voters who are particularly affected by rising fuel costs and tariffs, such as farmers, are tilting towards Democrats. Mr Trump is now promising $5,000 to every adult citizen if Republicans retain control of Congress on November 3rd. That will do little to reassure voters who still feel left behind.

epub_43.title: Democrats are rediscovering what an appealing politics of progress looks like
epub_43.text:
Democrats are rediscovering what an appealing politics of progress looks like
United States
| Lexington
Democrats are rediscovering what an appealing politics of progress looks like
Their competitive candidates in states such as Iowa show how the party can avoid approaching doom
Oct 29th 2026
Ever since Senator Tom Harkin retired after five terms in 2015, his fellow Democrats in Iowa have fared poorly. Republicans took control of what had been a divided state government and a divided congressional delegation, and Donald Trump won Iowa three times, most recently by more than 13 points. Now a bit hard of hearing and frail at 86, Mr Harkin is back on the stump, to support Democratic candidates who are mounting surprisingly strong challenges up and down the ticket.
As elsewhere, a lot of the campaigning in Iowa has been stupid and awful. Record sums are being spent to jam the airways with advertisements making nasty, misleading claims. Mr Harkin’s presence is something of a tonic, and not only because he is as genial and plain-spoken as ever. When he introduces Josh Turek, who is campaigning for Mr Harkin’s old Senate seat, and Mr Turek pushes himself forward in his wheelchair to take the microphone, the exchange supplies a poignant reminder of the sort of thing all this politicking is supposed to be about.
Mr Harkin was the champion of the landmark civil-rights law banning discrimination against people with disabilities. Mr Turek, who was born with spina bifida, was 11 when that law, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), passed in 1990. He calls Mr Harkin his political hero and says without the law, “every economic, every occupational, educational opportunity that I’ve been given would not have been there.” Like Mr Harkin himself, Mr Turek is quick to note something more. Mr Harkin counted on Republican allies to pass the bill. “It’s an amazing example of what we can do when we’re willing to work together,” Mr Turek says.
And that observation illuminates something else: that the struggle under way within the Democratic Party, which will probably grow more heated after the midterm elections, is not just a fight over policy between “progressives” and “moderates”. It is a contest between competing theories of how to make progress.
Mr Harkin is not surrendering the progressive label. He sees many of his differences with “my good friend” Bernie Sanders, the fiery leftist leader, as matters of style, even word-choice, not principle. He praises Mr Turek not only for having “a progressive agenda” but also for knowing “how to move it forward”. Mr Harkin does not note that Senator Sanders cannot point to any legislative achievement on the scale of the ADA.
Since Mr Harkin left the Senate, “progressive” has acquired a sharper edge. Mr Turek calls himself a moderate. Yet, like Mr Harkin, he also identifies as a prairie populist, in the tradition of the radical agrarian movement that united small farmers and trade unionists against the monopolistic powers of the Gilded Age. When Mr Turek talks about taxing billionaires, challenging big corporations and raising the minimum wage, he sounds no different from Abdul El-Sayed, who is running in Michigan and is the most prominent Senate candidate of the party’s populist left.
The candidates in Michigan and Iowa have important policy differences, though even those can blur. While Mr Turek says he opposes biological males competing in female sports, Dr El-Sayed has not taken a position, saying such decisions should be left to sports leagues. Unlike Mr Turek, Dr El-Sayed wants to abolish the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, yet he also says he supports applying immigration laws and securing the borders. Dr El-Sayed wants Medicare for All but says he would also back incremental expansions of public-health coverage favoured by Mr Turek. Dr El-Sayed wants to end military aid to Israel; Mr Turek would impose strict restrictions on such aid.
But their differences of style are stark. Dr El-Sayed has a combative, impatient approach, including to Democrats. He told donors he could intimidate Democrats who differ with him by putting “one ogre on a pike”, a reference to Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania. Mr Turek recoils from fighting even with Republicans. Dr El-Sayed has said Mr Trump should be impeached. Mr Turek has “no interest” in that. “We gotta get back to country over party,” he has said. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Mr Sanders’s likeliest heir, recently said a win by Dr El-Sayed would prove “anybody can win anywhere”. That is not so. Like Mr Turek, Dr El-Sayed is in a close race and may lose. But Michigan, where Democrats hold the governor’s office and both Senate seats, should have been less of a challenge.
The more inclusive style, rather than the combative one, has helped make Democrats competitive again this year not just in Iowa but in Alaska, Kansas, South Carolina and Texas. That model is the one Democrats should heed as they turn to the 2028 presidential campaign. Americans have been moving from Democrat-dominated states such as New York and California to Republican states including Florida and Texas. Congressional seats and electoral votes will follow along after the census in 2030. Expanding their electoral map is becoming an existential matter for Democrats. This may seem a paradox, and it will certainly be no easy feat in the last two years of Mr Trump’s polarising presidency, but to be viable as a party, Democrats need to become less partisan.
Republicans who are running scared this year are learning their version of that lesson. Mr Turek’s opponent, Representative Ashley Hinson, is calling herself a “bipartisan fighter for Iowa”. She barely mentioned Mr Trump at a rally in Manchester on October 25th. Americans, she said, were “feeling priced out of the American dream” because “a lot of people on, frankly, both sides of the aisle” have “forgotten how hard Iowans work”. The health-iest outcome of this refreshingly competitive election season across America would be a bipartisan awakening to the obvious: that most voters want less partisanship, more progress.

epub_45.title: Lula, the great survivor, makes history
epub_45.text:
Lula, the great survivor, makes history
The Americas
| Brazil’s four-time winner
Lula, the great survivor, makes history
His defeated rival has fled to the United States
Oct 29th 2026
EVEN BY BRAZIL’S standards, it was a week of extraordinary drama. On October 25th Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who most pundits thought was dead and buried after the first round of voting, won Brazil’s presidential election. That stunning comeback vaults Lula, as the 81-year-old left-winger is known, into an exclusive club of presidents who have won four democratic elections. Two days later his defeated rival, Flávio Bolsonaro—the son of Jair, a hard-right former president who is under house arrest for attempting a coup—fled Brazil after a Supreme Court judge investigating allegations of corruption ordered him to hand in his passports. He has taken his family to the United States.
No presidential candidate since the return of democracy in 1985 had lost the first round of voting and won the run-off. Lula trailed Flávio by 2m votes in the first ballot on October 4th. The candidates who were knocked out at that stage, who between them had received 8% of votes, also chose to back Flávio. Yet in less than three weeks Lula gained an extra 10m votes, many of them from people who had failed to turn out or spoiled their ballots in the first round (see chart 1).
Three things explain the turnaround. The first is a change in tactics. Ahead of the first round, Lula ran a disorganised and old-fashioned campaign. He wore a Panama hat to hide scars from a recent operation; that merely reminded voters of his age. His team barely spent anything on social media. Instead they handed out lots of stickers with his face on them. But between the two rounds Lula discovered both his mojo and the internet. He lost the hat and he began posting selfie videos on Instagram. His campaign got a huge boost from André Janones, a congressman from Minas Gerais, a bellwether state, who set up a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” which attracted over 10m members in two weeks. Mr Janones gave the members of this group “missions”, such as reposting an image of Lula on social media, which helped his messages go viral in the final stretch of the campaign.
Second, the government opened the taps. Lula raised handouts in Brazil’s flagship welfare programme by 15%. He pushed Congress into passing a law to reduce the working week by a day, without pay cuts. He pledged to make public transport free at weekends and forgive federal debts for sole traders, as well as to hand out $1,000 to a million of them. Incumbents in Brazil often make lavish giveaways before elections, but even so Lula has been generous. His team has not explained how he will fund these and other freebies, which are expected to cost 2% of GDP by the end of next year.
Finally, many Brazilians decided that Flávio was beyond the pale. Two televised debates helped rehash his dodgy past, especially his alleged links to Rio de Janeiro’s militias—groups of corrupt policemen who work as hitmen and extortionists. (Two weeks after the first-round vote, one of Flávio’s allies in Rio was arrested on charges of working with militiamen and drug-traffickers.)
The debates may have been decisive. In one of them Flávio, who is a lawyer, was asked about a case in which he defended a policeman accused of killing a five-year-old girl, which many viewers had not heard about. His arrogance turned voters off, not least when he mocked Lula for having nine fingers. (Lula lost one finger while working in a factory as a teenager.) “I was a minor and working at night, because either I worked or I did not eat,” Lula replied. That highlighted Flávio’s better-off background, and that he got his start in politics thanks to his father.
When his defeat was announced on October 25th, Flávio seemed defiant. He refused to concede (even though he had lost by a reasonable margin, having chalked up 48% of votes compared with 52% for Lula). He argued unconvincingly that a last-minute Supreme Court decision to keep polling stations open for an additional two hours, because of extreme weather and disruptions to public transport, had disadvantaged his campaign. He called for the vote to be annulled.
Yet then events moved very fast. Having failed in his tilt at the presidency, Flávio will in February lose the judicial immunity he has enjoyed as a sitting senator. Recently federal police have been investigating his ties to a businessman accused of massive money-laundering (both he and the businessman deny wrongdoing). The day after the election, the Supreme Court judge who is handling that case banned him from leaving the country.
Police say Flávio did not comply with a request to surrender his passports. Instead, on the evening of October 27th he and his family crossed the border into Argentina. The group then travelled to Miami via Ecuador (the US State Department had said in advance that the United States would be willing to grant them entry). Flávio’s brother, Eduardo, has himself been living in the United States since 2025. In June a Brazilian court sentenced Eduardo in absentia to four years in jail for trying to unduly influence the prosecution of his father—by lobbying Donald Trump to apply sanctions on the judges who sentenced him.
After arriving in the United States Flávio published a statement in which he called himself “the leader of Brazil”, said he was the victim of a “witch hunt”, and vowed to keep leading the opposition from abroad.  For the moment Mr Trump does not seem much inclined to back him, beyond permitting him to stay in the country. On October 26th Mr Trump told reporters that Brazil’s vote “looked like another rigged election” while adding that he “didn’t take sides” and saying “I like Lula, I get along with him very well.” On October 28th he said, “I won’t get involved”.
In theory, Flávio’s departure could prove a chance for Brazil’s right to make a fresh start. He became the right’s candidate only because his father anointed him as his heir. That decision sidelined politicians who would have been much more electable.  With Jair under house arrest and Flávio abroad, there could now be an opportunity for renewal.
All this has got Lula’s new mandate off to a dramatic start. His honeymoon is going to be short. Though he has won the presidency, right-wingers constitute the largest caucus in both houses. That will make it difficult for Lula to govern, especially since constitutional limits (and his age) mean that he cannot run again. He could become a lame duck from day one.
Brazil’s creaking economy must be his number-one priority. Thanks to his own spendthrift policies, the central bank has pushed up real interest rates to vertigo-inducing heights. Government debt-to-GDP has risen by over ten percentage points during Lula’s current four-year term. Markets panicked when his surprise victory was announced (see chart 2): the real fell by 8%  against the dollar—its worst day in more than a quarter of a century—and São Paulo’s stock index closed down 14%. Investors are demanding that Lula appoint a heavyweight as finance minister, rather than a party cadre, and that he set out a credible plan for lower spending. It is worrying that his pre-election giveaways suggest he will not choose to do anything of the sort.
Lula beat the odds to win the presidency. But he will need a lot more luck—and much good judgment—if he is to make a success of his fourth and final term.
■

epub_46.title: Donald Trump’s tantrums are an opportunity for Spain
epub_46.text:
Donald Trump’s tantrums are an opportunity for Spain
The Americas
| European hedge
Donald Trump’s tantrums are an opportunity for Spain
Can it get on better with its former colonies?
Oct 29th 2026
Getting Latin American leaders into one room is a feat. Getting them to agree on anything is tougher still. Only one president from the region turned up to the Ibero-American summit, a biennial gathering of leaders from Spain, Portugal and Latin America, when it was held in Ecuador two years ago—and that was the host. There are hopes Spain will do better when it holds this year’s pow-wow, in Madrid, on November 4th and 5th. The organisers are aspiring to get as many as 18 heads of state, or their deputies, to attend.
The timing is propitious. Donald Trump increasingly treats Latin America as the United States’ backyard. Though a wave of ostensibly Trump-aligned presidents have taken office, the region remains keen to hedge against his unpredictability by diversifying trade. Links with China are important, but also problematic. “I’ve never seen more desire for Europe,” says a veteran Latin American diplomat.
Spain has ties to the region that neither of the world’s superpowers can replicate. More than 4m people who were born in Latin America now live in Spain, many having arrived in the past decade. Back in the 1980s and 1990s Spain’s transition to democracy was a model for some of its former colonies. Felipe González, prime minister from 1982 to 1996, became an adviser to governments in the region. In 1991 Spain and Mexico convened the first Ibero-American summit in Guadalajara, laying foundations for a 22-member community loosely inspired by the Commonwealth of once British-ruled countries.
Spain’s influence has since waned. Spanish companies remain important investors in the region. But they have stepped back even as Latin America has strengthened ties with China. Some diplomats complain that Spanish governments have grown less interested. The current prime minister, Pedro Sánchez—who has called a general election for November 29th—wants to improve things.
That will require a change in approach. Mr Sánchez rubs along best with governments of the left. Ties with right-wing leaders have been fraught. In 2024 Spain temporarily withdrew its ambassador from Buenos Aires after Javier Milei, Argentina’s president, insulted Mr Sánchez’s wife in a speech. Spain has yet to accept the ambassador sent to Madrid by Colombia’s new president. Lawmakers complain the emissary has said rude things about Mr Sánchez on social media.
Yet even a shared worldview has not guaranteed good relations. On paper Mr Sánchez and Claudia Sheinbaum, Mexico’s left-wing president, ought to get on like churros and chocolate. But Ms Sheinbaum’s predecessor and mentor, Andrés Manuel López Obrador, picked a quarrel with Spain over its colonial past and demanded an apology from its king for the conquest. Spain’s foreign ministry reacted defensively; the dispute worsened when Mexico did not invite the king to Ms Sheinbaum’s inauguration in 2024.
Ms Sheinbaum has proved more willing to separate historical grievances from present-day interests. She has good reasons for doing so, notes Rafael Ch of Signum Global Advisors, a consultancy. The United States is Mexico’s biggest trading partner, but Mr Trump’s erratic policymaking is loosening ties. With economic growth sluggish, Ms Sheinbaum has little to gain from permitting a diplomatic quarrel with Spain to drag on.
Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s interim president, is likely to attend the meet-up in Madrid. Ms Rodríguez governs with Mr Trump’s backing, so Latin Americans are unlikely to make a fuss about her showing up. But it would be controversial in Spain. Opponents have long accused the Spanish left of indulging Venezuela’s grim regime. It would be refreshing—and good for Spain’s image—if the summit were to call loudly for the country’s democratic transition to speed up.
Those who gather in Madrid will discuss AI, disaster preparedness and mutual recognition of educational qualifications such as degrees. That kind of stuff will seem low-key. But other regional organisations, such as the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States and the Organisation of American States, are at a low ebb. So perhaps the most important thing is getting together at all.

epub_47.title: Back in Venezuela, María Corina Machado may speed the return of democracy
epub_47.text:
Back in Venezuela, María Corina Machado may speed the return of democracy
The Americas
| Homecoming queen
Back in Venezuela, María Corina Machado may speed the return of democracy
She will push for elections to happen sooner than Donald Trump had in mind
Oct 29th 2026
It was, as is her style, a homecoming laden with symbolism. On October 25th the first images to be released of
María Corina Machado’s
return to Venezuela  showed the opposition leader surrounded by supporters next to the statue of the Divina Pastora. The shrine, in a church near the city of Barquisimeto, depicts the Virgin Mary as a shepherdess guiding her flock.
Her return after a ten-month exile took millions of Venezuelans—and possibly the country’s ruling regime—by surprise. For months the wildly popular politician (pictured) had been promising to come back “soon” to Venezuela. She had been there (albeit in hiding) until December, when she left the country to collect the Nobel peace prize. In recent months she had made several attempts to get back. On each occasion it seemed the regime foiled her plans. This time she crossed the land border from Colombia.
Her presence in Venezuela will complicate the unusual, cosy relationship the administration of Donald Trump has formed with the
disreputable regime of Delcy Rodríguez
. Ms Rodríguez, who has quietly dropped the “interim” from her presidential title in recent weeks, has been running the country since January 3rd, when special forces captured her then boss, Nicolás Maduro, and took him to face drug-trafficking charges in New York.
Mr Trump claimed not to know about Ms Machado’s return when he was asked about it. “She is a very nice woman,” he said on October 25th. “She gave me her Nobel prize, so how can I say anything else?” In January Ms Machado handed the medal, which she won for her campaign for democracy in Venezuela, to Mr Trump (who claimed to deserve it more). She said at the time she made the gesture in gratitude for his “decisive support of our cause”.
She has plenty of reason to doubt the extent of that support. Mr Trump’s praise for Ms Rodríguez—whom he calls “terrific”—has always been fulsome. But he has long been ambivalent towards Ms Machado, a former congresswoman from a once wealthy industrialist family who was persecuted by Mr Maduro. She has called for new elections in Venezuela, to be held by next July, and says she will stand as a candidate. This has not got Mr Trump’s backing. “I don’t think they’re ready [for elections] yet,” he said in September.
His focus instead has been on portraying the capture of Mr Maduro and its aftermath as an unmitigated success. His government in August secured majority control of 65bn barrels of the country’s oil, about a fifth of its proven reserves, in an agreement with Venezuela and a private oil company. “We took over Venezuela very successfully and they’ve sent me as a gift a boatload of a million barrels of oil,” he bragged at a campaign event in Texas, on October 27th. He later quipped that maybe Venezuela “will become a prosperous 51st state”. He often claims that Venezuelans are “dancing in the streets” in celebration of all he has achieved.
Mr Trump’s problem, and Ms Machado’s opportunity, is that none of this is true. Few Venezuelans view his propping up of Ms Rodríguez, or their own economic situation, as a success story. Mr Trump’s own popularity in Venezuela has slumped in recent months. “He got rid of Maduro, which is good, but it is basically the same shit here,” says Eduardo, a computer technician in Caracas, the capital.
America insists that it has a plan with Venezuela, and that it is on track. On October 26th an official at the State Department said the next stage of the “transition” is to replace the members of Venezuela’s Supreme Court by mid-December, followed by an overhaul of the electoral council. The idea is that Ms Rodríguez would then at some point declare the presidency “vacant”, triggering elections within six months. Perhaps that would be in late 2027, or 2028. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said after Ms Machado’s return that the Rodríguez regime would not be allowed to wait out the process until the Trump administration ends: “We have timelines that are agreed to, and so far, they’ve met every one.”
Will Ms Machado abide by the same timeline? Or will she try to accelerate it? On October 25th a caravan of supporters accompanied her in a triumphant return to Caracas. For a giddy few hours, Venezuelans really were dancing in the streets. And it was not to Mr Trump’s tune.

epub_49.title: Binyamin Netanyahu has not won, but nor has he lost
epub_49.text:
Binyamin Netanyahu has not won, but nor has he lost
Middle East & Africa
| You win some, you lose some
Binyamin Netanyahu has not won, but nor has he lost
Refusing to work with the Arab parties may be his opponents’ undoing
Oct 29th 2026
Binyamin netanyahu took to the stage in the early hours of October 28th knowing he had almost certainly lost his majority. And yet Mr Netanyahu and his Likud party supporters were jubilant. Likud lost some seats but it is still Israel’s largest party. The coalition was punished by the voters for what most Israelis perceive as the failures by Mr Netanyahu that led to the massacres of October 7th 2023 and for his coalition’s divisive policies. But the beating was not nearly as severe as most pollsters had predicted. More important, Likudniks reckon that even though the opposition has won an outright majority, it is incapable of forming a coalition to replace their own. They are probably right.
With over 90% of the vote counted Mr Netanyahu’s coalition had won 53 of the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament. The
final result
, still being tallied as The Economist went to press, is not expected to change much: the prime minister will not have the seats to form a new government. Israel’s opposition is divided into two blocs. The main one, consisting of four mostly Jewish parties, is expected to win 48 seats. The second, made up of predominantly Arab parties, is on track to win 19 seats, the most Israel’s Arab minority has ever won. Together, the two blocs could command a clear majority.
But of the four Jewish opposition parties, only one, the left-leaning Democrats, has explicitly said it would go into government with the Arab parties. Two larger opposition outfits are much more reluctant. Yashar, led by a former Israel Defence Forces chief, Gadi Eisenkot, and Yachad (Together), led by two former prime ministers, Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, have been evasive. Avigdor Lieberman, leader of Yisrael Beiteinu, a nationalist opposition party, has categorically ruled out relying even informally on the Arab parties.
For their part, the Arab parties are willing to co-operate. Under Mansour Abbas, Ra’am, a moderate Islamist group, has been eager to be part of the government since 2018. Mr Abbas reckons that is the best way to promote the interests of Israeli Arabs. The Joint List, which is a bigger electoral alliance of Arab, communist and Palestinian-nationalist parties, has been warier. Joining a coalition would mean taking joint responsibility for policies, such as security, which it opposes. But on October 10th Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List, said that the group would use “all the tools” at its disposal to replace the Netanyahu government and that it would “serve as a safety net” for a new coalition, even if it would not become a member of it.
Before the election Mr Eisenkot and other Jewish opposition leaders acknowledged in private that they would need the Arab parties’ seats. They touted the idea of a minority government that would rely on a confidence-and-supply deal with the Arab parties. But they made no public overtures.
Mr Netanyahu had spent the campaign accusing his opponents of planning to bring the Arabs into government. In an ai-generated video, Mr Eisenkot was portrayed astride a wooden Trojan horse, with Mr Abbas and Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats, lurking inside. Mr Golan pointed out that there was nothing wrong with co-operating politically with Arab Israelis. Mr Eisenkot and the other party leaders ducked the question.
In the election of 1992, the Arab parties supported Yitzhak Rabin, the Labour leader, blocking Likud’s path to power. They did not formally join Mr Rabin’s government but backed it on crucial votes and in return got increased funding for their communities. The then leader of Likud, Yitzhak Shamir, accepted defeat without question. But his successor, Mr Netanyahu, made delegitimising the Arab vote one of his core political aims.
In his first election as Likud leader in 1996, Mr Netanyahu ran with the slogan “Netanyahu: Good for the Jews”. In 2015 he released a video on election day warning his supporters that “the Arab voters are heading to the polling stations in droves” and urged them to do the same. Accusations that his opponents planned to sit in government alongside “terror-supporting” and “Muslim Brotherhood” Arab parliamentarians have been a constant in his campaigns, even though in 2021, after failing to form a coalition, he himself talked to Mr Abbas about joining one. His hard-right allies kiboshed those talks. Mr Abbas joined a short-lived (previous) coalition led by Mr Bennett and Mr Lapid instead.
Mr Netanyahu was at it again this time. “The right-wing bloc has an overwhelming majority in the Zionist public, the Jewish public,” he said on election day. “It is simply forbidden to risk Israel and form a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties that oppose our very existence.”
He and his coalition had been languishing in the polls ever since the attacks of October 7th. When at last they went to the country, they were widely expected to be drubbed and turfed out of office. That the coalition was not thoroughly trounced is partly because Mr Netanyahu stoked anti-Palestinian fears. This may not have boosted his own popularity, but it helped reduce support for his opponents. “I detest Netanyahu and his coalition,” says Shmuel Davidson, a software engineer from Tel Aviv. “But I can’t vote for an opposition which may co-operate with the Arab parties who want to kill me.”
Most of the Arab politicians condemned the attacks of October 7th, but some were tone-deaf. A member of the Knesset from Ra’am described Hamas as “partly a charity organisation”. Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of Balad, one of the parties in the Joint List, called the massacre “an important historic event, militarily, politically and strategically” from which others could learn. Such statements helped Mr Netanyahu stoke Jewish Israeli fears that their Arab neighbours, who mostly identify as Palestinian, are on the opposite side in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Desperate to see the back of the ruling coalition, Arabs turned out on October 27th  in the highest numbers in decades. And their party leaders had been reaching out to their Jewish counterparts. “The Arab representation should bring influence and partnership,” said Mr Abbas on election night. “We are ready and prepared to pave the way for ousting the Netanyahu government,” Mr Jabareen posted on social media the next day. “Change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership.”
Their Jewish counterparts have yet to respond. In speeches on election night, Messrs Eisenkot, Bennett and Lapid all spoke of trying to form “a Zionist government”, without mentioning the Arab parties and their impressive gains. Since then, they have been silent. One opposition Knesset member suggested that, when the new legislature is sworn in on November 10th, Jewish and Arab opposition parties could co-operate in electing a new speaker and take control of parliamentary business. If such a move were successful, it could perhaps lead to coalition talks. But a senior aide to an opposition leader poured cold water on such ideas, saying it was more likely some of the parties would seek a unity government with Mr Netanyahu, rather than with the Arabs.
So far, in the Jewish opposition bloc, only Mr Golan has suggested a different course. “We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he said the day after the election, calling for “a government that serves all Israeli citizens”.
But Mr Netanyahu seems confident he can bide his time while the opposition blunders. Even without a majority, he will stay on as caretaker prime minister; he still seems hopeful that Donald Trump might yet agree to join him in further military strikes on Iran after America’s midterm elections. Israel has a unique opportunity, he declared on election night, with “our partner, President Trump, to remove the Iranian threat once and for all”. Should Mr Trump decide to join another attack, or to let Israel launch one, Mr Netanyahu feels sure some of his foes would join a unity government under his leadership, or that he would be able to run down the clock on coalition talks and gamble on another election in early 2027.

epub_50.title: Saudi Arabia wants Iran to call off the Houthis and make a deal with America
epub_50.text:
Saudi Arabia wants Iran to call off the Houthis and make a deal with America
Middle East & Africa
| An awkward errand
Saudi Arabia wants Iran to call off the Houthis and make a deal with America
But a summit meant to pressure the regime achieved little
Oct 29th 2026
FOR months Iran’s allies have battered Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones. They have damaged its most important oil pipeline and killed at least 17 people at Riyadh’s airport, which remains largely out of service. It raised a few eyebrows, then, when Khalid bin Salman, the Saudi defence minister, flew to Tehran on October 26th for a visit meant to “encourage dialogue”. Grinning, the brother of the Saudi crown prince even posed for photos with Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s top security official.
The meeting was a surprise; even Saudi state media seemed unprepared. Both sides scrambled to spin it. Iranian officials saw a demonstration of their strength: a top Saudi royal arriving like a supplicant. One hardline MP said a “helpless” kingdom had to “beg” for mediation with the Houthis, the Iran-backed militia in Yemen that has done much of the damage.
Prince Khalid did not travel alone, though. He was joined in Tehran by the Pakistani army chief and the head of Turkish intelligence. Both countries are fellow members of the Mecca pact, a mutual-defence agreement signed in Saudi Arabia in August. The Saudis cast the summit as a show of deterrence, in which three big Muslim powers jointly delivered a warning to an Iran that stood alone.
For all the drama, the summit seemed to achieve little. The Saudis raised two immediate concerns. One is the Houthis. Iran has little incentive to rein them in, though. Indeed, there were more missile attacks on Riyadh after Prince Khalid’s visit.
The other is the threat of renewed war between America and Iran. Donald Trump has warned Gulf states that he is preparing another round of strikes after next week’s midterm elections. America is sending warships, air-defence batteries and other equipment to the region. A third aircraft-carrier is due to arrive in November.
Much of the world is frantically trying to prevent this. Delegations from Qatar and Pakistan, which negotiated an earlier deal to halt the war, have made several visits to Tehran this month. European diplomats are working the phones. Even Vladimir Putin seems to be getting in on the act. He held talks in Moscow this week with Iran’s president and Qatar’s emir.
Yet this flurry of diplomacy has not produced a deal that both Iran and America will accept. The former insists on a narrow agreement centred on the Strait of Hormuz. If America ends its blockade of Iranian ports, lifts sanctions and makes other economic concessions, the regime has pledged to reopen the waterway within a week. Gulf diplomats are haggling over the timetable: perhaps Iran would agree to four days, rather than seven.
That misses a bigger problem. Mr Trump is uninterested in such a deal, which would essentially be a return to the short-lived memorandum of understanding he signed in June. The president wants Iran to make immediate concessions on its nuclear programme. So far, Iran is unwilling; it refused even to discuss the nuclear issue during the four-party talks in Tehran.
Diplomats in the region say Saudi Arabia offered Iran a carrot and a stick. If it makes concessions that enable a deal with America, the kingdom and its neighbours are willing to discuss a broader regional-security pact. If Iran refuses, and resumes attacks on Gulf states, the Mecca-pact countries will be ready to respond.
The risk is that Iran saw neither as credible. It doubts that Saudi Arabia shares its view of regional security, which includes booting American troops from the Gulf. As for the stick, the Saudis are already struggling to beat back the Houthis, and its new allies are reluctant to join offensive strikes.
After decades of relying on America, Gulf states are now engaged in trying to defuse a regional crisis themselves. It is a welcome effort—but for now, the threat of war still looms.

epub_51.title: South Africa’s “white party” looks for more black votes
epub_51.text:
South Africa’s “white party” looks for more black votes
Middle East & Africa
| Gogo a-go-go
South Africa’s “white party” looks for more black votes
Local elections will highlight the ANC’s steep decline and the role of race in politics
Oct 29th 2026
AS PART OF her campaign to become mayor of Johannesburg, Helen Zille has snorkelled in a water-filled pothole. She has directed cars when power cuts turned off traffic lights. She has paddled down a flooded street. The candidate from the Democratic Alliance (DA), South Africa’s second-biggest party, has taken an old BMW “spinning”, a popular pursuit in the city’s black townships. The 75-year-old grandmother has stepped up to a turntable (pictured) and been dubbed “DJ Gogo”.
These were stunts with a purpose. Ahead of local elections on November 4th Ms Zille wants to highlight the decay of the commercial capital under a coalition led by the African National Congress (ANC). Polls suggest the once hegemonic party will have its worst showing in a nationwide election since the end of white rule in 1994. Meanwhile Ms Zille could soon be the first white mayor of post-apartheid Johannesburg. Such a result would underline the decline of the party of Nelson Mandela—and perhaps point to the beginnings of a less racialised politics.
The ANC has been losing support for 20 years. But it is heading for a new low. An average of opinion polls in the past six months has the ANC at 32%, the DA at 27%. Five years ago the ANC won 46% to the DA’s 22%. The DA’s own polling reckons it could become the largest party in most of South Africa’s eight largest cities.
Among the roughly 80% of the South African population that is black, the ANC remains the most popular party. It benefits from residual loyalty because of its role in ending apartheid, its patronage and because it genuinely improved the country during its early years in office. But South Africans are increasingly tired of its graft and failure to run basic services. Johannesburg, which sells itself as a “world-class African city”, is the most glaring example. Nearly half of the bulk water the city supplies is never paid for because it is stolen or leaks out of pipes. It spends more money than it raises in taxes and fees, yet it consistently fails to repair infrastructure. The cost of fixing its infrastructure backlog is roughly 25 times its capital budget.
“This is our last chance to save Johannesburg,” argues Ms Zille. Based on her experience running Cape Town from 2006 to 2009, she pledges to get a grip on the finances, appoint leaders to city agencies on merit and root out corruption.
Whether she gets the chance will depend on her ability to form a coalition. The DA usually benefits from “differential turnout”: its core base among whites and other minorities is more likely to vote than black voters are. But since black Joburgers make up around three-quarters of the city, she will need enough of their votes, too.
Will she get them? Most former ANC supporters either do not vote or opt for an opposition party other than the DA. UmKhonto we Sizwe (MK), led by Jacob Zuma, a former president, targets Zulus, the largest ethnic group. The Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) is another black-nationalist party. Other urban voters are attracted by ActionSA, whose appeal is based partly on its ability to exploit concerns about illegal immigration. “A country without order is headed for disaster,” says Sanele Bhagathi, a voter from Johannesburg.
Many black South Africans are DA-curious but have resisted it because, fairly or unfairly, the DA’s brand is that of a “white party”. Sceptics see Cape Town, which is well run but has bleak mostly non-white outskirts, as a reason for caution. “I don’t believe the party cares enough about [that inequality], and they should,” says Thabo Nthuli, another voter in Johannesburg.
Yet governing in coalition with the ANC at a national level has helped detoxify the DA’s image and reaffirmed its reputation for competence. It is hard for opponents to suggest that the likes of Ms Zille want to bring back apartheid—a trope of the ANC—when as a journalist under white rule she exposed the regime’s abuses.
For many black voters Cape Town is a model of good governance. “I never used to have these problems or these failures,” says Mandisa Maphisa, who moved to Johannesburg from there. “I’ll be voting for the DA for effective service delivery that the party itself has proven is possible.”
The DA thinks it will double its share of the black vote, from around 4.5% to 9% nationally, meaning it could be the third-most popular party among black South Africans. Ms Zille will probably win a higher share, though she may not meet her target of 40% of the overall vote.
The shift away from the ANC suggests that politics is beginning to catch up with society. Most South Africans say they do not mind the race of their neighbour, their sons- or daughters-in-law or the president. In a survey published in April, 70% agreed that politicians use race and colonialism as an excuse for their own failures.
An increasingly diverse middle class shapes politics, too. In 2012 black households made up 29% of those with at least 75,000 rand ($4,500) in monthly income, notes the Liberty Institute, a research group at the University of Cape Town. By 2024 they had caught up with whites (41%). The share of multiracial marriages increased from 1% to 11% between 2001 and 2022. More South Africans socialise with people of other races than in the 2000s.
There is no guarantee that Ms Zille will end up as mayor. But if she can win over enough black voters to form a coalition in Johannesburg, that will draw “a line in the sand”, says William Gumede, an academic. “To get the South Africa we want, we need more blacks to cross the racial barrier.”

epub_52.title: Senegal tries to teach more children in their first language
epub_52.text:
Senegal tries to teach more children in their first language
Middle East & Africa
| Going local
Senegal tries to teach more children in their first language
The government hopes that will make them learn more
Oct 29th 2026
When Senegal’s government wanted to find out in which languages to teach children, it sent officials into schools to listen to them playing. In school playgrounds across the country, the surveyors found children speaking in Wolof and Pulaar, joking in Safi, and throwing in the occasional French word.
The mapping exercise is part of an initiative to foster teaching in Senegalese languages that began in 2021. Most schools in Senegal teach in French, the country’s only official language. But most children do not understand or speak it well. By starting to teach young children in local languages before transitioning to others, Senegal hopes that they will learn more.
At the moment, many children who attend French-speaking schools can barely understand their lessons. In Dakar, the capital, an estimated 55% of children do not speak French. In rural areas such as Fatick, in the south of the country, that share rises to 87%. The situation mirrors the rest of the continent. Most African schools teach in international languages, but only 10-15% of Africans are thought to be fluent in one.
They usually speak several of Africa’s 1,500-3,000 indigenous languages. But because most children receive no formal instruction in their first language, it often ends up insufficiently developed to form the basis for learning a new one required at school. As a result, many struggle to study properly in any language at all. Nhlanhla Mpofu, a researcher at the University of Notre Dame Australia, says that around 80% of nine- and ten-year-old children in a South African class she studied could read a sentence perfectly, but did not understand what it meant.
Local-language instruction seems to help. One study in South Africa in 2024 found that children who focused on learning to read in their home language also did better in an international one, whereas weaker students who focused on the international language read less well in their home language. In Senegal, the latest effort also appears to have improved reading scores. Yet previous local-language teaching programmes funded by the World Bank and USAID faltered there, in part because parents were unhappy that textbooks were poorly made, compared with those for classes taught in French.
One important decision is which local language to teach in, given how many different ones are spoken across Africa. Senegal, for example, has six constitutionally recognised languages in addition to the official French, but there are at least 30 in total. Language statistics are old and incomplete, says Fiona McLaughlin of the University of Florida, and preferring one language to others can be politically tricky. She estimates that Wolof is the first language for around 40% of Senegalese and that 90% speak it. But its spread and status as a lingua franca in Dakar have raised fears of “Wolofisation”, especially in the Christian south, where many associate the language with Islam.
To assuage such concerns, officials in Senegal make decisions about which language to recommend on a school-by-school basis. Schools are flexible, says Mamadou Ly, who runs Associates in Research and Education for Development, one of the organisations helping to implement the programme. For example, children in villages that predominantly speak Soninke in a majority-Pulaar region will learn in Soninke. In one case, a school started out teaching Wolof, but after two years some parents wanted their children to speak Pulaar. The school split the class so that both could be taught.
Perhaps the biggest challenge is reassuring parents that local-language instruction will not crowd out teaching in English, French or Portuguese. The languages of former colonial powers still dominate law, politics and business, making them essential for success. Senegal uses a gradual transition. Children start out learning in their chosen national language 80% of the time and in French 20% of the time. By age 12, the ratio reverses. “Children should be anchored in their culture, but should also be open to the world,” says Mr Ly.

epub_54.title: Serbia’s students found a new way to topple a strongman
epub_54.text:
Serbia’s students found a new way to topple a strongman
Europe
| Here comes everyone
Serbia’s students found a new way to topple a strongman
Like Viktor Orban, Aleksandar Vucic fell to an anti-corruption movement
Oct 29th 2026
For 18 months Pioneers’ Park in central Belgrade has been a political hotspot. In early 2025 it was taken over by protesting students. Then forces loyal to Aleksandar Vucic, the country’s leader, fenced it off and set up an encampment. On October 25th, the day of Serbia’s general election, a posse of black-clad men assembled; they seemed to be pro-government thugs. But they vanished after Mr Vucic unexpectedly announced that he had lost. By the next day the fences were down and the tents destroyed, as citizens symbolically reclaimed the park.
Taking back the country’s other institutions will be harder. Mr Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) ruled for 14 years, dominating the courts, the media and the economy. The scale of his defeat was unexpected. Opinion polls had shown the SNS running neck-and-neck with the opposition Student List, a mostly leaderless protest movement. Instead the SNS took just 39%. The students won 53%, giving them 141 MPs in the 250-seat parliament. They will try to restore the rule of law to the state that Mr Vucic captured.
Like Hungary’s Viktor Orban, who was defeated by a broad popular movement in April, Mr Vucic was felled by outrage at corruption. Membership in the SNS had become a requirement for career advancement in state-linked institutions and big businesses, a communist-style practice that led to cynicism and resentment. Mass demonstrations began in 2021 in protest against a proposed lithium mine. In 2024 the collapse of a railway-station canopy that killed 16 people was blamed on shady contractors; Serbs came to feel that government corruption had left no one safe. That sparked the student movement, which started in universities, staged huge rallies throughout the country, and then met in faculty-based “plenums” to select candidates for the elections.
How the Student List will govern is unusually unclear. None of its MPs has a political background; they are members of civil society selected for their expertise. Serbs wonder whether power will lie with the new ministers, or with the students who picked them. One possible prime minister is Dejan Soskic, a former head of Serbia’s national bank and now a Student List deputy. Once installed, he says, the government “will operate as any other”. The MPs have signed the movement’s manifesto, guaranteeing that the students will have “a very significant impact”.
That manifesto, though, is full of promises to “spend the public funding responsibly” but light on detail. The students aimed to attract every voter tired of the SNS, regardless of political leanings. The movement embraces everyone from hard-core nationalists to easy-going liberals. The final election rally, which drew 150,000 people, featured headscarf-wearing Bosniak Muslims, Orthodox flags portraying Jesus and cardboard cutouts of Novak Djokovic, the Serbian tennis champion.
In the long run the movement could break up into left, centre and right factions. On foreign policy, its programme suggests little difference from that of Mr Vucic. It opposes the independence of Kosovo and eschews sanctions on Russia. Mr Soskic is ambiguous about whether Serbia will continue to sell arms to Ukraine: the students “do not support the idea of having economic benefits from disasters”. But Serbia’s effort to join the European Union could benefit if its government makes progress on the rule of law.
Mr Vucic had resigned as president, for which he was ineligible to run again, in order to run for prime minister. Some had feared he might resort to fraud or violence rather than give up power. Fraud there was, but not enough to affect the outcome. Ana Brnabic, an SNS member who took over as acting president when Mr Vucic stepped down, says that as the results came in and it became clear there was no path to victory, “he said ‘There is no reason not to announce this…We lost, and that is it’.”
The SNS is primarily a patronage machine, handing out jobs, public contracts and money. Having lost that power, it may not prosper in opposition, or even survive. Efforts to purge its apparatchiks have begun. This week supporters of the Student List angrily confronted the owner of a pro-Vucic newspaper, and demanded the resignations of editors at the public broadcaster, which had refused to report on the student protests. Ms Brnabic calls such demands “revolutionary terror”. An openly gay woman of partly Croatian descent, she says that since the election she has received threatening messages calling her a “Croatian whore” and a “dead lesbian”.
Yet the SNS still has resources. It is deeply entrenched in the organs of the state. Mob bosses are widely reported to be collaborating with Serbia’s security services and with senior politicians. The Student List campaigned under the slogan “Serbia or the Mafia”, but breaking the nexus between the state and organised crime is dangerous. One former prime minister who tried it, Zoran Djindjic, was assassinated in 2003 for his pains.
In one way Mr Vucic’s defeat differs from Mr Orban’s. Hungary’s opposition was headed by Peter Magyar, a charismatic social-media front man with an indefatigable appetite for campaigning. Serbia’s is amorphous and decentralised. That has been a strength, but could become a weakness in office. Mr Vucic has predicted that the students will collapse, and that he will be back in power in two years. Perhaps. But they have shown other countries a new way to beat a strongman.

epub_55.title: Poland is growing less religious, but not less right-wing
epub_55.text:
Poland is growing less religious, but not less right-wing
Europe
| Faith no more
Poland is growing less religious, but not less right-wing
As belief in Catholicism declines, secular far-right parties are rising
Oct 29th 2026
For most of the day, Gabriela’s classroom in Wroclaw, a city in south-western Poland, is a hive of activity. But on Thursdays, as religion class starts, most of the kids trickle away. Religion lessons are optional and limited to one hour a week, but even that is sometimes too much for 12-year-old Gabriela, who says she envies the kids who get to opt out. Of the 18 pupils in her class, only three take religion.
Poland is one of Europe’s most religious countries, with 92% of adults identifying as Catholic. But religiosity is declining. The share of adults who do not practise at all has doubled in under a decade, to 22%. Sunday Mass attendance has fallen from 45% in 2005 to below 30%. Church weddings, baptisms and priest numbers have dropped, and the church has been forced to look abroad for recruits. At a seminary in Kielce, in southern Poland, nearly a third of the trainee priests are from Africa.
The exodus is especially acute among the young. From the 1990s, when Poland scrapped communism, until the early 2010s the share of secondary-schoolers in their final year who took religion courses hovered around 90%. By last year it had dipped to 35% (see chart). The share who are non-believers is 24%, four times the figure for adults. Youngsters everywhere tend to be less religious than their parents, but in Poland the generation gap is unusually wide. “Secularisation here is happening faster than anywhere else,” says Andrzej Kobylinski, an academic and priest.
One factor is economic growth, which tends to boost secularism. Poland’s record on that front is extraordinary: GDP per head, adjusted for purchasing power, has quadrupled in two decades, propelling the country to about the same real income level as Spain. Meanwhile, a rash of clerical sexual-abuse scandals in the late 2010s tarnished the church’s reputation.
Another element was an informal alliance between church leaders and the right-wing populist Law and Justice (PiS) party, which governed from 2015-23. That alienated many youngsters, and women of all ages: hundreds of thousands protested in 2020 after the constitutional court, dominated by PiS appointees, imposed an almost total ban on abortion. Covid left a mark, too. Attendance at mass plummeted during the lockdowns, and has not recovered. Support for abortion and same-sex marriage has risen in the past decade.
But a more liberal society has not always made for liberal policies. Donald Tusk, the prime minister, heads a government spanning centrists, progressives, leftists and conservatives. During his campaign in 2023 he pledged to ease the abortion ban, but splits in his coalition have prevented that. A ruling by the European Union’s top court has forced Poland to accept gay marriages conducted abroad, but the country’s own laws have no provision even for same-sex civil unions. In July the president, a PiS ally, vetoed legislation that would have granted some rights to same-sex partners.
Rather than weakening the conservative opposition, secularisation is reshaping it. The Konfederacja (KWiN) party is challenging PiS as Poland’s main opposition. Although many of its politicians are Catholic hardliners, KWiN’s agenda pays little attention to the church. It focuses mainly on Euroscepticism, manosphere vibes, low taxes and stopping migration.
“Secularisation is not a threat to the right,” says Krzysztof Bosak, KWiN’s co-leader. Religion takes up “a very small fraction of our overall political message”. That may explain the party’s appeal among the young and religiously indifferent. Polls suggest it enjoys more support from the young than any other party.
Meanwhile PiS has seen its support fall to under 20%. In hopes of winning back voters from KWiN and the Confederation of the Polish Crown, an even more extreme (and often antisemitic) far-right group, PiS this year picked a nationalist Catholic as its candidate for prime minister. But that alienated the party’s moderates. In July a group of 40 MPs headed by Mateusz Morawiecki, a former prime minister, left PiS to form a new centre-right grouping, Development Plus.
In the past, says Aleks Szczerbiak of the University of Sussex, the conservative recipe for success in Poland was to be “left-wing on economic issues, right-wing on moral and cultural issues, and very religious”. That formula has expired, he says. Now the right’s binding force is no longer faith but fear—whether of immigrants, woke culture or the EU. Mr Kobylinski says this mirrors developments elsewhere in Europe, pointing to the secular, populist-right Alternative for Germany.
The good news for Mr Tusk is that with less than a year before a general election, his ruling Civic Coalition (KO) is in first place in the polls. The bad news for him is that KO and its allies lack the votes to form a government. For now, PiS and the far right together have a big enough share to form a majority. The right is deeply divided; in the last campaign KWiN vowed never to rule with PiS. But should they overcome their differences and take office, it would be as a more secular yet more extreme right-wing force than ever.

epub_56.title: Europe’s biggest steelworks may be nearing its end
epub_56.text:
Europe’s biggest steelworks may be nearing its end
Europe
| Iron or lungs
Europe’s biggest steelworks may be nearing its end
A court will soon decide whether Italy’s polluting Taranto plant must close
Oct 29th 2026
In the 1970s the steelworks at Taranto, on Italy’s southern coast, were among Europe’s largest, with 20,000 workers churning out millions of tonnes of steel a year. Today the plant is down to 8,000 employees, and this month it halted production. In July a court in Milan ordered it shut down by October 25th to install pollution controls. The owners appealed, and the government of Giorgia Meloni, Italy’s prime minister, allowed it to keep its furnaces warm so that production could resume. This week Italy’s highest court will decide whether they must be turned off, which could spell the plant’s end.
The steelworks’ chimneys tower over the city, spewing out toxins. In the nearby district of Tamburi residents sweep red dust from their balconies every day. Studies have documented elevated rates of cancer and respiratory disease, as well as reduced cognitive performance among children. One study found over 1,000 excess deaths between 2011-19 near the plant; another found deaths from lung cancer were 30% above the regional average.
Grazia Parisi, a local paediatrician, says she sees growing numbers of children with respiratory illnesses and conjunctivitis. Her patients include children with leukaemia and brain tumours. When children get a cough, mothers fear the worst. “We are afraid to breathe, eat or let our children play in the fields,” says Dr Parisi.
Among those suing the plant is Aurelio Rebuzzi, whose son Alessandro suffered from cystic fibrosis. He died at 16. In a church next to the plant, under a mosaic of Christ pointing at a steel factory, Mr Rebuzzi recalls doctors urging him to take his son away. “But Alessandro refused, saying ‘It’s not me that should leave my city that I love, but those who came and polluted it.’”
The government fears a shutdown would hurt Italian manufacturers and devastate Taranto’s economy. The plant was owned by the state when it opened in 1964. It was privatised in 1995, but has struggled to cope with international competition and with court penalties for pollution. The state has intervened repeatedly to indemnify the plant and bail it out.
In mid-October workers blocked roads to protest against the shutdown. Oronzo Spagnulo, a union organiser who has worked there for 26 years, said the government should make steelmaking cleaner while preserving jobs. His father, who also worked at the plant, died of brain cancer. The workers struggle to balance concern for their livelihoods with their health. Angelo Bicchieri, a safety officer, says residents who do not work at the factory see the workers as complicit: “They hate us.”
Ecco, an environmental think-tank, says the plant could switch from coal to natural gas and then green hydrogen at a cost of about €11bn ($12bn). But the workforce would shrink to 3,200. The government says European green-deal funds are available, and it hopes to find new private owners to fund the rest. But the shutdown order makes the plant less attractive.
Some residents reject even the clean-steel idea. They would prefer the region to stop making steel and shift to agriculture and tourism. Europe’s steel output has shrunk by one-third over the past two decades. If Taranto’s steelworks were to follow the trend, it might be no bad thing.

epub_57.title: Another deadly train crash puts Spanish infrastructure in question
epub_57.text:
Another deadly train crash puts Spanish infrastructure in question
Europe
| Spanish railways
Another deadly train crash puts Spanish infrastructure in question
It is the second collision on the same line this year
Oct 29th 2026
For the second time this year crushed train carriages lie on their sides in the Spanish countryside. On the morning of October 28th a high-speed train operated by Renfe, the state rail company, ploughed into a stationary train south of Toledo. At least 68 people died, and 58 were seriously injured. Survivors described horrific carnage in the first carriage of the Renfe train and the rear three of the stationary one, operated by Iryo, an Italian-controlled competitor.
In January, in a similar tragedy on the same line, 46 people were killed when an Iryo train derailed and was hit by one from Renfe. Until then Spain’s high-speed network, the world’s longest after China’s, was a source of national pride. Now Spaniards are in shock. “It’s not acceptable in a country like Spain” to suffer two serious rail accidents in a year, said Pedro Sánchez, the Socialist prime minister, at the scene. “The whole of Spain is grieving.”
This week’s accident happened after the continuous automatic train-control system, which controls signalling on the line, stopped working. Trains were halted. But in a decision that Oscar Puente, the transport minister, called “inexplicable”, a traffic controller ordered the Renfe train to resume its journey, with fatal consequences 17 minutes later.
“Spain has a right to know what’s happening with its infrastructure,” said Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative opposition. Mr Sánchez promised an investigation. But they tend to be slow and inconclusive in Spain. A police report blamed the January crash on a defective track repair but that has yet to be confirmed.
Liberalisation of the network in 2021 has led to a big increase in traffic. The government’s critics say that spending on maintenance has not kept pace. And some say both Renfe and Adif, the state rail-infrastructure company, have been stuffed with political appointees. A general election is due on November 29th; most of the candidates have suspended campaigning during three days of official mourning. Soon enough, Spaniards will give their verdict on whom they blame.
