epub_58.title: The Kremlin is shutting down Russia’s last free newspaper
epub_58.text:
The Kremlin is shutting down Russia’s last free newspaper
Europe
| Final edition
The Kremlin is shutting down Russia’s last free newspaper
Novaya Gazeta is closing after being placed on a state enemies list
Oct 29th 2026
A large modernist building in the heart of Moscow, a former printing press, with a modest nameplate: Novaya Gazeta. Journalists packing up books, belongings, memories. The rustle of cardboard and screech of packing tape. Boxes piled in the newsroom, under a street sign: “Politkovskaya Square”, named after Anna Politkovskaya, a renowned reporter for the newspaper, killed 20 years ago this month.
A young staff member sits down next to others taking a break, just to spend a little more time with colleagues. A trolley rolls down the corridor, carrying photographic prints. “It’s as if my whole life has gone by,” says the newspaper’s accountant. A crestfallen camerawoman records the final days of the last liberal media outlet in Russia.
Dmitry Muratov (pictured), Novaya Gazeta’s publisher and a Nobel peace-prize laureate, was on his way to Paris on October 19th to commemorate Politkovskaya’s murder when he learned the paper was being evicted from the building it had occupied for three decades. Its financial channels would be blocked, thanks to being branded a “foreign agent”. Next day he learned that Sergei Sokolov, the editor-in-chief, had been detained and questioned.
On October 26th Mr Muratov and Mr Sokolov gathered the paper’s remaining staff in the basement of the building next door, telling them to leave their phones outside. The previous night someone had broken into the newspaper’s offices, so it was unsafe to talk there. It was a sign of escalation, Mr Muratov explained. They might be declared an extremist organisation and their “members” arrested. The staff agreed it was time to close down the newspaper launched in 1993, the year Russia adopted its post-Soviet constitution. “We haven’t died, they’ve killed us—along with the constitution,” says Mr Muratov. “You can only laugh at Article 29 of the constitution: ‘Censorship is prohibited’.”
The closure of an independent anti-war newspaper in a country run by a militaristic dictatorship was hardly a surprise. What was astonishing was that it managed to carry on for nearly five years after Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine and isolated Russia from the West. Its licence had been revoked and its website blocked, but it continued reporting, finding ever more ingenious ways to reach readers.
Novaya Gazeta's journalists had been exposing the state’s violence against its own people since the war in Chechnya in the late 1990s, which secured Mr Putin’s grip on power. Six of its journalists had been killed, including Politkovskaya. “I have it in for Putin,” she wrote in 2004, “because of his cynicism...because of endless war…because of lies.” Russia was heading towards fascism, she warned.
On October 7th 2006, Mr Putin’s birthday, she was gunned down entering her apartment block. War was bound to follow sooner or later, says Mr Muratov: “When people are treated like dust and institutions are destroyed, violence inevitably spills beyond our borders.”
It was Novaya Gazeta that revealed that the regular Russian army, not rogue separatists, were fighting in Donbas in 2014. The paper was first to report that the Wagner mercenary group was controlled by Evgeny Prigozhin, who later led a mutiny against Mr Putin and died soon after in a plane crash. In 2018 Prighozhin had funeral wreaths and severed rams’ heads sent to the newspaper’s offices.
The day after Mr Putin ordered the invasion of Ukraine, Novaya Gazeta came out in both Russian and Ukrainian with the headline “Russia. Bombs. Ukraine.” Days later, after the Kremlin criminalised the word “war” and imposed de facto military censorship, the newspaper put out an edition with the headline “No Words” on the front page, followed by blank sheets of paper. When distributors stopped delivering it to newsstands, readers came to its newsroom and bought up the entire run.
After the invasion, two-thirds of the newspaper’s editorial staff moved to Latvia and launched Novaya Gazeta Europe. Mr Muratov and about 30 others decided to stay in Moscow. Unable to cover the war in Ukraine, they reported on its consequences in Russia: political prisoners, economic deterioration, psychological trauma and censorship. Some young journalists joined up. “Give me a job,” said one young woman when she applied. “Any subject, anything—I just need a place where I can say out loud that I’m against it.”
The newspaper provided comfort and dignity to those who opposed the war but did not want to leave Russia. Ordinary Muscovites went there in order not to feel alone. “It was a place where you could feel as though you were in a normal world, one where criminals are not hailed as heroes,” one reporter says. But even as Mr Putin escalates his attacks on Ukrainian cities, he is demolishing the few remaining free public spaces inside Russia.
Novaya Gazeta “was our city”, says Mr Muratov. “They’ve destroyed this city, and we’re leaving. But we are not leaving our work.” He will donate many of the newspaper’s artefacts to its readers, or “accomplices”, as he calls them. On October 29th, the day of remembrance of the victims of Stalinist repression, the journalists began reading out a long list of current political prisoners. A stone from Solovetsky island, the site of one of the first gulag camps, has been placed in “Anna’s garden”, a patch of green in front of the building which they have planted in Politkovskaya’s memory.

epub_59.title: Europe is gearing up for a future war Russia is already waging
epub_59.text:
Europe is gearing up for a future war Russia is already waging
Europe
| Charlemagne
Europe is gearing up for a future war Russia is already waging
Living in a phoney peace
Oct 29th 2026
For eight months after France and Britain formally declared war on Germany in September 1939, remarkably little happened. The period became known as the “phoney war”: a curious interlude during which western Europeans purported to be fighting while in fact living at peace. (Not for long, alas.) Today Europe faces the inverse predicament. In theory no part of the continent west of Ukraine is at war with Russia. But peace ain’t what it used to be. Month after month Kremlin-paid stooges harass European airports with drones, sabotage railway lines, torch shopping centres, threaten defence-company executives, hack computer systems and spread morale-sapping disinformation on social networks. None of this amounts to conventional warfare—but neither does it feel like not-warfare. Call it the phoney peace. Russia is keeping Europe permanently off-balance, displaying too much belligerence to ignore, yet not enough to trigger direct retaliation.
War and peace, to borrow a Russian phrase, used to be mutually exclusive. Today in Europe they exist concurrently. This poses a dilemma: how much should Europe worry about threats of future invasion, and how much about the current reality of aggression? On one hand, the continent is gearing up for an old-fashioned war against Russia of the sort Leo Tolstoy might recognise, involving artillery and troop movements (and missiles and drones, these days). On the other, it is already embroiled in a different sort of conflict, one fought with sabotage and propaganda. The danger is that Europe fixates on the hard war Russia might wage tomorrow—the clear-cut one that generals have spent their careers preparing for—while neglecting the murkier one already in full swing.
For now, much of Europe’s focus is on the tanks-crossing-borders threat. That is unsurprising: spooks from various countries think Russia might try to launch an invasion of NATO territory by 2030. Military materiel is thus being ordered, soldiers trained and battalions positioned accordingly. Defence budgets have soared to meet the challenge. Before 2022 most NATO countries fell short of the target of spending 2% of GDP on defence. Now they are (mostly) on track to meet a revised target of 3.5%.
Arguments rage over how these new billions should be spent. Should European countries keep buying American weapons, or pay more to develop their own? Are tanks obsolete? Such trade-offs are best left to those who know one end of a howitzer from the other. Some investments would help fend off both conventional and unconventional threats. Take drones, the break-out weapons of both the Ukraine war and Russia’s low-grade attacks on other parts of Europe. Learning to deal with them will deliver rich dividends both on future battlefields and in today’s murkier situation, when drone incursions have become routine.
Debates over what kit to buy risk obscuring a broader question: what is the right split between spending on defence versus on security more broadly? Much of that 3.5%-of-GDP splurge has been conceived around the risk of a war of territorial conquest that seems foolhardy even for the mercurial Vladimir Putin. Russia has spent five years trying to win a three-day war against its neighbour; taking on NATO would be a curious choice of encore.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin is already waging a war of sorts on Europe. For what else to call the constant stream of sabotage and provocation? Researchers at the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism, a Dutch outfit, have documented over 180 such incidents linked to Russia since 2022. Some amount to little more than souped-up vandalism, carried out by petty criminals hired over the internet for a few hundred euros. Others are so reckless that casualties seem inevitable sooner or later. In 2024 incendiary devices planted in parcels passing through European logistics hubs threatened to bring down cargo aircraft. In August an explosives-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig airport in Germany.
Europeans are hardly oblivious to the need to fight off so-called “grey-zone” warfare. Alongside the pledge to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence, NATO members committed to devote 1.5% to broader security needs, including protecting critical infrastructure, improving civil resilience and so on. But the latter target is loosely defined, and mainly encompasses existing spending. Nor is money the only obstacle. Territorial defence is expensive, but it is familiar territory for military types, albeit fuzzier now that drones have muddied the waters between conventional and unconventional fighting. Protecting Europe against sabotage and dirty tricks—both deterring attacks and minimising their impact—is a messier business. It often requires police forces, local authorities and private companies to work together. Nordic countries have long taken such matters seriously. In Germany they are now part of the public debate. Others need to catch up.
The lesson is not that spending on security—the stuff needed to counter low-level aggression—should come at the expense of territorial defence. On the contrary: it is precisely because NATO’s hard-power deterrence is so credible that Russia has resorted to unconventional warfare. Europe needs to get better at preventing such attacks, and at minimising the damage if they succeed. But how to push back against Russia—which often denies being behind attacks—without entailing dangerous escalation?
There is one easy way for Europeans to show the Kremlin that its campaign of intimidation is futile. Much of the Russian mischief is ultimately intended to undermine European support for Ukraine. In November European leaders will have to agree a new aid package to keep Ukraine solvent while it fends off its invader. A generous offer would send a strong message: Russian sabotage will not cause Europe to waver in its support. The current peace, phoney as it is, can be sustained only with steadfast resolve.

epub_61.title: Britain’s defensive budget did little to tackle deeper problems
epub_61.text:
Britain’s defensive budget did little to tackle deeper problems
Britain
| Playing it safe
Britain’s defensive budget did little to tackle deeper problems
The government hopes to win voters over with small treats now and the promise of reform later
Oct 29th 2026
When Andy Burnham entered office in July, the football-mad prime minister promised to go on the attack. His government would oversee “the biggest changes in the last 40 years”. Britons fed up with the status quo would “start to believe again”. That ambition calls for a striker at the Treasury, a game-changing chancellor. Unfortunately John Healey’s first budget, on October 28th, was all defence. It dealt with the immediate worries: modest tax rises shored up the public finances, and even more modest handouts eased the cost of living. But the budget left the big problems, whether on reforming Britain’s broken tax system or finding the money for its spending ambitions, untouched.
To be fair, Mr Healey was playing on a boggy pitch. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), a fiscal watchdog, cut its 2027 growth forecast from 1.6% to 1%, blaming the energy crisis caused by war in the Middle East. The conflict pushed estimated inflation for 2027 from 2% to 3.4%. Borrowing costs will be £12bn ($16bn) a year higher on average in the medium term. By 2031-32 debt-interest spending will consume 4.2% of GDP (£160bn a year), more than double the pre-pandemic level.
The chancellor’s game plan was to show “fiscal discipline” and give “Britain some breathing space on the cost of living”. On both counts, Mr Healey achieved short-term success but set himself up for long-term failure. The government is on track to meet its fiscal rules, with debt coming down and day-to-day spending covered by tax revenues by 2029-30. The deficit is forecast to fall by half, from 4.2% this year to 2.1% in 2029-30. If Mr Healey pulls this off, he will be doing much better than the French or the Americans.
Mr Healey chose to shrink his margin against the fiscal rules, to £15bn from £24bn in March. As the rules only bind in 2029-30, he snuck in higher spending early on (see chart 1). Holding the margin at even that level then required a medley of small, fiddly tax tweaks. Taxes on savings and property income will go up by two percentage points, raising £1bn a year in steady state. A time-limited surcharge on bank profits will raise £1.5bn. Gamblers and large operators of private-hire cars will also have to cough up. All these changes made the system messier, but none poses existential challenges to Britain’s competitiveness.
Although it is welcome that Mr Healey did not degrade the public finances further, he should not be mistaken as a paragon of fiscal responsibility. Debt is expected to be 96.7% of GDP in 2029-30, up from 95.5% now. If the government cannot stabilise debt even outside a crisis like the covid-19 pandemic, it will have less firepower when the next one hits.
Worse, few believe Labour will stick to its spending plans. Mr Healey delighted in setting a target to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030. (He could hardly have done otherwise, having resigned as defence secretary under Sir Keir Starmer over a refusal to set such a target.) He was hazy on how to pay for this important move, punting the decision to next year’s spending review. The OBR reckons that, under current plans, most departments face real-terms cuts of 2.6% a year in the last three years of the forecast. The government is unlikely to get that past its backbenchers—and Mr Burnham himself wants more money for priorities such as a National Care Service.
The story on the cost of living is similar. The budget continued Mr Burnham’s strategy of giving the electorate cheap goodies, like a mascot lobbing sweets into the stands at half-time. Most households will receive £100 to help with their heating bills. An energy tax-cut will be extended until July, with taxes on fuel also frozen until then. But although the public might temporarily enjoy a sugar rush, these measures will not disguise the fact that this is a grim period for living standards.
The OBR thinks that household disposable income will fall in real terms this year, and grow weakly thereafter (see chart 2). By the end of the decade it will be only 1% higher than before the pandemic. Ultimately it is economic growth, not handouts, that will improve living standards. The Prosperity Alliance, a pro-growth lobby stuffed with technocrats, calculates that if growth had continued along pre-2008 trends the median household would be £16,000 a year better off.
Yet the budget did little to improve the prospects for growth. There were some good measures, like a plan for building data centres more quickly and a greater focus on making cheap bills the
foremost priority of energy policy
. The devolution of tax-raising powers to local areas should also incentivise local politicians to push for growth. But Mr Healey could have gone much further. Britain’s sclerotic planning system, choc-a-bloc with veto points, remains mostly intact. The country’s sky-high visa fees put off the world’s brightest from joining British companies. Britons might have to wait until December to find out more about the government’s plans to move people from welfare to work.
The biggest disappointment was Mr Healey’s failure to reform Britain’s tax system, which disincentivises growth at every turn. He left stamp duty on home sales, which stops people moving to better jobs, untouched. He failed to remove the high marginal tax rates (like 62% for those earning between £100,000 and £125,140 a year) which stop people from working longer hours. If anything, the chancellor made the system more complicated. Pensioners on £13,000 a year now face a 53% marginal tax rate if they want to make a bit of money on the side. More small businesses will be exempt from commercial-property taxes, but adult gaming centres and vape shops are exempt from the exemption.
Blame for a lacklustre budget should ultimately be laid at the foot of the team captain, the prime minister. Mr Burnham hopes to win voters over with small treats now and the promise of radical reform later. That misunderstands how governing works. The time for big moves is early, while a government still has authority and years to let its policies pay off before an election. Mr Healey mounted a successful defence. But only goals win games.

epub_62.title: Britain’s energy system gets half an overhaul
epub_62.text:
Britain’s energy system gets half an overhaul
Britain
| Danger! Low voltage
Britain’s energy system gets half an overhaul
But bills will remain uncomfortably high
Oct 29th 2026
British households and businesses have struggled with expensive energy for years. Firms in the country pay more than in any EU member state. Domestic consumers are near the top of that undesirable league table (see chart).
Cheaper rather than greener power was the promise from John Healey, the chancellor, in his budget on October 28th. He signalled a shift away from prioritising low-carbon electricity generation at all costs. “From this point, our Labour government priority is first and foremost cheaper energy,” he said.
He proposed a handful of short-term measures and some longer-term ambitions. Most Britons will get a one-off payment of £100 ($133) this winter. A previous decision to remove value-added tax from bills temporarily will be extended. The “standing charge” on gas bills, a daily payment to stay connected to the network, will be removed and a planned levy which would have funded hydrogen energy products is cancelled. Largely, this doesn’t change the underlying costs; it just moves them around.
In the longer run, Mr Healey said, the government will approve green projects only if they cut costs for consumers. He promised that more “fixed-price contracts” for renewable energy will make Britain less reliant on volatile international markets for natural gas. (Left unsaid was that this could also lock in higher prices if markets go down.)
A target of generating almost all electricity from zero-carbon sources by 2030, which looks increasingly hard to reach, stays in place. Allies of Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, and Ed Miliband, her predecessor, insist cheap power was already a priority. The short-term subsidy will be “cold comfort for households”, according to the Resolution Foundation, a think-tank; average annual bills are forecast by EDF, an energy provider, to jump by 27% (or nearly £500) in January and another 8% in April.
Abolishing the standing charge puts more burden onto the variable part of the bill, pushing up the unit price of gas and making bills more expensive for heavy users. Shifting green levies onto general taxation only moves the burden to taxpayers. Mr Healey made a welcome pledge to adopt new rules to speed up the construction of nuclear power stations, but this will take years to have any effect on bills. He is resisting calls to introduce more localised pricing for electricity, which could make markets more efficient. The government has approved the exploration of a new gasfield in the North Sea, but ministers are divided over whether to give the green light to an oil project nearby.
Alarmingly, it is not clear whether the grid could handle cheaper energy if this pushed up demand. The country’s power infrastructure came close to blackout during a summer heatwave, according to a leaked report from the National Energy System Operator, which runs the system. Cheap or green? Neither matters much if the lights go off.

epub_63.title: Do immigrants from some countries commit more sex crimes?
epub_63.text:
Do immigrants from some countries commit more sex crimes?
Britain
| Making sense of the census
Do immigrants from some countries commit more sex crimes?
A hard look at Britain’s data suggests so. But it is hardly an epidemic
Oct 29th 2026
In Bristol last November three men and a 17-year-old boy, all Afghans, gang-raped a 17-year-old girl over several hours. Beforehand they had groomed her on Snapchat and plied her with alcohol; afterwards they fled to France in a lorry. The French authorities returned them to Britain, where they were convicted and, on October 6th, sentenced to long jail terms. In court the girl described how “listening to it all again from the lawyers kept me reliving everything that happened to me”.
Such horrors fuel suspicion of migrants. So did a recent state-issued booklet about Britain for asylum-seekers. Page five clarified that the legal age of consent is 16 and that rape is a serious crime. “I’ve never heard of someone who decided not to rape because they received a leaflet,” said
Kemi Badenoch
, the Tory leader. The clumsy campaign fed the idea that some immigrants—notably men seeking asylum—are responsible for a disproportionate share of sex offences. Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary, claims that “Afghans are over TWENTY times more likely to commit sex crimes than Brits.”
Is that true? The government does not publish crime rates by immigration status. The limited data it does release are raw counts of offences by those of each nationality, from a countrywide police database. The “20 times” claim was based on there being 13,000 Afghans in Britain, an estimate from the Office for National Statistics’ Annual Population Survey. That figure is unreliable, however, having been extrapolated from a sample of fewer than 60 individuals. In 2021 the ONS stopped publishing this population estimate owing to plummeting survey-response rates.
The Economist’s analysis suggests that the “20 times” claim is a wild exaggeration. But our numbers are hardly reassuring.
The Migration Observatory, a think-tank based at Oxford University, obtained figures through freedom-of-information requests to the Ministry of Justice. These count cautions and convictions in England and Wales, split by offenders’ nationality, between 2010 and 2024. The data detail 8m crimes, of which 106,000 are sex offences ranging from rape to consensual sex in public. The police’s recording of offenders’ nationality is messy, but we found that four-fifths of sex crimes were committed by British people. Just 0.39%—409 offences over the 15-year period—were committed by people who said they were Afghan.
Whether 409 crimes is a lot or a little depends on how many Afghans are in the country. In March 2021 the last census reported 14,300 Afghan passport-holders living in England and Wales, and another 7,100 without a passport who said they were Afghan: a total population of 21,400.
The census is just a snapshot in time. Since 2021 some 3m people have settled in Britain and the foreign-born population has risen from 16% to 19% of the total. After the Taliban seized Kabul, in August 2021, some 38,000 Afghans flocked to Britain over the next year and a half. Accounting for those who later left and those who became citizens, we estimate that the Afghan population of England and Wales had doubled to 45,000 by the end of 2022.
To capture more than the snapshot we analysed convictions during a three-year period, 2020-22, and averaged our population estimate over those three years. We then standardised our estimate to account for age and sex (men commit 98% of sex crimes, for example, and Afghans are about ten years younger than the population at large). This suggested Afghans are convicted of sex crimes at seven times the British rate—a far cry from Mr Timothy’s “over 20 times”, but disturbing nevertheless (see chart). Our number is still uncertain: it may be skewed by a few serial offenders, by quirks in reporting and detection rates for such crimes.
Evidence from other countries, using different methods, suggests that this may not be solely a British problem. The perception is certainly not. “The main group, of the worst crimes, like raping, like killing people…the main category are Syrians and Afghans,” Alice Weidel, leader of Germany’s populist Alternative for Germany party, told The Economist. In Austria, Denmark, Finland, Germany and Sweden immigrants from the Middle East, North Africa, Central Asia and the Horn of Africa are over-represented among suspects and convicts—especially for sex crimes. Where age-standardised analysis exists for those countries, the over-representation shrinks, as in Britain, but it does not vanish.
Looking at convictions by ethnicity, rather than nationality, is less unsettling. The Ministry of Justice produces detailed data on prosecutions and convictions by age and sex for 18 ethnicities. We used these to repeat our age-standardised analysis, for the same 2020-22 window. Our results suggested that Pakistani (an ethnicity, not a nationality, in those data), other Asian and other non-black minority men were no more likely to have been convicted of sex offences than white British men.
It should not be surprising that conviction rates differ between nationalities. Ben Brindle of the Migration Observatory notes that many migrants will have witnessed violence, or come from poor backgrounds. This drives criminality, and being socially isolated and jobless in Britain doesn’t help. “Just as large differences in conviction rates exist among British citizens, they will be present across different nationalities, too,” he says.
And the numbers need to be kept in perspective. In 2010-12 Afghan nationals were convicted of 92 sex crimes; in 2022-24 the total was 102. Ten additional sex crimes, after the Afghan population has roughly tripled, is not an epidemic.
■
Editor’s note (October 26th 2026): This article has been changed to clarify the wording on sex offences by ethnicity.

epub_64.title: Prince William builds a high street
epub_64.text:
Prince William builds a high street
Britain
| Urban planning in Cornwall
Prince William builds a high street
Go ahead and laugh. Your local shopping street will soon resemble it
Oct 29th 2026
Nansledan is a peculiar place. Few homes in the quarter-built settlement, near Newquay in south-west England, are more than a decade old. Yet they are a stylistic mixture of Georgian, Victorian and Art Deco. Street names are in the little-known, hard-to-pronounce Cornish language: Bownder An Mengleudh, Lergh Trewolek, Stret Myghtern Arthur. The unnervingly friendly residents occasionally spot Prince William, who in effect owns the land. But perhaps the strangest thing about Nansledan is that it is building a commercial high street.
Of all the features of the British urban landscape, the high street is the most troubled. A YouGov poll this year found that more people think their local one is in a bad state than think it is in a good state. High streets have suffered “decades of decline” and been “hollowed out”, declared Andy Burnham soon after becoming prime minister in the summer. Changing shopping habits mean many shops are vacant or occupied by charities, vape dealers, slot machines and barbers.
Few suburban developers create high streets these days. “You can always get more money in the short term by building another house,” says Hugh Petter, the master planner of Nansledan and a partner at adam Architecture. But the new Cornish burgh has an unusual owner in the Duchy of Cornwall, a centuries-old outfit that provides an income to the heir to the throne. The duchy, which thinks on much longer timescales than most builders, is trying to create a suburban small town, not just a collection of homes. And it reckons it has cracked the high-street problem.
Because Nansledan’s high street is still in the concrete-and-steel phase of construction, it is simple to see the thinking behind it. As far as possible, given the gentle slope on which the place is taking shape, the shop floors are built on the same level. The idea is that traders can start operating from a single small shop, then sprawl sideways into neighbouring properties if they succeed. Sam Kirkness, the executive director of development at Nansledan, says the shops could also be converted into houses, although he hopes that does not happen.
Behind the new high street two large buildings are rising. One, clad in timber, will become a Tesco supermarket. The other will be a market hall, modelled on a much-admired building in Altrincham, a posh suburb of Manchester. The shops around the market hall, most of which are likely to sell food, could be reconfigured even more radically than those in the high street. It should be possible to chop up or amalgamate commercial spaces in a great many ways.
The instinct that shopping streets need to bend and change as businesses grow or fail is a good one. “A lot of units on high streets are simply too big,” says Jan Kattein, a London-based architect (who is not involved with Nansledan). Mr Kattein, who has renovated many British high streets, argues that towns and cities need more small spaces where entrepreneurs can test a business idea cheaply. The tiny “micro-retail” spaces that he and other architects have wedged into courtyards and odd corners of cities are often in high demand, he points out.
The new commercial strip in Nansledan would be no more than a feature of a small Cornish development were it not for one thing. When it comes to urban planning the Duchy of Cornwall is hugely influential. In the 1990s it began to build Poundbury, a ridiculously named (and, in parts, ridiculous-looking) town in Dorset. Some of the things pioneered in Poundbury, such as tucking cars into courtyards and scattering social housing among market-rate housing, are now common in new suburban housing estates.
Amanda Langley, who lives in Nansledan and runs a chocolatier there, says that she often sees “Nansledan tourists”—urban planners and visitors who are curious about the new settlement. It is a peculiar place. But, if the duchy’s previous developments are a guide, it will not stay unusual. Prepare to see other high streets that look just like the one in Nansledan.

epub_65.title: London’s courts can thrive under AI—but they are also at risk
epub_65.text:
London’s courts can thrive under AI—but they are also at risk
Britain
| Ruling the future
London’s courts can thrive under AI—but they are also at risk
An outgoing top judge gives some parting advice
Oct 29th 2026
HOW DOES Britain, with no frontier lab to its name, thrive in a world of rampant artificial intelligence? Part of the answer lies in the courts. London can be a place where claimants bring a new generation of disputes relating to AI—if it puts in some hard graft, says Sir Geoffrey Vos. He steps down this week as the Master of the Rolls, the second-most-senior judge in England and Wales who oversees the civil courts. He has some parting advice.
Sustaining London’s success, he says, relies on ensuring that English law can give certain and predictable answers to the novel legal problems that AI will throw up. “What this says to the world is, if you want a law which is really thinking about the problems of our modern age, English law is one of those laws,” says Sir Geoffrey, “so come here to resolve those disputes.”
He has led a task-force that has set out to define what the common law implies for a range of hypothetical AI problems. Is a human liable if an AI tool libels someone, or if an AI architect designs a faulty building? Is a radiologist negligent if they failed to use an AI tool that could have detected a tumour? A forthcoming paper will deal with agentic AI tools, which carry out tasks autonomously on behalf of a user. The challenge, says Jacob Turner, a barrister and member of the task-force, is that “AI is the only technology that we have ever developed in the history of civilisation that is able to make its own decisions.”
The task-force is an attempt, Sir Geoffrey says, to “short-circuit” questions that the courts might take years to settle—much as it took years for the courts to decide in the 18th century whether shares were a form of property. “You can’t afford to wait ten years for the Supreme Court to tell you that you’re liable if you fail to put guardrails in place in agentic AI and thereby cause people harm,” he says. “Those things are critically important if people are going to choose English law to determine their technological commercial problems.”
Since the 1970s, London’s lawyers have earned a handsome living by welcoming successive waves of international disputes, thanks to a reputation for honest judges and courts offering a Rolls-Royce service. But so far the AI dividend has been modest, with only a handful of blockbuster cases. Last November the High Court largely rejected claims by Getty Images, a media company, that an AI firm had infringed copyright while training its models. Many more are turning up in American courts. And there is stiff competition from rival centres such as Singapore and Dubai.
London’s courts have thrived because English law governs business and transactions across much of the world. But this historical dominance is at risk, Sir Geoffrey suggests. Industries are racing to adopt AI through contracts with the big labs. The dominant ones are either American or Chinese, and operate according to American or Chinese law. “You’ve got now a sort of basic default position that everything you’re doing is going to be powered by AI, and that AI will be prima facie supplied under American law.” The upshot, he says, is that “a lack of digital sovereignty can lead to a lack of legal sovereignty.”
The Master of the Rolls is a post dating to the 13th century, and popular stereotype portrays English judges as ageing technophobes. In Sir Geoffrey’s case, hardly.  In recent lectures he has issued blunt warnings to lawyers: hopes to shield the legal industry from AI with prohibitions on its use are a “hopeless avenue”. They must “be in the vanguard” and “adapt or die”.
People already routinely ask AI for legal advice. Sir Geoffrey has suggested that if the judiciary appears Luddite or “protectionist”, it risks losing public trust. “It’s extremely undesirable for judges to be baked in history, and not behaving in the same way as other members of our society,” he says. He has little time for the complaint that AI submissions are prone to errors and hallucinations; the tech will improve. “I would be asking far more existential questions…how can we best use AI within the justice system to deliver justice to the people we serve in a way they will trust.”
In England official guidelines say that AI can “assist” judges, but it “must not displace reasoning…or the exercise of judicial discretion”. The dividing line is “hard to draw”, says Sir Geoffrey. He recently visited Shenzhen, where an AI-based court system is credited with a sixfold increase in judicial output by reading texts and providing draft reasons for judges to cite.
Ultimately, he stresses, these are limits for Parliament to decide, not judges. But, he has argued, human judges will be irreplaceable as the last resort for people’s rights: machines are incapable of the idiosyncrasy or empathy that fully independent humans enjoy. That is essential, he reasons, if the public is to accept a court’s verdict; people may well have more trust in an idiosyncratic human judge who is 90% reliable, but who they feel has listened to their grievance, than they would in a perfectly reliable machine, he says. There is, perhaps, more to justice than just spitting out the right answer.

epub_66.title: Did Harry Kane have to leave England to win the Ballon d’Or?
epub_66.text:
Did Harry Kane have to leave England to win the Ballon d’Or?
Britain
| The Hurrikane
Did Harry Kane have to leave England to win the Ballon d’Or?
The Premier League’s greatest strength is also a weakness
Oct 29th 2026
The Men’s Ballon d’Or is the most prestigious individual prize in world football. This year’s ceremony was held in London to mark 70 years since Stanley Matthews, an Englishman from Stoke, won the very first Ballon d’Or in 1956. Few Britons have followed his example. It is 25 years since Michael Owen became the sixth British player to do so. On October 26th Harry Kane, England’s captain, became the seventh (and, excluding Scotland’s Denis Law and Northern Ireland’s George Best, the fifth Englishman).
The prize is well-deserved. Mr Kane stands out even among the superstars at Bayern Munich, a German club that have won their domestic league in nine of the last ten seasons. Watch him play and you will notice that he is much more than a goalscorer. But he is a goal machine. Mr Kane scored 61 goals for Bayern last season—19 more than any other player in Europe’s top five leagues and the highest tally anyone has managed since the 2014-15 campaign. Add the six he scored to become England’s all-time top World Cup goalscorer, and (with all due respect to Kylian Mbappé of Real Madrid and Lamine Yamal of Barcelona) it would have been a robbery had he not won the prize.
But Mr Kane’s brilliance is not new. In 2017, playing for Tottenham Hotspur, he became the first player in seven years to outscore Lionel Messi (a record-holding eight-time Ballon d’Or winner) and Cristiano Ronaldo (a five-time winner) over a calendar year. He scored 56 goals in 52 games for club and country, an astonishing record. Yet he came just tenth in the vote for the Ballon d’Or. Why?
Partly because he was playing in the Premier League. Since the league was created in 1992 only three of its players have won the Ballon d’Or (Mr Owen plus Mr Ronaldo, when the Portuguese superstar was at Manchester United, and Spain’s Rodri, when playing for Manchester City). That is not because Premier League players are scrubs. It is instead because the league’s competitiveness makes it difficult to rack up the accolades, and the goals, expected of a Ballon d’Or winner.
Historically, Europe’s top goalscorers have played in countries like Spain—where two clubs rule over an otherwise middling league. Those same European clubs tend to dominate the Champions League, the elite European contest, which carries a lot of weight in Ballon d’Or nominations; at Tottenham Mr Kane scored many goals but won no major trophies. English clubs have won just six Champions League titles since 2000. With talent more evenly spread, a Premier League season is gruelling. On October 14th Man City played Paris Saint-Germain (PSG), the French and European champions. PSG were able to rest eight of their starting 11 players in their previous game. Man City managed two, and were beaten convincingly.
The Premier League, with its large revenues and eye-popping wages, will always attract top talent. But true superstars rarely make England their home. Competitiveness, long the league’s greatest strength, is also its greatest weakness.

epub_67.title: What happens when a place degenerates and gentrifies all at once?
epub_67.text:
What happens when a place degenerates and gentrifies all at once?
Britain
| Bagehot
What happens when a place degenerates and gentrifies all at once?
It says a lot about the state of the British state
Oct 29th 2026
When Gail’s, a chain of artisan bakeries, opened a store in Brixton, an always-lively part of London, on October 16th, it did not receive a warm welcome. Posters appeared of a sourdough loaf altered to look like a bomb. A petition against the store attracted 1,326 signatures. Naturally, once opened it was rammed with Brixtonians buying ham-and-cheese croissants for £5.40 ($7.20). Its windows provided a panorama of travellers streaming down the steps into Brixton Underground Station. Just before 4pm on Saturday October 24th it offered a view of a man pinning someone down and stabbing at him repeatedly.
Welcome to Brixton, where degeneration and gentrification are never far apart. To gauge the state of the British state, ignore the budget, which took place in Westminster on October 28th, and scoot down to Brixton. The area has always been the sharpest example of social change. It was a symbol of post-war immigration before it became a byword for inner-city decline and racial strife. It has since been a tale of rebirth. Gentrification ripped through the area. Handsome Victorian terraces went from five figures to six figures to seven figures. Now it is, again, a picture of something rotten. Call it degen-trification, where an area is both on the up and falling apart, all at once.
Bad behaviour increased after lockdown, says Ayesha Hazarika, a broadcaster and an organiser of Action on Anti-Social Behaviour, a local residents’ group. An area that was always vibrant if edgy instead became scary. Residents complain of drug addicts defecating and masturbating in public. Robberies are up by over 40% year-on-year in 2026 so far; sexual offences by a similar rate. Robert Jenrick, an MP for the populist-right Reform UK, filmed himself marching around Electric Avenue hunting shoplifters, safe in the knowledge he would find some. A few metres from Gail’s, past the site of the stabbing, someone has daubed “Destroy Brixton Gentrification”. A baffled resident might channel Mahatma Gandhi’s reputed thoughts on Western civilisation: “Gentrification? I think it would be a good idea.”
Brixton both confirms and denies the online caricatures of London as a hellhole, depending on where one looks. Is it a no-go area? Far from it. Every evening, young Londoners erupt out of Brixton Underground Station, flicking a Revolut or American Express at the ticket barrier before scurrying into Brixton Market, a once-rundown 1920s affair but now a yuppy playground. Chishuru, a Michelin-starred Nigerian restaurant, started here; as did middlebrow fare from Franco Manca to Honest Burgers, which became successful chains. Jay Rayner, Britain’s finest food critic, lived down the road, and slapped his approval on anything good.
As it is for London’s yuppies, so it is for the city’s crackheads, who barge through the barriers at Brixton station to sample the local delights. Brixton is blessed with, by all accounts, Michelin-grade crack cocaine, and so people travel from far and wide as they would for any new small-plates joint. At night a curiously well-manned hot-dog stand appears outside the station. It serves glass-eyed Zoomers, staggering out of the Tube. It also serves skeletal figures with a determined look who have cajoled generous passers-by into paying for a hot-dog with a flick of an iPhone. The addict is then taken round a corner and handed a small package. Brixton could well be the only place in Britain where it is possible to pay for crack with contactless.
Brixton is the story of a state that has lost the capacity to care. Every part of it has bigger things to worry about. What is a little fare-dodging when Transport for London has a backlog of £4bn in repairs on its Underground network? However well-paid Tube station staff may be, expecting them to deal with knife-wielding assailants is a bit much. Anyway, aren’t the British Transport Police supposed to do that? Though London’s main stations are well-staffed by men with guns, far fewer officers are available for workaday antisocial behaviour on the rest of the Tube.
In any case, Brixton Underground Station is a short walk from a police station. Arresting a drug addict or a small-time street dealer is easy. But where would they go? England’s crown courts have a year-long wait; its prisons are full. At its last inspection HMP Brixton was England’s most crowded category-C prison, for offenders on the path to redemption. Prisoners are doubled up in single-occupancy cells. And about 40% of prisoners said it was easy to score drugs within its walls. (That said, HMP Brixton does have an acclaimed restaurant, The Clink, staffed by inmates serving pan-fried lemon sole in a lemon-butter sauce for £26.)
Can’t the council step in? It already does. It spends the best part of £250,000 a night—about £100m a year—on temporary accommodation for the homeless. This is not largesse born of being a borough in one of the world’s richest cities: with a projected cumulative deficit of £93m by 2030, Lambeth is almost broke, due to obligations from Westminster being dumped on councils without funding to match. Expecting it to treat hundreds of crack and opiate addicts who live in Lambeth on top is unfair. The result is an inordinately expensive system that fails everyone from taxpayers to the people sleeping rough at Brixton station.
When an area tears in two directions, it becomes a discourse monster proving everyone’s priors. For reactionaries it is a harbinger of what Britain will become without hanging ’em, flogging ’em or deporting ’em. For progressives it is austerity made manifest, a land of inequality incarnate where a banker will leave a £1.8m home and step over human shit on his way to work. Sometimes England’s extremes are all in one place and make the solutions offered in Westminster seem inadequate. Just take a trip to Gail’s in Brixton and look out of the window to see.

epub_69.title: To understand African politics, just listen to the music
epub_69.text:
To understand African politics, just listen to the music
International
| The ballot or the ballad
To understand African politics, just listen to the music
Artists have captured a continental spirit of revolt
Oct 29th 2026
“In the town where I grew up I have become a stranger, as though I belong to no land.” So sings Teddy Afro, Ethiopia’s biggest pop star, on “Das Tal”, a hit song released in April. It is a denunciation of the violence and repression convulsing his country. Days after its release more than a hundred people in Addis Ababa, the capital, were reportedly arrested for listening to it in public. Police are said to have warned nightclub owners in the city not to play it. Teddy’s studio was raided and two of his associates were reportedly detained.
Such cartoonish thuggery might seem excessive. But the Ethiopian government and other African regimes have good reason to fear musicians. Opposition parties in Africa tend to be weak or divided. Civil society is typically supine, the media often cowed. But on a continent teeming with disaffected youth, music remains a lively political battleground. In many countries, musicians have emerged as the most authentic—and at times the most dangerous—voices of dissent. “If you want to understand our politics, you should listen to the music,” says an Ethiopian analyst.
This may come as a surprise, since Africa’s best-known musical exports these days are politically anodyne. Afrobeats, for instance, might owe its name to Fela Kuti, a ludic Nigerian radical repeatedly jailed by military juntas. But most of its current stars specialise in “club bangers”, apolitical anthems for the discotheque. South Africa’s music scene once produced anti-apartheid icons like Miriam Makeba and Hugh Masekela. It is now most famous for Amapiano, a hypnotic and hedonistic genre of electronic dance music.
Some link these shifts to the rise of an African middle class and a well-heeled African diaspora. Both prefer revelry to revolution. “They say money don’t buy you happiness,” sings Teni, a Nigerian artist. “But I want all the money in the world.” She means it: when Afrobeats stars like her hold concerts back home in Nigeria, the tickets can cost more than the average Nigerian earns in a month. Hip-hop fans in South Africa say their genre has been similarly gentrified since the end of apartheid. “It’s music tied to a discourse of a new black bourgeoisie, enjoying the fruits of freedom,” says Oliver Layman, a South African researcher at Cornell University.
Beneath this affluent crust, however, magma seethes. Millions of young Africans have no jobs or only bad ones. They blame corrupt leaders for embezzling their futures, but have few outlets for their anger. Previous generations of the downtrodden at least had clearly defined common interests. Peasants might pick up guns and fight for land; factory workers could unionise and go on strike. Today Africa’s vast, informal underclass is more diverse and less coherent. Unskilled day-labourers have different interests from jobbing tradesmen. Motorbike delivery riders have little in common with barbers or maids.
Little unites Africa’s
“generation hustle”
apart from a deep sense of disaffection. But nearly all disaffected young Africans listen to music, and a generation of musicians has given form to their spirit of revolt. Singing mostly in local languages, many are heavily influenced by reggae and hip-hop, drawing on those genres’ emotive themes of poverty, defiance and black liberation. Their music often transcends ethnic and occupational divides. It has sometimes transformed amorphous anger into co-ordinated political action.
The most famous example is Robert Kyagulanyi—better known by his stage name, Bobi Wine. Mr Wine rose to prominence as a self-styled “ghetto president”, singing songs about life in the slums of Kampala, Uganda’s capital. He has since run twice to be the country’s actual president, making him one of the few serious challengers to Yoweri Museveni in his 40 years in power. “Maybe his background as a musician meant he had his finger on the pulse in a way that others did not,” muses an adviser to Mr Museveni. “Everything that I’m saying now, I had already said in my music,” says Mr Wine, whose nom de plume is a tribute to his hero, Bob Marley.
Musicians have orchestrated social eruptions in other countries, too. In 2023 the death (from illness) of Azagaia, a Mozambican rapper, brought thousands of people into the streets for a funeral procession. It quickly morphed into a protest against the iniquity of the elites Azagaia had railed against in his music. Those demonstrations were the overture to a
mass uprising
that nearly toppled the government the next year. Azagaia’s song “Povo no Poder” (“People in Power”) served as the posthumous anthem of the revolt.
Another rabble-rousing singer, Hachalu Hundessa, commands near-mythic adulation among the Oromo, Ethiopia’s largest ethnic group, who have long felt marginalised. His songs helped inspire youth protests that brought Abiy Ahmed, the prime minister, to power in 2018—the first Oromo to hold the job. In 2020 Hachalu was assassinated, sparking a
week of chaos
and violence that left at least 166 dead. Many young Oromos soured on Mr Abiy (whom the musician had criticised), blaming his government for their idol’s death. Protesters came to blows with security forces over where his body should be buried, as though the singer were a saint.
The continent is littered with other examples of musical dissent. Y’en a Marre (We’re Fed Up), a pressure group founded by rappers from Senegal, is credited with helping force an autocrat from power in 2012. In 2015 Martial Pa’nucci, a rapper from the Republic of Congo, organised mass protests against an attempt by Denis Sassou-Nguesso, the country’s dictator, to change the constitution. Pilato, another rapper, led an anti-corruption march on Zambia’s parliament in 2017. One of the leading critics of the kleptocratic dictatorship in neighbouring Zimbabwe is a dancehall singer called Winky D. The ruling party, Zanu-PF, has threatened to ban his work, accusing him of fomenting a “regime-change agenda”.
Bolshy music does not always emanate from a single talisman. In 2024, when Kenyans poured onto streets in opposition to tax increases, some protesters sang struggle songs that can be traced back to the Mau Mau, an anti-colonial rebel movement. Others belted out the lyrics to “Anguka Nayo” (“Fall With It”), a mindless party song by Wadagliz, a Kenyan rap duo. The message was that the government should fall: some club bangers, it turns out, work rather well on the barricades.
Kenyans also made satirical TikToks mocking William Ruto, their imperious and increasingly authoritarian president. In a viral trend, many videos were set to “Kasongo”, an old song by Orchestra Super Mazembe, a Congolese band, about a wayward husband who mistreats his wife. “Kasongo” has been a ubiquitous nickname for Mr Ruto ever since. He hopes to win a second term next year. “One term for Kasongo!” has become an opposition rallying cry.
Mixing music with politics can be a risky business. In 2016 Luaty Beirao, an Angolan rapper, was charged with plotting a rebellion and jailed. Kizito Mihigo, an outspoken Rwandan gospel singer, was arrested in 2020 and found dead in his cell a few days later. This year Mr Wine was forced to flee Uganda after the country’s army chief
threatened to castrate
him. “Unfortunately, I could not counter a man with a sword with poetry, and so I ended up in exile,” the ghetto president laments.
Some artists wield a sword themselves. Many practitioners of
famo,
a genre of accordion music popular in Lesotho, are part of criminal gangs with tentacular influence over political parties and the state. Members of Tinariwen, a Grammy-winning band from northern Mali, once fought for Tuareg separatists against the Malian government. Bootleg cassettes of their early songs were passed around by fighters in the desert, in a kind of Saharan samizdat. Some are said to have been written by Iyad ag Ghali, though he later abandoned the Tuareg-nationalist cause: Mr ag Ghali is now the leader of JNIM, west Africa’s most powerful jihadist group.
The civil war in Sudan has produced a flood of new jihadist music, according to Sudan War Monitor, a research group. The songs praise fighters in Islamist militias aligned with the national army, and exhort prospective new recruits to join. Ethiopia’s civil war has spurred a somewhat analogous outpouring of ethno-nationalist music from Tigray, a rebellious northern province. “There are no love songs any more,” a rebel musician told Deutsche Welle in 2021. “Now every [song] is a struggle song.”
It would be wrong to suggest that all African music is anti-establishment. In Ethiopia Mr Abiy’s government is said to have tried to ingratiate itself with Oromo musicians of late. In April two prominent Oromo singers released a musical rebuttal to “Das Tal”, Teddy Afro’s indictment of Mr Abiy’s rule. The counter-diss track casts Teddy as a malign nostalgist for the Ethiopian empire, which many Oromos regard as an oppressive system under which Teddy’s ethnic group (the Amhara) subjugated their forefathers. Another recent hit boasts that Oromos now rule the roost in “Arat Kilo”, the palace in Addis Ababa where Ethiopia’s emperors once lived and where Mr Abiy currently resides.
One popular song from last year even lauds Mr Abiy’s
controversial ambition
to reconquer a Red Sea port in Eritrea, which seceded from Ethiopia in 1993. “When we command the rain, it falls; when we call for clear skies, they open,” it runs. “Proud Oromo…move onwards to the Red Sea.”
Across Africa, musicians are often paid by politicians to compose songs for election campaigns or perform at rallies. Mere months after Kenya’s tax revolt in 2024, Wadagliz performed “Anguka Nayo” at a government jamboree, with a beaming Mr Ruto clapping along beside them. “Those dictators that are smart are quick to co-opt,” Mr Wine observes. They offer musicians “lives of luxury and opulence”, and demand obedience and flattery in return.
And yet Africa’s dissident artists are unlikely to pipe down. “Africans and music are synonymous,” says Ndungi Githuku, a Kenyan musician and activist. “Why is the government afraid of this? It’s very simple—the government cannot sing.”
■
Sign up to the
Analysing Africa
, a weekly newsletter that keeps you in the loop about the world’s youngest—and least understood—continent.

epub_70.title: Donald Trump may love the Middle East to death
epub_70.text:
Donald Trump may love the Middle East to death
International
| The Telegram
Donald Trump may love the Middle East to death
The folly of wanting a Middle East run by nationalist strongmen and made rich by global commerce
Oct 29th 2026
IF President Donald Trump loathed the Middle East, that unhappy region might be better off. Were he filled with cold disdain for Israel, Iran or the Arab monarchies of the Persian Gulf—as happened with other second-term presidents—he might by now be trying to walk away. Instead, as war clouds gather again over Iran and its neighbours, Mr Trump cannot stop meddling.
Not so long ago Middle Eastern rulers relished the attentions of the Trump clan and its patriarch. At last they had an American president who praised their iron-fisted governance and shared their transactional, show-me-the-money approach to foreign relations. Even their interior design strikes a chord with Mr Trump. “I’m seeing perfect marble. This is what they call perfecto,” swooned America’s president last year, touring the Emir of Qatar’s palace. On that same visit in May 2025, the applause from Gulf leaders was heartfelt when Mr Trump hailed the “miracle” they had collectively wrought, in a speech in the Saudi capital, Riyadh.
Seventeen months on, in such cities as Abu Dhabi, Doha and Dubai, that Riyadh speech is recalled with grief and exasperation. Officials, scholars and investors talk with fury of America’s and Israel’s war on Iran, which is wrecking the very model of modernisation that Mr Trump claims to admire.
In his Saudi address, Mr Trump paid tribute to Middle Eastern rulers for two broad achievements, reflecting his beliefs about what makes for a viable world order. First, he hailed the region for embracing national pride and for staying loyal to traditional values. Middle East rulers thrived by ignoring outsiders “giving you lectures on how to live”, enthused Mr Trump. Second, he praised the region’s absolute monarchs and leaders for their love of money. Specifically, he lauded them for seeking peace through prosperity, and for capitalising on the Gulf’s position at the crossroads of lucrative trade, shipping and aviation routes. Mr Trump described a Middle East of gleaming cities, technology companies and Formula One racetracks forging a future defined by commerce, not “the ancient conflicts and tired divisions of the past”.
Back then, before the war on Iran, the Middle East’s rise seemed to involve both of Mr Trump’s favourite ideas working as planned. It was a region of autocratic palace-builders, reaping great wealth from oilfields and gasfields beneath their feet. It was at the same time a place of bustling container ports and airports open to the globe. Such resource-rich countries as Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates were moving to diversify their economies away from oil and gas. Harnessing their cheap energy, spare land and other resources, they planned to build AI data centres and other hubs for industries of the future.
Mr Trump’s war puts all that into doubt. It has also exposed a contradiction at the heart of his vision. There is a fatal tension between his praise for unyielding nationalism as the foundation of successful societies and his hopes for a globe made peaceful by shared prosperity. For especially in the Middle East, aggressive, rule-scorning chauvinists are destroyers of peace and plenty.
Mr Trump may believe that countries asserting their self-interest is the blueprint for international stability. That is news to Gulf neighbours of Binyamin Netanyahu in Israel, of the Islamic regime in Iran or the Houthi rebels in Yemen. As seen from the Gulf, though the leaders of Israel, Iran and the Houthi rebel movement are very different political actors, a common thread links them. All are seen to seek legitimacy by appealing to narrow ideological, religious and civilisational beliefs (or ancient conflicts and tired divisions, as Mr Trump might say). All are willing to use force to defend and advance their goals.
Conflict is especially deadly for the sort of economic activity which the Gulf hopes will generate future wealth. Marble palaces can be fortified. Oilfields and gasfields can be secured by national armies backed by American firepower. But when Iranian drones or Houthi missiles close Gulf shipping lanes, smash into airports or bomb data centres, as has happened several times this year, the damage goes beyond an individual site. Middle Eastern rulers hope to attract footloose foreigners, whether they are investors, shippers, air passengers or expatriates raising families in gleaming, low-tax cities. In the Gulf, there is brave talk of installing air defences at data centres or building them underground. But airports cannot be buried. Nor can desalination plants. Attack that sort of asset too often, and business will move.
Seen from Gulf capitals, the American-Israeli war on Iran is an attack on connectivity as an economic model. A Gulf official quotes a leader sighing that if he could pick his country up and move it to Latin America, he would, but instead his homeland is 45 minutes by speedboat from Iran. Several Gulf officials are both angry with Iran for striking them, and desperate for a reset of relations with that country. They dread a deal that leaves Iran controlling the Strait of Hormuz like a protection racket. But rather than risk Iranian regime change, they would prefer an Iran engaged in global trade, so that it, too, has incentives to see arteries of commerce kept open. An argument heard often in Doha or Dubai is that the austere, fanatical Revolutionary Guards have little to lose from an endless conflict. For there to be even remote hope for the region, Iran needs political leaders who are more accountable to their people, and focused on their well-being, Gulf neighbours insist.
Though Mr Trump has little interest in accountability for leaders, he does claim to want Iran to choose a path of economic development. For now, though, his attacks have left Iranian hardliners stronger than before. Hence the gloom in the Gulf. Once, its rulers swooned as Mr Trump praised them. Now, they fear he may love their region to death.

epub_72.title: American bosses are desperately trying to de-MAGAfy
epub_72.text:
American bosses are desperately trying to de-MAGAfy
Business
| Feeling blue
American bosses are desperately trying to de-MAGAfy
Ahead of the midterms, corporations want to win back favour with the Democrats
Oct 29th 2026
American bosses once acted on the knowledge that, in politics, the wheel always turns. Parties came in and out of power, and so companies curried favour with both Republicans and Democrats regardless of who controlled the White House or Capitol Hill.
Many bosses have abandoned that even-handedness over the past two years. Companies identified a window of opportunity to advance their agendas, says Reggie Babin of Akin, a lobbying shop. Since Donald Trump’s return to power, pushing through long-desired mergers or securing regulatory changes has often meant abandoning bipartisanship—and dignity, judging by the many corporate donations to Mr Trump’s
garish new ballroom
.
In a few days, however, the president is
predicted to emerge
from the midterm elections with a far weaker grip on Washington. Accordingly, much of corporate America has been desperately trying to scrub off its spray tan and deflate its lip filler. But rebuilding ties with the Democrats will not be easy.
One way this shows up is in the people businesses appoint to handle government relations. In January 2025, the same month Mr Trump was inaugurated, Meta elevated Joel Kaplan, its longtime Republican-whisperer, to be the social-media giant’s chief emissary. On October 20th it announced that Mr Kaplan will be leaving the business. Paramount Skydance, which recently completed its takeover of Warner Bros Discovery with the president’s blessing, has hired a former staffer from the Biden administration to help court the Democrats. Other companies that have enlisted former Democratic aides in the past six months include Palantir, a maker of data-analysis tools, as well as Polymarket and Kalshi, two prediction markets.
The tilt away from Mr Trump can also be seen in America Inc’s donations. Businesses are barred from giving candidates money from their own coffers. But they can co-ordinate donations by setting up political action committees (PACs), which solicit voluntary contributions, mostly from their executives. Those executives can also give to candidates directly or through trusts.
The Economist examined federal filings covering donations by business leaders and their families across these channels. In the second quarter of 2026, the latest period for which data are available in full, 33% of their giving went to Democrats, up slightly from 31% across 2025. Yet that vastly understates the shift, as a disproportionate share of mega-donors support Republicans. Strip out the ten biggest—including Elon Musk—and 51% of donations in the second quarter went to the Democrats, up from 36% throughout last year.
For the most part, America Inc still draws the line at supporting socialists. Of the $287m that executives donated to Democrats in the first half of this year, a mere $9m has gone to progressives, including those endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America. Take out the donations given by Saikat Chakrabarti, most of which went to the entrepreneur’s own unsuccessful primary bid, and the figure drops to just over $4m.
America’s bosses, however, may find that even moderate Democrats have become unreceptive to their overtures. Stopping data centres is not the only anti-corporate rallying cry that has pervaded the midterms. In Iowa big agriculture is the villain; in Alaska it is big fish. One former Democratic official sums up the party’s new outlook on corporate America bluntly: “We demand blood.”
In Silicon Valley the nervousness is palpable. Chris Hughes, a co-founder of Facebook and friend of the Democrats, notes that many tech bosses spent much of the past two years “running around Washington” trying to shape regulation in their interests. One venture capitalist predicts “a reckoning” after the midterms for those who cosied up to Mr Trump. “History is not going to look back particularly favourably on those who leaned in.”
Sensing the threat, some have gone on the attack. Consider the contest for a Senate seat in Ohio. Sherrod Brown, the Democratic candidate seeking to return to the Senate, is a vocal critic of the crypto industry. Fairshake, its flagship PAC network, is spending $55m in a bid to prevent his comeback. But some prominent industry figures—including Chris Larsen, co-founder of Ripple, a crypto-infrastructure provider—have opposed the effort, worrying that it will create animosity with Democratic lawmakers, and that Mr Brown is unlikely to forget the attacks if he wins. Mr Larsen has donated through other channels to the Democrat’s campaign.
The blue wave
may end up smaller
than polls suggest. Yet even if the Democrats take the House of Representatives only narrowly and lose the Senate, they will be able to cause businesses grief. Control of the lower chamber would grant committee chairs the power to subpoena company files and call executives to testify. That could cause embarrassment, or worse.
Washington lawyers say they have been fielding calls since the start of this year about potential investigations. In some cases they have already been hired to parse employees’ actions and communications for indiscretions that could become public, and have been working to pick and train telegenic witnesses from their clients’ ranks. Edward O’Callaghan of Cahill, one law firm, says he has been counselling some businesses to pre-emptively meet influential members of Congress in a bid to avoid public hearings. Where Democratic support seems unlikely, they can instead equip Republicans with favourable information to use in a hearing.
In many respects the next two years will be trickier than a complete change of power. At the same time as companies try to avoid congressional scrutiny, they must maintain good relations with Mr Trump and those in his orbit who could seek the presidency in 2028. “They can’t ignore the fact that there’s still two years of business” with the current administration, says Mr O’Callaghan. Pennsylvania Avenue may soon resemble the Strait of Messina. Few will sail through unscathed.

epub_73.title: Don’t expect supersize profits from Anthropic soon
epub_73.text:
Don’t expect supersize profits from Anthropic soon
Business
| Floating point
Don’t expect supersize profits from Anthropic soon
Lurking in its IPO prospectus are warnings of challenges ahead
Oct 29th 2026
Breakneck growth is commonplace in Silicon Valley. The rise of Anthropic is something else. In the first quarter of last year—when Claude Code, its hit programming tool, was first released—the artificial-intelligence lab pulled in $376m of revenue. By the second quarter of this year that figure had risen 30-fold, to $11.6bn, surpassing corporate mainstays such as McDonald’s or 3M.
In a few weeks this darling of the AI revolution will undergo an initial public offering (IPO) that will be, if not the largest of all time, then certainly close to it. On October 26th it publicly filed supporting paperwork that gave the outside world a closer look at its finances.
Anthropic’s rapid growth is all the more remarkable because, unlike many zippy startups, it has already reached profitability. In the second quarter it eked out an operating profit of just under $1bn, at an 8% margin, having lost $1.7bn in the preceding three months (see chart).
The company is particularly eager to draw attention to its spending on computing power, which fell from 251% of sales in the first quarter of 2025 to just 48% in the second quarter of 2026. Anthropic claims that improvements in its AI models have made it faster and more efficient to develop and serve its technology, allowing the company to make the most of its limited resources. Its personnel costs also fell from 58% of revenue to 16% over the same period as it saw the benefits of scale.
But can Anthropic’s stunning performance continue? A closer look suggests caution is warranted: growth is slowing, the company is paying higher prices to access scarce computing power and a resulting shift towards directly purchasing AI chips will guzzle up much of the cashflow Anthropic would otherwise be on course to generate. Earlier investors who had hoped for a public valuation as high as $2trn may thus be disappointed.
Anthropic’s scorching revenue growth has put a target on its back. Claude Code made it an early leader in the race to automate programming. Silicon Valley colossi such as Meta and Microsoft became huge customers, spending billions of dollars on the lab’s technology. More recently those customers have been pushing staff to use internally developed alternatives. At the same time, OpenAI, Anthropic’s arch-rival, has been gaining ground with its own offering, Codex, the daily use of which has risen tenfold since early August. And after the short-lived craze for “
tokenmaxxing
” earlier this year, companies of all stripes have been more closely monitoring their spending on AI and imposing limits on their engineers.
This month Anthropic told shareholders during a private gathering that revenue in the third quarter was up by about 45% from the preceding three months, a third of the growth rate it achieved in the second quarter. In its IPO prospectus the company warns that, as the market matures, growth could slow “more rapidly than we anticipate”. Moreover, it is increasingly reliant on the tech giants to push its products. Almost half of Anthropic’s revenue now comes from sales made through the cloud businesses of Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft. The company has also upped its investment in advertising to help build demand for its products. Its spending on sales, marketing and distribution partnerships (including with the big cloud providers) absorbed 18% of revenue in the second quarter of 2026, up from 6% in the first three months of 2025.
Another problem Anthropic faces is that, like other AI developers, it is struggling to secure the computing power it needs to serve customers. Its prospectus warns investors that use of “short-term compute” could go up in the near term, weighing on its margins. For example, Anthropic has agreed to pay SpaceX about $3.1bn per month to use its Nvidia chips into 2029. (Anthropic is able to back out from early next year with 90 days’ notice.)
That explains why the lab is starting to develop more of its own computing infrastructure, rather than relying solely on cloud providers. This strategy should help keep operating costs under control, but also provides forewarning that the business will become a more capital-intensive enterprise in the long run. The initiative, called Anthropic Direct, involves procuring chips from providers such as Broadcom, which develops custom silicon, and installing them in rented data centres. That could make it harder to start throwing off the kind of free cashflow investors might hope for, and require the business to raise more money.
In Anthropic’s prospectus, its founders argue that its spending plans “may seem irresponsibly large at first glance”, but are justified by the exponential trajectory that AI is on. “We will aim to be bold but sane,” they write. With a technology so mind-bending, striking that balance may prove surprisingly difficult.

epub_74.title: Seven hot new sources of leadership inspiration
epub_74.text:
Seven hot new sources of leadership inspiration
Business
| Bartleby
Seven hot new sources of leadership inspiration
From amoebae to impalement
Oct 29th 2026
We’re thrilled to share the highlights of our winter catalogue. Following the success of our recent titles on the leadership lessons of Genghis Khan and Alexander the Great, we are bringing you a series of books with management takeaways from absolutely anyone and anything we can think of. Galleys are available on request.
“Start With Die: Leadership Lessons from Vlad the Impaler” by Derek Fromage. “When a man or a prince is strong and powerful he can make peace as he wants to; but when he is weak a stronger one will come and do what he wants to him.” In this contrarian take on the effects of appalling brutality within organisations, Derek Fromage, author of the bestselling “Dare to Bleed”, looks at the career of Vlad III. You’ve read the case for psychological safety. Now learn how Vlad’s high-stakes leadership philosophy can work for you.
“Rhyme and Reason: The Kindergarten CEO” by William Winkie. If you think nursery rhymes are for toddlers, think again. The traditional songs of childhood are crammed with management insights. Great leaders are consistent: it’s frankly confusing to be marched to the top of the hill and then marched straight back down again. Great leaders set shared goals: what’s the point in Polly putting the kettle on if Sukey is just going to take it off again? Great leaders understand the strengths of their team members: who can eat no fat, say, and who can eat no lean. Features practical takeaways on the use of tuffets.
“Meteor: The Katie Zacharia Story.” Sometimes, it all comes down to one moment. No one has any idea who you are, but the eyes of the world are suddenly upon you. Can you seize your opportunity? Katie Zacharia did. In less than 15 minutes at the podium in the White House briefing room, she showed everyone just what she was capable of. To find out how to go from obscurity to household name, read Katie’s stunning new memoir. Because meteors don’t always rise.
“Wham Bam! Lyrics and Leadership” by Eddie Vintner-Twist. To understand their employees, leaders have to inhabit their worlds. And there is no less obvious way to do that than to listen to 1980s pop songs. From the stigma of joblessness (“Wham, bam! I am a man; Job or no job, you can’t tell me that I’m not”) to fears of the apocalypse (“Ninety-nine red balloons; Floating in the summer sky”), celebrated music journalist Eddie Vintner-Twist squeezes every last drop of meaning, and more besides, from the lyrics of his youth.
“Singular: What the Amoeba Can Teach Organisations in the Age of AI” by Renée Roper. Artificial intelligence makes it possible to run organisations that are leaner than any in history. But how can businesses grow without adding complexity? The secret can be found in nature. The amoeba is a single-celled organism that can adapt to any environment. Rather than creating permanent layers of bureaucracy, it uses temporary extensions called pseudopods to change its shape and make progress towards its objectives. If you want to run a unicorn, you have to think like an amoeba. Features a foreword by Sam Altman (not that Sam Altman).
“The Trojan War MBA”. Felicity Jetsam takes six famous episodes from the story of the Trojan War and reveals the workplace dilemmas behind them. If the CEO humiliated you in public by poaching one of your minions, should you follow the example of Achilles and go on strike? Agamemnon’s decision to sacrifice his own daughter in order to propitiate an angry goddess may seem a little harsh, but what if you had to set aside your own interests in order to calm a furious board member? And if you saw a large wooden horse outside your office, are you sure you wouldn’t bring it inside?
“Four the Win! Why Table Legs Are The Ultimate Team Players” by Madge Trestle. The top of a table may take the glory, but the legs make everything possible. Without legs, a table would be just a piece of wood on the floor. Table legs cannot operate independently from their peers. They must always act together; even slight deviations in length cause everything to wobble. Features case studies on some of the most celebrated table legs in history, including the one in the Stauffenberg plot and some others that currently escape us.
Step inside the world of work with our
Bartleby newsletter
. Each week our white-collar oracle muses on the agonies of office life.
