epub_75.title: After its Odyssey, IMAX hits the big time
epub_75.text:
After its Odyssey, IMAX hits the big time
Business
| IMAXmaxxing
After its Odyssey, IMAX hits the big time
Its popularity reflects a shift in how audiences think about cinemas
Oct 29th 2026
IMAX IS ALMOST 60 years old. Richard Gelfond, its boss, is in his 70s. In the 32 years since he acquired the supersize-screen business from its Canadian founders, IMAX has been through near-death experiences and the wilderness years of the covid-19 pandemic. Then came Nolanomics. First was “
Oppenheimer
”, the 2023 tour de force directed by Christopher Nolan. This summer brought “
The Odyssey
”, by far the highest-grossing film of all time for IMAX. Between June and September IMAX screens, which make up less than 1% of the global cinema total, generated 5.8% of worldwide box-office revenues. Mr Gelfond describes the success in Homeric terms. “I’m now a grandfather,” he says. “I thought I could enjoy this with my children. I didn’t think it would take until my grandchildren to get there.”
Nolanomics has underpinned a tripling of IMAX’s share price over the past three years (see chart). Analysts expect record earnings when the company unveils its third-quarter results next week. Yet some on Wall Street fret that it has become a one-hitmaker wonder. Talk of a potential takeover has played a part in its surging share price.
In an interview with The Economist, Mr Gelfond says he expects IMAX to continue to grow next year, buoyed by what he hopes will be a wider slate of blockbuster releases and a shift in the way audiences approach
entertainment
. He points out that interest in IMAX has grown particularly quickly among Gen Z. Youngsters are “overdosing” on digital entertainment through their smartphones. But they are also increasingly willing to pay a premium for richly produced communal experiences such as a night at an IMAX. “There’s just a global craving to be with other people enjoying entertainment together,” he says.
IMAX is well-positioned to cash in on that desire, for three reasons. The first is brand. Only 41 of its 1,800 screens are the auditorium-size 70mm variety, projecting physical film twice as wide as the 35mm standard. They have a scarcity value as well as a visual richness that cinephiles love, helping explain why tickets for “The Odyssey” on some of these screens sold out a year in advance.
Even for IMAX’s other screens, which rely on digital projection, that reputation rubs off, helping to make a visit feel like an experience, rather than just another trip to the cinema. That, in turn, results in premium prices—though still far cheaper than a live concert or sports match.
IMAX’s reputation attracts not just audiences but film-makers. Some devotees, such as Mr Nolan, make use of special IMAX cameras (including for the entirety of “The Odyssey”). Less fanatical directors still value the prestige that comes from their films being shown on IMAX screens. One of the most anticipated movies of next year, “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew”, made by Greta Gerwig of “Barbie” fame, will run in IMAX theatres before its release on Netflix, a streaming platform.
IMAX’s second strength is its business model. It does not own or operate cinemas. Instead it sells or leases its projection and sound technology to them, then takes a cut of their revenue. Studios also pay it to show their films. Its presence is global: 60% of revenue comes from countries outside North America, including China, with a decent share of productions shown in languages other than English.
Mr Gelfond says that IMAX has deals to increase the number of screens by 500 over the next few years. But it is a slow and fiddly process. To kit out a giant cinema near Frankfurt, Mr Gelfond says IMAX had to paint the screen in a hockey arena with a secret formula, fold it and fly it to the venue. “You can’t just snap your fingers and there’s an IMAX theatre,” he says.
IMAX’s brand and business model reinforce a third strength: barriers to entry. Alicia Reese of Wedbush, a broker, says that IMAX has a several-year head start on would-be rivals. Even if they could catch up technologically, it would take time to build credibility with audiences and film-makers and match IMAX’s global reach.
Still, competition is heating up. Disney, an entertainment giant, has recently created an umbrella brand, Infinity Vision, that it hopes will serve as an alternative to IMAX. Rather than a new technology, Infinity Vision is a certification programme that will let various other supersize-screen brands claim Disney’s stamp of approval.
It will soon be put to the test. On December 18th IMAX and Infinity Vision will go head to head, launching “Dune: Part Three” and “Avengers: Doomsday” on their respective screens. Yet both may well end up benefiting if “Dunesday” turns into a reprise of the “Barbenheimer” battle in 2023, which spurred cinema-going after a quiet few years. Already 2026 is shaping up to be the best year for the box office since the pandemic, thanks not to larger audiences but higher ticket prices—including for large-format showings. Moviegoers are not IMAXed out yet.

epub_76.title: India’s ultra-cheap internet is about to get more expensive
epub_76.text:
India’s ultra-cheap internet is about to get more expensive
Business
| Byte back
India’s ultra-cheap internet is about to get more expensive
Blame Jio, the country’s telecoms disrupter, going public
Oct 29th 2026
The impact of Jio, India’s biggest telecoms provider, can be seen everywhere in the country’s megacities. Delivery drivers scroll through short-form videos as they wait at red lights; shop assistants keep a family video chat running all day underneath the counter; security guards wile away the long, boring hours sharing memes and ogling foreign beauties. Jio’s super-cheap plans have allowed Indians to feast on all the internet has to offer.
Public investors can now buy a seat at the table. On October 28th Jio’s shares began trading on India’s two main bourses. The listing, which valued the company at 10.3trn rupees ($108bn), is the largest ever in local-currency terms (and the second-biggest in dollars). Jio’s shares closed 27% above their listing price at the end of the first day of trading.
The debut was a triumph for Mukesh Ambani, one of India’s richest magnates, who began building Jio in 2010 when few Indians could afford smartphones. Jio is one of the rare pieces of Reliance, Mr Ambani’s sprawling conglomerate, that he, rather than his father, can take credit for building. Reliance’s original telecoms arm, which Mr Ambani’s brother Anil inherited, went bust in 2019.
For internet-hooked Indians, however, the listing may not be such good news. Jio’s valuation suggests significant price rises may be coming. To maintain its revenue growth—around 15% in the latest financial year—it needs to either find more customers or make its service dearer. Market penetration is already high: India has 1.3bn wireless connections, 92 for every 100 people, rising to 147 connections per 100 people in cities. And thanks in part to Jio’s bargains, the telecoms industry has fallen from around a dozen companies in 2016 to just four today, two of which are vestigial. Jio enjoys a market share of 39%; its main rival, Bharti Airtel, controls 38%. (Vodafone Idea, which is heavily indebted, holds 15%, with state-run BSNL on 7%.)
That points to growth through higher prices. At present Jio earns an average revenue per user of around 214 rupees ($2.28) a month, for which subscribers get an average of 44 gigabytes (GB) of data. At 4.9 rupees per GB, Jio costs a third less than the industry average in India (and 2% of what American telecoms charge). Narrowing that gap would be the fastest route to more revenue. Motilal Oswal, a local broker, predicts a 15% increase in Jio’s prices by December. Airtel, which typically follows Jio with tariff rises of its own, has seen its share price jump by 11% in the past month in anticipation.
Might India’s data addicts revolt? After all, Jio’s rise was built on being startlingly cheap. When the firm first launched, users on its introductory offer enjoyed free high-speed data, helping it reach 100m subscribers in 170 days. Indians remain price sensitive: when the two big telecoms companies raised their fees in July 2024, Jio lost 16m subscribers in four months, with many switching to BSNL. But that did not last. Sluggish streaming speeds and patchy coverage on the former monopoly’s network brought many customers back.
Mr Ambani might also try to expand Jio’s other businesses, including its fixed-line offering and streaming service, which account for a fifth of its revenue. The tycoon has pledged to bring “
affordable intelligence
” to India, mirroring the cheap internet he brought a decade ago, and could peddle various AI services via Jio.
He is also plotting a satellite-internet offering similar to Elon Musk’s Starlink, the rollout of which has been held up by regulatory hurdles. (Mr Musk recently blamed “certain oligarchs” for the delays.) It would be an odd fit for Jio, which has benefited from India’s high population density: a 5G tower in one of the country’s packed cities covers tens of thousands of people, keeping down costs. Satellite internet is most appealing in areas that are remote and sparsely populated—which in India typically means poor. Jio had agreed to a distribution partnership with Starlink. Why, then, would it need its own satellites? Because one customer matters above all for Mr Ambani: a government that would rather not depend on Mr Musk.

epub_77.title: The world’s biggest maker of spectacles faces a crisis
epub_77.text:
The world’s biggest maker of spectacles faces a crisis
Business
| Blindsided
The world’s biggest maker of spectacles faces a crisis
EssilorLuxottica has been rocked by a petty feud
Oct 29th 2026
Two years before his death in 2022, Leonardo Del Vecchio, the Italian billionaire who built EssilorLuxottica into the world’s biggest eyewear-maker, handed control of the business to his trusted confidante, Francesco Milleri. To his heirs, Del Vecchio left equal stakes in a holding company, Delfin, which owns 32% of EssilorLuxottica, alongside stakes in various other Italian companies.
For a time, there was harmony. At its peak in November last year the market value of EssilorLuxottica, which owns brands including Ray-Ban and Oliver Peoples, reached €148bn ($172bn), nearly triple what it is was worth when Mr Milleri took charge. Since then it has plunged back down to €81bn amid a governance crisis brought about by Leonardo Maria Del Vecchio (pictured), the 31-year-old heir who until August served as the company’s strategy chief. Investors fear that the dysfunction is set to coincide with a period of technological upheaval for the company.
Over the past month the crisis has spilled out into the open—in sometimes bizarre fashion. First came a podcast in which Leonardo Maria lamented a lack of love from his father, shared his struggles with drug abuse, boasted of his sexual exploits (2,000 women, many seduced by singing Enrique Iglesias’s “Hero”)—and declared that his former mentor Mr Milleri should be “nervous” about his handling of EssilorLuxottica. Then in a rambling radio interview on October 26th the wayward heir claimed that Mr Milleri had been appointed chief executive only as a caretaker with the job of finding a successor, which he had failed to do.
Mr Milleri says he has known Leonardo Maria since he was a baby and has treated him like a son, which makes their falling out all the more painful. EssilorLuxottica’s underlying business has continued to perform solidly. On October 20th the firm reported that its revenue was up by 9%, year on year. Insiders say that the feud instead stems from Leonardo Maria’s bitterness over the failure of his plan to become the leading shareholder in Delfin by acquiring the stakes of two of his siblings, Luca and Paola, for €10bn. Mr Milleri, who chairs Delfin’s board, supported the plan, but three of the five directors refused to agree to the conditions imposed by Leonardo Maria’s lenders, including guaranteed dividends to help cover the interest bill. The heir blamed Mr Milleri for failing to win the board over.
Leonardo Maria’s desire for change at Delfin is understandable. “The governance is broken,” argues Bernardo Bertoldi, an expert on family businesses at Turin University. Delfin is set up such that each of its eight equal shareholders—the founder’s six children, his stepson and his widow—in effect has a veto over the many decisions that require an 88% supermajority. The elder Del Vecchio’s hope had been to keep his family united through the need for consensus. In practice, the structure he created is too rigid, argues Mr Bertoldi.
Even so, for EssilorLuxottica’s investors, the drama is worrying. Mr Milleri’s current term will end in April. The dysfunction at Delfin could put his reappointment in doubt (though the holding company’s board has expressed its support). “Concern about governance has weighed heavily on the stock,” says Luca Solca of Bernstein, a broker.
The uncertainty has coincided with growing nervousness about the long-term impact of smart glasses on EssilorLuxottica’s business. For now the technology is giving a boost to the company; a partnership with Meta, a social-media giant, to develop Ray-Ban smart glasses has been a notable success. But other Silicon Valley titans, including Apple and Google, also have their sights on the opportunity. Eventually their products could eat away at EssilorLuxottica’s traditional eyewear business, much as smart watches have hurt sales of timepieces.
Mr Milleri says he is confident that EssilorLuxottica will emerge a winner from the technology—which he reckons could one day replace the smartphone—pointing to EssilorLuxottica’s beloved brands and global retail network. He will have to hope the Del Vecchio heirs do not get in the way of his vision.

epub_78.title: Why it’s a bad time to be a rat-killer
epub_78.text:
Why it’s a bad time to be a rat-killer
Business
| Snared
Why it’s a bad time to be a rat-killer
Private equity and artificial intelligence are nibbling at sales
Oct 29th 2026
It is a good time to be a rat. A warmer climate makes breeding easier. Busier cities provide more rubbish to eat. Bed bugs, too, are doing well, thanks to growing pesticide resistance. Then there are the termites, which have been spreading northwards, chewing through ever more of states like New York and Ohio.
Demand for pest-control has been growing for decades. Over the past ten years global spending has nearly doubled, reaching $29bn last year. The industry may be buzzing, but the world’s two biggest pest-control companies—Rollins and Rentokil—are not. Rollins’s share price has fallen by 44% this year. Rentokil is down by 23%.
The modern pest-control industry can trace its origins to these two giants. Orkin, Rollins’s flagship service, was hatched in 1901 when Otto Orkin, a 14-year-old immigrant from Latvia, began selling rat poison door-to-door in Pennsylvania. Rentokil was the name of the fluid that in the 1920s cleared Westminster Hall’s roof of the deathwatch beetles that kept falling on parliamentarians’ heads. Since then the pair have dominated the industry. Today they account for half the revenue of America’s 100 largest pest controllers.
So what has got under investors’ skin? Rentokil is, in part, caught in a trap of its own making. Its takeover of Tennessee-based Terminix four years ago was so badly bungled it prompted investors to sue. The company’s growth has stunk ever since.
But now Rollins, too, is plagued by poor performance. It blamed slow growth early in the year on bad weather, which it said prevented technicians from reaching customers. “They had never used weather as an excuse before,” says Manav Patnaik of Barclays, a bank. The weather improved, then the company missed earnings expectations for its second quarter. And its third.
Two bigger threats are creeping into view. First is private equity. The pest-control industry is attractive to PE in part because it is defensive—people dislike living with bed bugs, and will pay to purge them whatever the state of the economy. Service providers can also keep their claws stuck into customers. In America roughly 80% of pest-control revenue is recurring, as people subscribe to regular pest-proofing in places where infestations are common.
PE-owned businesses have quadrupled their share of the revenue of America’s 100 biggest pest-controllers since 2020, to over 16%, partly by gobbling up smaller providers and merging them. That has made competition fiercer and acquisitions costlier for the incumbents, whose combined market share has slipped from 53% to 51% over the past decade.
The second scourge is AI. According to Bernstein, a broker, customers are increasingly turning to chatbots rather than search engines to find pest-controllers. Because bots scrape sites like Reddit, which attract more—and rosier—reviews for local firms, these get recommended more often. The giants, meanwhile, inspire rage. “I cannot stress this enough to anyone looking for rodent removal…DO NOT HIRE ORKIN!”, writes one Redditor.
That explains why search traffic for Orkin fell by 48%, year on year, between May and July. (Search activity for Terminix has suffered less badly—for now.) Data centres face increasing local opposition. Less appreciated is how the technology they support is helping small businesses compete. In the pest-control industry, AI has brought on a rat race.

epub_79.title: Weil’s collapse and the death of corporate loyalty
epub_79.text:
Weil’s collapse and the death of corporate loyalty
Business
| Schumpeter
Weil’s collapse and the death of corporate loyalty
Superstar talent is alluring. It is also dangerous
Oct 29th 2026
And just like that, an institution that existed at the apex of corporate America for nearly a century is more or less finished. Weil, Gotshal & Manges, a firm of lawyers, has suffered what can only be described as a run on the bank.
It started last month when a top mergers lawyer left for Cravath, Swaine & Moore. Other competitors began lining up outside the General Motors Building in Manhattan, where Weil is based, trying to hire its lawyers. The committee of partners responsible for saving Weil, no doubt handicapped by efforts to save themselves, failed to stop the exodus. The partner due to take the top job decided she wouldn’t bother. Merger talks collapsed. Weil, which is best known for advising on the bankruptcies of Enron and Lehman Brothers, has now hired bankruptcy lawyers itself and is preparing to wind down. The balance-sheet of a law firm is a simple combination of office chairs and brains. When the brains start to leave, the end cannot be far away.
Law firms have collapsed before. Fear of being the last partner in a broke partnership means weak ones can disintegrate suddenly, as John Morley of Yale has written. Yet never has a name as famous fallen on such hard times so quickly. Weil is, by any measure, an extremely successful business: its partners earn, on average, almost $6m a year. The ability of Weil’s lawyers to extract enormous fees from their clients is not the problem. Rather, it is the newfound ability of superstar lawyers to extract enormous pay from their own firms, and the damage they do to them when they up and leave. Such professional fleet-footedness was unthinkable a decade ago—and marks the passing of something far more important than any law firm.
In the 20th century mass layoffs severed the bonds of goodwill between ordinary workers and corporations. Yet the reward for winning the contest that is Western capitalism was still a career in an institution that resembled a medieval guild. Partnership at an investment bank, a consultancy or a law firm was the best-paid option. Success in the marketplace liberated the individual from market forces, providing a secure perch in his professional life, and also in his social life, with admission to clubs, boards and perhaps an apartment in a co-operative building near Central Park.
Such elite collectivism barely exists today. Bankers abandoned it first. In 1999 Goldman Sachs, the archetypal Wall Street partnership, followed its rivals and went public. Its bosses are still called partners, but are nothing of the sort. Smaller merger-advisory houses, which sought to recreate the old partnerships, have mostly listed their shares so their founders can cash out. The legal professions’ collectivist impulses lasted far longer, because its firms never needed to raise capital. Yet the market came for them eventually, too. In recent years the “lock step” compensation model, where individuals are paid on the basis of tenure rather than performance, has given way to one where the top lawyers can name their price, and come and go far more easily. A governance model resembling a stuffy but staid co-operative has been replaced with one closer to the businesslike but impersonal condominium.
Weil is the first great law firm to suffer the death of elite collectivism. It is unlikely to be the last. That is because it is hard to say what Weil might have done differently, and what exactly marked it out for ruin. The result is disorienting: an industry of hundred-year-old stalwarts, any one of which could at any time suffer a debilitating run if the wrong lawyer defects. The partnership structure, once an instrument of stability, is now a liability. Paying an individual anything other than the fees he commands from clients is not an incentive to collegiality, but an invitation to leave. The names on the door are not an indication of shared values, but the dignified parts of an increasingly efficient corporate constitution. Loyalty counts for little; history, nothing at all.
What might law firms look like after the legal industry’s Lehman moment? Lawyers can see their future in other parts of the economy where the elite collective has been supplanted by the elite individual. It is visible in every arena where the very best is worth much more than the runner-up: from the football player to the programmer to the rapper. Consider hedge funds such as Citadel or Millennium. Portfolio managers owe no obligation to each other. There isn’t much chatter between them. Often they are in competition. Each knows what share of his profits he will be paid, and roughly what level of losses will get him sacked. It is easy enough to move on to the next shop. Such traders are, in essence, the world’s best-paid gig workers.
Any firm that derives most of its value from superstar human capital should respond to Weil’s demise with superstar anxiety. How might order be reimposed? There are legal mechanisms. Finance imposes non-compete agreements, sometimes stretching out years, to make it harder for its staff to leave (these have never been used by law firms). There are illegal mechanisms, too. Leave the mafia and it might relieve you of your fingers. But the most durable ties are cultural. On Wall Street that might once have been supplied by the division between Jewish and Protestant firms. What would similar connections look like today?
Silicon Valley has an idea, though it is unlikely to travel well. The competition to hire the best artificial-intelligence researchers is the most extreme example of the war for superstar talent; firms are frequently raided for their top researchers. Yet the frontier labs are about the only elite businesses around today that carry the collectivist impulses that once dominated. Mostly that has to do with competing belief systems about the dangers posed by their technology. Wall Street’s lack of an existential philosophy is an existential problem.

epub_81.title: The countries making a fortune from the US-China rivalry
epub_81.text:
The countries making a fortune from the US-China rivalry
Finance & economics
| A rare opportunity
The countries making a fortune from the US-China rivalry
Critical-mineral profits could transform a lucky few
Oct 29th 2026
FOR BETTER or worse, many poor countries’ fortunes hinge on their natural resources. Since their industries are less sophisticated and their service sectors smaller than in rich places, an underground bounty can make a big difference to their economic prospects. Rising global demand for oil or ores can spur growth, attract investment and fill fiscal holes. Many finance ministers in the poor world fondly recall the last commodity “supercycle”, when rising China’s insatiable demand pushed up the price of metals and fossil fuels. Oil sales helped to nearly double Angola’s GDP between 2002 and 2008.
Now the world may be entering another supercycle, propelled by the race between America and China to secure supplies of minerals critical to artificial intelligence, electrification and other technologies expected to define the 21st century. Chinese minerals diplomacy, which has helped to secure deals with at least 19 countries since 2000, is alive and well. Donald Trump’s administration has already signed mineral-themed agreements with more than 20. Today the rivals are both courting a much smaller group of countries capable of getting minerals out of the ground quickly.
On October 16th the World Bank said it would quintuple, to $20bn, a fund to help countries capture some of the surging demand. Yet in order to succeed, their governments cannot rely only on their subterranean resources or their cosiness with America and China. They must also show ability to supply stuff at speed.
The urgency is palpable. In May 2025 Mr Trump was forced to rein in tariffs he had imposed on Chinese goods, after China retaliated by restricting exports of seven rare-earth minerals used to make semiconductors and weapons. America wants to break China’s chokehold. It has stockpiled minerals, offered producers guaranteed prices and poured billions into mining projects, while chivvying private investors to do the same. One Texan investor says administration officials approached him on eight separate occasions.
The wheedling has worked. According to officials, in 2025 the American government and American firms spent $15.4bn on foreign mines, up from nearly nothing in 2024, and more is expected this year. At least a tenth of that came from EXIM, a government-owned bank, and the Development Finance Corporation, a bank that once doled out loans to clinics and climate activists but has been repurposed by Mr Trump and given $205bn to play with. In response, Chinese state-owned mining giants splurged well over $30bn abroad, far more than in 2024 (see chart 1). The superpowers’ combined investments have not been this high since the last supercycle started to unwind a decade ago.
So far the biggest beneficiary has been the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Most Western investors abandoned the vast, conflict-torn, landlocked central African country when prices of tin, diamonds and other of its abundant resources collapsed. This enabled Chinese firms to scoop up distressed assets for a song. The Chinese have pledged $1bn to expand a copper mine and propose to build a much bigger one that could churn out up to 500,000 tonnes per year, making it one of the largest copper projects in the world.
Now America is back, too. A government-financed fund is in talks to buy 40% of one of the last remaining Western-owned operating mines, a copper concern run by Glencore, a Swiss-based company. Private firms have followed. KoBold Metals, a Californian startup, is probing lithium deposits in the DRC’s Manono region. Virtus, an unlikely coalition of ex-spooks and soldiers, has bought a cobalt and copper venture with headquarters in Dubai.
The DRC is so indigent that the cash is already transforming its economy. In 2025 foreign mining investment was equivalent to roughly 8% of its GDP. It was more than double the total of foreign direct investment (FDI) the year before. The DFC has expressed interest in contributing up to $1bn to build the Dilolo-Sakania Railway, which will plug into a rail link to Angola and will be the DRC’s biggest infrastructure project in a decade. The Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative, a non-profit in Norway, reckons that mining will generate $8bn in government revenues between 2026 and 2030. Should other mines continue to produce at similar rates, the industry will yield $20bn for the state, roughly equivalent to a year’s spending.
Two other big winners are Brazil and Kazakhstan. Neither is so poor as to be materially enriched in an instant as the DRC has been. But they are nevertheless benefiting mightily from American and Chinese interest.
America’s approach has been the more focused. In Brazil it has set about building a rare-earth empire. In September USA Rare Earth, a listed company in which the government has a stake, took over Serra Verde, the only producer of four of the scarcest such minerals outside Asia. The firm has already spent $2.8bn acquiring the mine. A further package pulled together by the Department of War and a loan from the DFC will push American investment to nearly $5bn.
In Kazakhstan America is eyeing tungsten, which is vital to high-tech arms-manufacturing. In November 2025 Kaz Resources, a firm backed by the administration and by investors including Eric Trump and Donald Trump junior, two of the president’s sons, is stumping up $1bn to develop deposits at Kairakty, first explored in 1958, and Northern Katpar. The deal is equivalent to nearly a twentieth of Kazakhstan’s annual FDI inflow. A further $1.6bn could come via the DFC and EXIM.
China’s bets in both countries have been broader. Last year Chinese firms invested around $6bn in Brazil, more than in any other country. A third of that went on mines producing minerals including nickel, copper and gold. In Kazakhstan, China, like America, wants tungsten: Kaz Resources had to pay over the odds to fend off a Chinese firm lobbying for a licence, according to two American officials involved in negotiations. But last year China and Kazakhstan also agreed on deals worth over $10bn that included copper and gold projects, as well as a tungsten mine.
Last year Mr Trump’s officials spoke about recruiting countries to America’s camp while pressing them to spurn Chinese advances. Most, they said, would have to pick a side. The experience of the DRC, Brazil and Kazakhstan shows that this is not how things have played out so far.
American and Chinese mineral-hunters are piling into the same handful of countries because only so many have lots of half-finished, old or dormant mines that can be completed or revived quickly and cheaply. China has long prized speed, in contrast to the preference of private-sector Western miners for the slower process of finding promising new assets and carefully optimising returns over their lifetimes. Now America is becoming impatient—and so behaving more like the Chinese.
Last year just five countries—the DRC, Brazil and Kazakhstan, plus Zambia and Canada—accounted for nearly 80% of the two superpowers’ combined mining investments abroad. With the exception of Canada, for which Mr Trump seems to feel special contempt, Sino-American rivalry is paying off for these fortunate few. On a visit to Beijing in March, DRC officials obtained commitments from China to share more data and invest more in local processing. China has also agreed to share the ownership of its Congolese copper project with the local state-owned diamond miner. According to the two American officials, the Kazakh government managed to extract a bigger stake in the Kairakty joint venture than America first offered.
In the short run, smash-and-grab may benefit the superpower rivals, too. China started to produce lithium in the DRC earlier this year. America’s expansion of Serra Verde, the Brazilian mine, should be up and running in a year. The Kazakh project should begin production by 2030.
Yet the strategy has its limits. It relies on others to prospect for and develop existing deposits, even as prospectors and developers grow more cautious. Miners’ exploration budgets have never recovered from the end of the last supercycle (see chart 2). Despite forecasts of surging demand for copper, which may outstrip supply by 8% within ten years, the world’s biggest producer of the red metal, Chile, has cut back output, largely owing to underinvestment in decaying assets.
Higher prices should in theory attract investment in new projects. At least 30 countries possess viable deposits of copper, for instance. But these can take a decade or more to pinpoint and develop. In the meantime, all the meddling by the governments of America and China is confusing the price signals miners rely on to decide whether an untapped deposit is worth the hassle. The result is more investment paralysis—but, for the lucky few places with ready deposits, it’s payday.

epub_82.title: China’s stock markets are the great global exception
epub_82.text:
China’s stock markets are the great global exception
Finance & economics
| Fast bears
China’s stock markets are the great global exception
If the country is winning the future, why are its investors so glum?
Oct 29th 2026
ACCORDING TO Moonshot AI, a leading artificial-intelligence firm
based in Beijing
, “What truly matters lies beyond the reach of human sight.” That is one reason why its Chinese name translates as “Dark Side of the Moon”. (Another may be the founder’s love of Pink Floyd.)
The startup, which hopes to list in Hong Kong next year, illustrates many of China’s AI strengths. Its founders are talented and dedicated. Its Kimi K3 model, which it has just upgraded, is lean and powerful. The country is determined to make the most of the new technology. Its economy, like America’s, Taiwan’s and South Korea’s, lies firmly within the orbit of the global AI boom. But unlike those places, where optimism waxes and wanes, China’s stock market has been dark.
The pessimism is plainest in tech-heavy stock-market benchmarks, such as the ChiNext index in Shenzhen. It has lost about 40% in four months. The bearishness has spilled over to broader indices, such as the CSI 300, which tracks large-cap firms listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen (see chart 1). In October this index met the conventional definition of a bear market, having fallen by 20% from its June peak.
For about a decade China’s regulators have instead sought to cultivate a “slow bull market” that would lift consumer sentiment and raise money for new companies without running wild. In the first half of 2026, they seemed to be getting their wish. The CSI 300 made a slow advance. CXMT, a chipmaker, listed in Shanghai in July, raising 66.6bn yuan (a lucky number worth almost $10bn). The “national team”, state-owned financial institutions that prop up the market when required, felt confident enough to offload some of the stocks they had bought in past crises (see chart 2).
Things changed around the middle of the year. The culprits include AI scepticism and local fiscal caution. Doubts about end-user demand for AI apply with extra force in China. Mainland companies are notoriously reluctant to pay for software. And competition for their custom is fierce. Kimi’s success, for example, poses a threat to listed rivals such as MiniMax.
China’s stocks have also suffered from the government’s budgetary inhibition. Many investors had hoped for a concerted effort this year to lift the economy through infrastructure investment and handouts for households. But the government has relied more on foreign demand to keep growth going. This year’s export boom has allowed it to turn its attention to fiscal repair, not fiscal expansion.
The irony is that much of that boom has been AI-related. The value of Chinese semiconductor exports, for example, more than doubled in the first nine months of the year. The world’s AI spending has supported Chinese growth, obviating the need for fiscal stimulus. And that unexpected austerity has weighed on domestic demand, depressing the stock market. The AI gods give; they also take away.
Lately the national team seems to have returned to action, putting a floor under the market. Exchange-traded funds held by Central Huijin, part of China’s sovereign-wealth fund, have recorded strong inflows, notes Larry Hu of Macquarie, a bank. The government is also mobilising investment for what it calls the “six networks”. These include the power, computing and communications systems an AI-led economy will need. Economic growth has picked up and the CSI 300 has edged back above the symbolic 4,000 mark for now.
Contrary to popular belief the “dark” side of the moon gets two weeks of sunlight a month, just like the visible side. China’s markets will hope that their day in the sun comes soon.

epub_83.title: The never-ending absurdity of global oil markets
epub_83.text:
The never-ending absurdity of global oil markets
Finance & economics
| Laws of thermokinetics
The never-ending absurdity of global oil markets
Despite stronger Gulf exports, Brent is near its Iran-war peak
Oct 29th 2026
EIGHT MONTHS into the Iran war the oil-market riddle keeps deepening. Since early September exports from the Middle East have climbed. They exceeded 17m barrels per day (b/d) in the week to October 23rd, just 4m b/d below 2025 levels, reckons Vortexa, a data firm. Yet in the same period the price of Brent futures, the international benchmark for crude, has jumped by a fifth, to $115 a barrel, nearing its April peak (see chart).
Three factors explain why oil is so pricey, starting with a change in China’s appetite for crude. In March its government, worried about supplies, banned exports of refined products. Refiners drew on stocks and consumers used less fuel. The result was a near-halving of crude imports between February and June, by 6m b/d. That was a big reason why the largest oil-supply shock in history did not push prices higher.
In June a detente between Iran and America caused prices to drop. Chinese refiners lobbied to lift the export ban: with Gulf exports still blocked and Russian refineries pummelled by Ukraine, refiners’ margins elsewhere set records. From July China resumed exports and imports rebounded. In the three weeks to October 16th they were more than 3m b/d above June’s level—enough to absorb some of the jump in Middle East exports, notes Neil Crosby of FGE NexantECA, a consultancy.
Chinese imports have since edged down. But a second factor—a rise in freight costs—is still forcing up prices. The way China has been buying has played a part in this: rather than purchasing on pre-agreed schedules, it chased better prices on the spot market, creating demand for tankers that was harder to plan for and costlier to secure, according to Tom Reed of Argus Media, a price-reporting agency.
Meanwhile, the rise in Gulf exports via the Strait of Hormuz has added to tanker demand. Such voyages need fleets of state-owned tankers to shuttle clandestinely through the strait, collect cargo, then transfer it in the Gulf of Oman to other vessels that may wait for days. That ties up more vessels, pushing up freight costs worldwide. These once made up 4-7% of the cost of delivering oil to Chinese buyers; by October they accounted for 25-30%.
Such costs have spilled into the wider market. Producers in Latin America and west Africa, farther from buyers, have discounted their crude to stay competitive; North Sea drillers, by contrast, command a fuller price. This “geography premium” has opened up a spread between the cheapest and priciest grades that recently neared $60—and pulled Brent a bit higher.
But demand and freight do not fully explain why Brent sits far above “fair” value, which JPMorgan Chase, a bank, puts some $20 below the recent price. The gap reflects the third factor: fear that further violence could slow Gulf exports again. In October Iran has struck at least 30 vessels, the highest monthly tally of the war by far. Yemen’s Houthi rebels have attacked Saudi Arabia’s cities, airports, refineries and the country’s (recently repaired) East-West oil pipeline. In the month to October 22nd, seven of the eight days on which Brent moved by more than $2.50 a barrel brought news of peace talks or worsening tensions, counts Morgan Stanley, another bank.
Mr Trump has hinted he might strike Iran again after America’s midterm elections on November 3rd. Markets are waiting to see if he does: low trading volumes in Brent futures give every bullish bet outsize weight. If he holds off, prices will probably fall back within days. But large-scale bombing, alongside major Iranian and Houthi attacks, could push prices to $130-140 a barrel, reckons Jim Burkhard of S&P Global, a data firm.
China holds ample oil stocks, and rich countries retain strategic reserves; both will probably be tapped if prices go so high.  And the Brent futures curve, refining margins and forward freight prices suggest markets fear disruption will last well into 2027. In April traders were close to panic. Now they are nearer to resignation.

epub_84.title: In an AI blow-up, would insurance pay out?
epub_84.text:
In an AI blow-up, would insurance pay out?
Finance & economics
| Buttonwood
In an AI blow-up, would insurance pay out?
Credit default swaps are back in vogue amid fears of a debt disaster
Oct 29th 2026
IN 1912 FRANZ REICHELT, a tailor and inventor, ascended to the first level of the Eiffel Tower to offer a demonstration. He had designed a suit which could double as a parachute. After mixed results with mannequins, he decided it was time for a manned test—and fell to a grisly end. Today owners of credit-default swaps (CDSs), a form of insurance designed to pay out when borrowers go bust, likewise find themselves in mid-air with an untested parachute.
CDSs can be used to hedge exposure to debt, or to speculate. But are they a good way to do either? The instruments gained notoriety in the global financial crisis of 2007-09, then got their wings clipped during the euro-zone debt crisis. In 2011 the Greek government’s initial restructuring of its debt failed to trigger CDS payouts. Although the contracts were eventually activated in 2012, by then many investors had lost faith. They lost more in 2014, after Portugal’s central bank split the failing Banco Espirito Santo in two and the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA) judged its CDSs to apply to the stronger offshoot. Some investors who held the old bank’s bonds faced huge losses—and Reichelt-like protection.
Despite these setbacks, the CDS is back in vogue. Concern over
France’s public debt
has driven the cost of related five-year CDSs to its highest in 14 years. In America the cost of insuring against a default in the next five years by Oracle, a cloud-computing giant going all-in on
artificial-intelligence data centres
, has quadrupled in the past 12 months. If the world’s mounting pile of debt comes crashing down, many CDS investors can expect a hard landing.
In some ways CDSs have been made less flaky. For example, changes to the terms of standard contracts in 2014 made it clear the redenomination of government debt into currencies other than the euro would count as a default, which was not explicit before. Bond exchanges, where an old liability is forcibly swapped for a new one more favourable to the borrower, also now count as a CDS-triggering default.
But although some of the old holes have been patched up, new tears have appeared. Since the last big update to ISDA’s rules 12 years ago, corporate defaults have become as unfashionable as skinny jeans, thanks to furious legal innovation by firms facing bankruptcy, especially in America. Many now opt for liability-management exercises (LMEs), creative restructurings of their debts that avoid lengthy court battles. Since 2024 LMEs in America have outnumbered conventional defaults.
Investors waited months for a CDS payout after Altice France, a telecoms firm, announced an aggressive LME restructuring in 2024. Holders of CDSs covering the debt of Ardagh Group, a European packaging manufacturer, faced an even rockier ride after its LME in July the same year. Prices of Ardagh CDSs fell at first, when it appeared that they would not be triggered. The payouts eventually landed, but not before investors again began to question the swaps’ merit.
At least Altice and Ardagh are based in Europe, where restructuring is considered a credit event that can (in principle) trigger a CDS. Not so in North America, home to almost all of the AI companies being buffeted by the credit-market storm. The businesses making chips, building data centres and otherwise involved in the fast-moving AI economy are reaching for complicated financing arrangements. Their loans are backed by things like data-centre leases and “remaining performance obligations” (customers’ promises to pay them for computing capacity). Suppliers are lending money to their customers, sometimes while borrowing loads themselves. Such complexity is a recipe for a nasty and uncertain restructuring.
Defenders argue that CDSs still provide protection in the event of a default. The sophisticated investors who most commonly buy such products are often prepared for protracted legal battles and willing to weather the volatility.
This makes CDSs sound like resource-intensive bets on distressed debt in the mould of Oaktree Capital or Elliott Management. Yet that is not how they were envisaged. Their original purpose was to make it easier to hedge exposure to debt by offering a predictable payout in the event of non-payment. When the payout is no longer predictable—and requires investors to turn into Howard Marks or Paul Singer, the hard-charging founders of Oaktree and Elliott, respectively—CDSs look as threadbare as Reichelt’s wings.

epub_85.title: The task facing the new head of India’s biggest private bank
epub_85.text:
The task facing the new head of India’s biggest private bank
Finance & economics
| Damage control
The task facing the new head of India’s biggest private bank
HDFC Bank needs revitalising
Oct 29th 2026
HDFC Bank started on a shoestring. In its first makeshift office, in a textile mill in Mumbai in 1995, rats gnawed at computer cables taped to the floor. Paper clips were meticulously accounted for. Staff held meetings under a peepal tree. Even as the bank grew, they were asked to bring in their own tea mugs.
Such prudence paid off. HDFC Bank soon became a formidable institution, known for efficiency, conservative lending, tight control of bad loans and steady profits. It is now India’s biggest private lender. But when Anup Bagchi, its new chief executive, took charge on October 27th, he inherited a difficult legacy.
In 2023 a $40bn
merger
with Housing Development Finance Corporation (HDFC), a related housing-finance giant, created one of the world’s largest banks. The logic was compelling. HDFC Bank’s cheap current- and savings-account deposits could help fund HDFC’s vast mortgage book, which had relied on dearer bonds, bank loans and longer-term deposits. The enlarged bank could also cross-sell home loans, cards and insurance to a bigger customer base.
Reality proved harder. The loan-to-deposit ratio jumped from 85% to 108%, raising funding costs and then squeezing the net interest margin. Liquidity requirements obliging banks to park deposits at the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and in government bonds became more onerous (as a mortgage lender HDFC had been exempt from some stricter rules applied to banks).
Broader forces affecting all banks added to the strain. Savers began moving money from low-yielding bank accounts to mutual funds on user-friendly apps, forcing banks to be more generous. And in February 2025 the RBI began cutting its policy rate after holding it steady for two years. (The central bank reversed course only this month.) While loan rates fell, banks were still paying higher deposit rates locked in earlier, explains Nitin Aggarwal of Motilal Oswal, a financial-services firm.
Some also questioned HDFC Bank’s governance. They included Atanu Chakraborty, its own chairman, who quit in March citing differences over “values and ethics”. (The RBI found no evidence of misconduct.) In July HDFC Bank’s board fined three executives 100,000 rupees ($1,050) each after the bank reportedly channelled 450m rupees to a state road-building agency, ostensibly to sponsor a safety campaign. The sum allegedly matched the gap between the formal deposit rate and the higher rate promised to the agency.
The share price has fallen by a third in the past year. But not all is gloom. In the year to September loans were up by 16% and deposits by nearly 19%, helped by an
RBI scheme
to attract foreign-currency deposits. In the latest quarter net profit rose by 5% year on year, to 195bn rupees. The return on equity (a gauge of profitability) was 14%—not shabby, but down from 17% the year before the merger.
So how should Mr Bagchi start earning his annual pay-packet of up to $3.7m? “Changing the culture and replenishing the talent pool” should be priorities, reckons Tamal Bandyopadhyay, author of two books on HDFC Bank. “The top and medium tiers of the bank have been faction-ridden in the past few years.” Many “victims of the cross-fire” quit, he says.
Mr Bagchi spent 34 years at the ICICI group, HDFC Bank’s fiercest competitor. He ran ICICI’s securities and life-insurance arms and helped build its banking franchise. But the turnaround could be a long one. Big bank consolidations show that “a larger balance-sheet alone does not guarantee stronger returns,” says Devang Rajkotia of Moody’s, a rating agency. A banker who has pitched to Mr Bagchi praises his “attention to detail”. He will need it.

epub_86.title: Christine Lagarde departs at a moment of peril
epub_86.text:
Christine Lagarde departs at a moment of peril
Finance & economics
| Monetary policy
Christine Lagarde departs at a moment of peril
Her successor as ECB chief will have an unenviable job
Oct 29th 2026
It’s official: Christine Lagarde is leaving the European Central Bank. Madame la présidente is likely to become the new boss of the World Economic Forum in Geneva and thus host of the great annual Davos gabfest. The 70-year-old former managing director of the IMF steered the ECB through the covid-19 pandemic and the inflationary shocks that followed.
She will depart in February, nine months ahead of schedule, at a moment of jeopardy. Her home country, France—where she was once finance minister—is going fiscally rogue. Failure to sort out credible budget plans has sent its bond yields soaring. The spread over the German benchmark is now as high as it was during the worst of the euro-zone crisis in the early 2010s (see chart). Marine Le Pen, a right-wing populist who once called for the single currency’s abolition, may next year enter the Élysée Palace. Ms Lagarde’s successor will have an unenviable task: persuading France to cut spending.
Her tenure began in more innocent times. In 2019 the euro crisis was well behind the bank, and government debts were falling fast. The ECB’s main problem was working out how to get inflation—then just above 1%—to the target of 2%. It was hardly a crisis. So policymakers sought other jobs, such as making central banking more environmentally friendly.
The idyll did not last. Three successive tests battered the ECB soon after Ms Lagarde took over. The first came a few months into her tenure, when covid reached Europe. Investors rushed to safety, which in Europe meant German debt rather than that of the periphery. At first, Ms Lagarde argued the ECB was “not here to close spreads”. Markets did not take the suggestion well.
She was caught in the perennial vice facing European policymakers. Soaring spreads can mess with the ECB’s ability to run monetary policy: what good does a cut to the bank’s policy rate do if a country’s actual borrowing costs rise by far more? Yet market discipline is also what stops politicians from borrowing heedlessly and dumping their problems at the ECB’s door. Ultimately, the danger of a fiscal crisis on top of a pandemic was too much to bear. Ms Lagarde set up a large bond-buying programme. The ECB had become the bloc’s crisis lender of not-quite-last resort.
Her second test was inflation. Pandemic stimulus, supply disruptions and the energy shock caused by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine ultimately pushed euro-zone inflation above 10% in 2022. At first, Ms Lagarde was reluctant to raise interest rates. Like many other central banks, the ECB hoped the surge might prove transitory. It waited longer than most before acting. After wages started climbing and inflation broadened across the economy, the bank was forced to raise rates by 4.5 percentage points between July 2022 and September 2023. Inflation returned to around 2% by late 2024.
Europe is still reckoning with the third test: hefty debts. Interest rates started rising in 2022, putting pressure on the most indebted countries. In July that year Italian borrowing costs began to rise much faster than German ones, prompting Ms Lagarde to devise a new “transmission-protection instrument” to keep spreads contained. There was a clear case for stepping in during the pandemic. But was the repricing really so disorderly this time? Markets did not seem unduly alarmed. Investors learned that the ECB would intervene to manage bond disorder—so long as countries stuck to some basic rules of prudent macroeconomic management.
And what about countries that do not? That is the question that will bedevil Ms Lagarde’s successor. The French presidential election, in April and May 2027, is unlikely to bring much clarity. Ms Le Pen has suggested spending cuts to bring down debt, but her ideas are thin and her party would command no majority to pass legislation, much like the current minority government. Even if a centrist wins, the odds of progress do not look much better. As French spreads continue to climb, the ECB must prepare for a stand-off with its second-biggest member.
The appointment of Ms Lagarde’s successor will be a highly political affair. In quintessential European fashion, that means haggling over several jobs at once. The ECB’s six-strong board will need three new members by the end of next year. So far, a Dutchman, two French nationals and an Italian have steered the euro through its first quarter of a century. It is arguably Germany’s turn to lead the bank. The problem is that Ursula von der Leyen, head of the European Commission, is herself German and her term runs until 2029.
Thus the two main contenders are from elsewhere: Pablo Hernández de Cos, the Spanish head of the Bank for International Settlements, a club for central banks, and Klaas Knot, a former governor of the Dutch central bank.
Mr Hernández de Cos may be attractive to German officials. They could try to persuade France he is a soft-money dove, which would then necessitate a German becoming the bank’s chief economist so as to strike a balance between southern tolerance for higher inflation and teutonic firmness when governments come begging for lower rates. Such a line-up would also give Spain—economically strong and in good fiscal shape—an overdue turn running the bank.
But the French are not so easily fooled. Mr Hernández de Cos is not really a dove. And they have accepted that the next boss will have to be in a more German mould. To them, Mr Knot, the Dutchman, is acceptable—provided the chief economist is French. Their main contenders for that job are also women. That matters, because Ms Lagarde and Isabel Schnabel, the only two women on the executive board, are both leaving and, embarrassingly, all 21 national central-bank governors on the monetary-policy council are men.
So German policymakers may return to the remit of the ECB’s new boss. Top of the list is to explain to politicians in Paris that high interest rates on French debt are of their own making, and that fiscal measures will be needed first, to restore trust, before any help arrives from the central bankers. Such a message, Germany may well conclude, would sound best in blunt, phlegmatic Dutch.

epub_87.title: Ignore AI and ask for that pay rise
epub_87.text:
Ignore AI and ask for that pay rise
Finance & economics
| Free Exchange
Ignore AI and ask for that pay rise
Fear of a technological revolution may be suppressing wages
Oct 29th 2026
Imagine unwinding after a long day at work by reading about the end of work. A post on Reddit tells you that “The entire point” of artificial intelligence is to “ensure you have zero ability to work for a living”. You visit Blind, an anonymous confessional for anxious tech workers, where employees trade horror stories of two-year job hunts yielding nothing but automated rejections. The best thing you can do, you decide, is to future-proof yourself by mastering the new tools. But then you read that AI is said to have made short work of the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture. Time to change job after all? “At this point, it seems easier to get into Harvard than get a new job,” warns another Redditor. Harvard rejected you, so best to stay put. At least your boss likes you.
The doomscrollers are not alone. Across America, workers increasingly fear that AI will take their jobs. Yet for now, the more immediate threat may be to their pay. Average hourly wages in the private sector have risen by just 3% in the past year. Prices have risen faster still, pushing down real wages. That is all the more surprising given productivity is growing healthily, which ought to support pay rather than squeeze it. During the dotcom productivity boom of the late 1990s, for instance, real hourly wages grew by more than 2.5% a year. Some Americans were even cheerful.
Might AI have something to do with it? As the technology takes over more tasks, firms may need fewer workers, weakening demand for labour and holding down wages. Such fears received fresh fuel on October 26th, when Microsoft offered buy-outs to 60,000 employees to contain costs while making gargantuan investments in AI. But evidence of widespread job losses attributable to AI remains thin. Unemployment is low; layoffs are scarce. In a recent survey by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, just 4% of service firms using AI reported laying off workers in the past six months because of it, while roughly as many reported hiring more workers as hiring less. Researchers at Stanford University, studying payroll records for millions of Americans, have likewise found little evidence of widespread AI-driven displacement.
Even so, fear of AI could still be having an effect, by causing workers to cling to the jobs they have rather than seek new ones. Businesses’ demand for workers remains healthy, judged by job openings. But workers are reluctant to jump ship. The Economist estimates that Americans are quitting 13% less often than job openings and the unemployment rate would predict, based on the pattern of the past 25 years. In professional and business services, a sector filled with AI-exposed jobs, the quit rate is nearly a third lower than in 2019, and almost as low as it was during during the global financial crisis of 2007-09. Wage growth in the sector has tumbled, too. When workers are happy to stay, employers face less pressure to raise pay to keep them.
Consider the reaction to Microsoft’s offer: “Taking a buyout means you may never have a job in tech ever again,” warned one viral post on X. And workers seem more spooked by the prospect of finding another job than by that of losing their current one, making them all the more determined to stay put. A survey by the Boston Fed found that just one worker in ten was concerned about AI-related job losses, but that six in ten expected AI to lead to layoffs in their industries. Another survey in July showed that Americans’ confidence in finding a new job was near a record low, even as they saw little increase in the risk of losing the one they had in the short term.
Research supports the idea that workers are acting on their fears by doing nothing. Economists at the Atlanta Fed examined how workers’ expectations about the labour market affect their decisions to switch jobs. They find that a rise of ten percentage points in the perceived risk of not finding work is associated with roughly 13% fewer job switches, even after accounting for differences among workers and in local labour-market conditions. All told, changing expectations may explain roughly half the decline in job-hopping since 2022.
Economists have long understood that expectations can become self-fulfilling. Bank runs occur when nervous depositors withdraw their money, bringing down the very bank they fear might fail; expectations of inflation can spur spending and wage demands, helping to push up prices. Something similar may be happening in the labour market, though the panic works in reverse. AI anxiety may cause workers to cling to their jobs, leaving employers fewer vacancies to fill—roughly half of job openings come from firms replacing departing workers. This in turn leaves other workers with fewer opportunities, further weakening labour’s bargaining power. Karl Marx wrote of an “industrial reserve army” weighing down the “active labour-army”. Today, the mere spectre of an agentic army may be doing the same.
Still, dismal scientists cannot blame dismal thinking alone. Even if AI isn’t fuelling firings, it does appear to be slowing hiring in some sectors, particularly of young workers. Other factors may also explain workers’ new clinginess. Homeowners paying rock-bottom mortgage rates may be reluctant to move for a new job and a pricier loan. And the Great Resignation of 2021-22, when Americans switched jobs in large numbers, may have left many happily settled with their employers. Not all job-hugging is driven by fear.
Workers may have more power than they think. AI should make them more productive—and more valuable. But they will have to claim their share. The Boston Fed survey found that workers who felt AI had boosted their productivity were more than four times as likely to report willingness to ask for a pay rise. Just as pessimism can sap bargaining power, confidence can strengthen it. Doomscrollers of the world, know your worth!

epub_89.title: Treatments for age-related infertility are being developed at last
epub_89.text:
Treatments for age-related infertility are being developed at last
Science & technology
| Stopping the biological clock
Treatments for age-related infertility are being developed at last
Startups hope to improve IVF by revealing the biology of infertility
Oct 29th 2026
FOR MANY well-known reasons, women around the world are increasingly choosing to have babies in their mid-30s and into their 40s. They face a considerable challenge: genetic errors in their eggs increase as they get older, leading to fewer pregnancies and more miscarriages.
In-vitro fertilisation
(IVF) has long been the only solution offered to these women but, as it stands today, it is not fit-for-purpose and can be an expensive and heartbreaking gamble. If they can tolerate the financial, physical and emotional burden, would-be mothers are advised to try the process as many times as they can bear.
Change may be on its way. Two European startups want to increase women’s chances of having a baby with treatments to improve the viability of human eggs. They are building on research that has peered deep inside the human egg to explain exactly why baby-making becomes so error-prone as women age. By identifying the molecules and processes responsible for faulty eggs, the companies hope to improve IVF outcomes for older women.
A woman’s oocytes (immature eggs) are some of the oldest cells in her body. They were formed when she was a fetus; her ovarian reserve peaked in the millions while she was still in her mother’s womb. By puberty, the stock has plummeted to 300,000-400,000. She will continue to lose oocytes every month up until reserves are virtually depleted at menopause.
It is not only the quantity of oocytes that drops with time: so does their quality. Older ones are more likely to carry chromosomes in abnormal numbers. Healthy human cells have 23 pairs of matching chromosomes. As egg cells develop, each pair is joined and lined up carefully, ensuring that they can be split such that half—one complete set—are discarded. This leaves mature eggs with 23 single chromosomes that can partner with the corresponding number in a sperm. If something goes wrong in the process, an “aneuploid” egg can be formed: one that has either too few or too many chromosomes.
Aneuploidy is a leading cause of infertility. In women in their 20s over 20% of oocytes have an incorrect number of chromosomes. The share rises to 50% in those over the age of 40. No one has yet developed a solution to the problem.
Around the beginning of the decade a team led by Melina Schuh of the Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences in Göttingen, Germany, began mapping out the molecular causes of aneuploidy. They showed that levels of cohesin, a molecule which holds chromosome pairs together as an egg develops, decline with age. Diminished cohesin disrupts the chromosomal choreography and can result in aneuploid eggs. The team also found that a protein called Shugoshin 1 (derived from a Japanese word meaning “guardian spirit”) plays a crucial role in preventing cohesin’s decay, and thus lowers the risk of oocytes turning into aneuploid eggs.
In January 2025 Dr Schuh and her collaborator Agata Zielinska founded a company, Ovo Labs, to turn these discoveries into treatments. Ovo Labs is developing a product called EmbryoProtect 1, based on Shugoshin 1, that can be injected into immature egg cells before aneuploidy develops. In lab experiments the team injected EmbryoProtect 1 first into mouse eggs and later into more than 100 human eggs donated by IVF patients.
Early results appear promising. “When a mouse gets older, 60% of the eggs become chromosomally abnormal,” says Dr Zielinska. “But when you treat an old mouse egg with EmbryoProtect 1 you can see that you almost fully eliminate the chromosomal defects.” A first generation of healthy mouse pups has been born by fertilising eggs treated with EmbryoProtect 1. When the team injected oocytes with the product, they found that the proportion that developed chromosomal errors fell by roughly half compared with an untreated control group.
Dr Schuh says data from Ovo Labs and her laboratory at the Max Planck Institute show that in oocytes from women aged 34-40, the proportion of chromosomally normal eggs more than doubled after treatment. Dr Zielinska and her collaborator Debojit Saha, now at Princeton University, presented these results, which are not yet peer reviewed, at the annual meeting of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine, in Baltimore, on October 26th and October 28th. If their findings translate into clinical practice, women undergoing IVF could have “substantially more” chromosomally normal eggs available for their IVF cycles, says Dr Schuh.
A second startup, U-Ploid Biotechnologies based in Oxford, was created by Alexandre Webster and Chloe Charalambous, two former members of Dr Schuh’s lab. Instead of replicating Shugoshin 1, the firm has developed a molecule called Lyvanta that slows down separase, an enzyme which cleaves Shugoshin 1, leading to less cohesin and, eventually, more aneuploidy.
In experiments on mice publicised in 2025, Lyvanta reduced the incidence of chromosomal defects in 84% of eggs. U-Ploid is now testing their molecule in human cells. In preliminary results also presented in Baltimore, it said that treating immature eggs with Lyvanta had almost doubled the number which matured to be chromosomally normal. The team said that 66% of cells treated with Lyvanta did not have any chromosome errors, compared with 36% of untreated eggs.
Ovo Labs is exploring two further approaches to reduce aneuploidy. One is an engineered cohesin that would help its natural counterpart hold chromosomes together as eggs mature. The first results are expected to be published in a scientific journal on November 5th.
The other approach builds on an understanding of how immature human eggs shed their excess chromosomes. That process involves microscopic spindles which line up the chromosomes inside the egg as it divides. Dr Schuh’s research has shown that this spindle structure is particularly unstable in human eggs, even in younger women, in comparison with other mammals. This could explain why one in five eggs from women in their 20s is aneuploid, as well as why miscarriages are common even in younger women.
Comparisons with mice, cows and pigs revealed that human oocytes have very low levels of a spindle-stabilising protein called KIFC-1. Injecting KIFC-1 back into human egg cells reduced the risk of aneuploidy. Dr Schuh says Ovo Labs is exploring this avenue in the hopes that boosting spindle stability could improve IVF outcomes for both younger and older patients.
Rita Vassena, a fertility specialist and industry veteran at CooperSurgical, an American health-care firm based in Connecticut, calls preclinical data from both U-Ploid and OvoLabs “encouraging” but cautions that the technologies “will need to prove their short- and long-term safety and efficacy”. Still, says Dr Vassena, “Fixing the problem at the source brings about an unprecedented potential for treatment-efficiency gains.”
Demand will be high if any of these approaches pass clinical testing. In America more than 40% of women seeking fertility treatments were over 38 in 2018. In Britain, one in six patients starting IVF in 2023 was aged 40 and above. The researchers at Ovo Labs and U-Ploid say they frequently have to turn away women wanting to get in early on clinical trials that do not yet exist.

epub_90.title: China increasingly depends on copying American AI
epub_90.text:
China increasingly depends on copying American AI
Science & technology
| Copycats
China increasingly depends on copying American AI
Model distillation infuriates America, but may end up holding China back
Oct 29th 2026
Consider a water-skier. Surfing in the wake of a speedboat, they may at times go faster than the vessel pulling them along—but they never overtake it. Lately some experts have turned to this analogy to describe China’s race with America for supremacy in artificial intelligence. They suggest that the impressive progress of Chinese labs largely relies on the pace of their American peers pushing out the frontier. If America speeds up, so might China. If America were to throttle down, Chinese labs would slow too.
The reason is “distillation”: the training of an AI model on the output of another, rather than from scratch. As ai becomes more capable, the extent to which Chinese firms are distilling the best American models has become an urgent question. America’s companies need users to pay for their expensive models rather than use cheap knock-offs. And America wants to stay far ahead of China: President Donald Trump has said that “Whoever wins AI, wins.” Yet the widespread distillation of frontier AI models may not be quite as bad for America, nor as good for China, as it seems.
The idea of distillation is simple. In the early stages of training, large language models (LLMs) are usually taught to mimic text on the internet. Distillation teaches them instead to mimic other LLMs. The words generated by American models exhibit precisely the sorts of skills and reasoning Chinese developers want their own models to learn. As such, their output is useful fodder for training.
American developers on the frontier have no more advanced models to distil, and the text on the internet is all but exhausted. They instead increasingly rely on a less efficient technique called reinforcement learning (RL). It involves setting a goal for their model, such as solving a complex maths problem, and letting it experiment in search of a solution. American firms now spend more than half of their computing resources on RL-related techniques, up from a twentieth in early 2024.
Chinese firms can thus distil the capabilities that American models learn through expensive RL training. Like a student with a tutor, their AIs learn faster than American ones working things out alone. A small model trained by DeepSeek, a Chinese lab, on 800,000 examples produced by their most powerful model went from a score of 15% to 46% on a popular mathematics test, according to a study published in the Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics in July.
Far more data are needed to match the capabilities of frontier models—but Chinese labs appear to be distilling at scale. A report published in September by Anthropic found that five Chinese firms had collected more than 180m messages from its models in five months. Chinese models bear a measurable resemblance to American ones (see chart), and sometimes even identify themselves as Claude or ChatGPT.
How much does distillation matter? Much of China’s progress in ai is homegrown. More than half the world’s top AI researchers are of Chinese origin, as measured by papers presented at NeurIPS, the main global AI conference. But brainpower goes only so far. Advanced computer chips are today the main driver of AI progress, and America’s tech giants individually have more than all of their Chinese competitors combined. Distillation helps Chinese firms compensate. Researchers reckon Chinese AI is about three to six months behind the best American models. Without distillation the gap could almost double, estimates Saif Khan of the Centre for Technology & Statecraft in Washington.
Anthropic and OpenAI are keen to cut the rope. They have moved to end an exploit, found in August, that gives Chinese firms access to the reasoning that their models produce while solving problems. They have also stepped up their detection of distillation campaigns. Anthropic has begun charging for Claude requests even if the model senses what is going on and refuses to respond—making failed attempts at distillation costly.
Anthropic has said these new measures may not be lastingly effective, but have so far reduced the amount of data harvested by distillers by 90-99%. As a result it might give up about 5-7% of its revenue; distillers are still users, after all. The company argues that Chinese model-makers were releasing near-frontier models without guardrails against misuse, and that such models posed a national-security risk.
Yet, if they succeed, American labs may come to regret closing off access to their rivals. Chinese researchers have their doubts about the wisdom of relying on distillation. Few believe that training on American models is ethically wrong—frontier labs built their own systems on freely obtained internet data. But some bosses think that relying on the technique will condemn China to permanent second-place. Researchers at Chinese labs further suggest that, if it happens, recursive self-improvement—AI models that autonomously build their own successors—may rely on sophisticated RL infrastructure which distillers will not have.
Zhang Yiming, the founder of ByteDance, a Chinese internet firm, told his staff in July that the company would not use distillation to soup up its models. LatePost, a Chinese tech blog, paraphrased Mr Zhang’s comments, saying that distillation “will, at best, allow us to continually close the gap [with the frontier], but it will be difficult to truly surpass”. Mr Zhang acknowledged that letting go of the cord that tethers Chinese progress to the American frontier was leading ByteDance to fall behind. But the firm, unlike some of its rivals in China, has other streams of revenue and can afford to offer inferior models while it becomes more self-sufficient.
As for America, distillation is an annoyance, but may be better than Chinese firms skiing their own way to the frontier. The technique could make it easier to regulate ai, too. Mr Trump’s administration has been reluctant to slow down the progress of AI while it is made safer, lest America hand the competitive advantage to China. But if China is like a water-skier, it might not overtake even a slowing towboat.
