epub_91.title: Why dogs catch yawns from their owners but not other dogs
epub_91.text:
Why dogs catch yawns from their owners but not other dogs
Science & technology
| Pack mentality
Why dogs catch yawns from their owners but not other dogs
Studies of wolves suggest the effect may be a result of domestication
Oct 29th 2026
YAWNING IS CONTAGIOUS. And not only among humans. The mimicry has been seen in chimpanzees, elephants, pigs, wolves and even, allegedly, parrots. Its purpose, however, remains unclear. Many suspect it is a form of behavioural mirroring that helps animals strengthen social bonds and enhance group cohesion. In chimpanzees, for example, contagious yawning is more common among individuals who know one another.
Dogs yawn too. But, though these wolf-descended canids often do so after their owners, yawning after other dogs is rare. It therefore looks likely that, as part of the evolutionary process which created Man’s Best Friend, the bond-forming role of yawning has been transferred from one species to another. Federica Amici of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, and Paolo Ciucci of La Sapienza University in Rome, teamed up to investigate by comparing the yawning behaviour of purebred wolves with that of wolf crossbreeds carrying dog DNA.
Domestication is probably central to the story. Researchers suspect that over the course of 30,000-40,000 years living with (and being bred by) people, dogs have developed traits which made them more aware of human behaviours. Along the way, this process seems to have diminished their awareness of their own kind too. But that raises the question of what happens when dog genes migrate into wolves.
Drs Amici and Ciucci, and a group of their colleagues, headed to wilderness enclosures in the mountains of Germany and Italy to investigate. There they observed 20 captive purebred wolves and 13 captive canids that were the result of wolves and dogs crossbreeding in the wild for two or three generations. The animals were in small packs of eight and 12 among the purebreeds, and three, four and six for the crossbreeds. Each wolf was closely observed for 22 15-minute sessions. Yawns were studiously noted, as was the behaviour of other animals in the enclosure.
The researchers’ findings, as reported in Animal Cognition, were striking. When purebred wolves witnessed a yawn, there was a 41% chance they followed suit within two minutes. Such copycatting was seen only 24% of the time in the crossbreeds—supporting the idea that dogs’ shift to copying human yawns rather than those of their own kind is, indeed, a genetically evolved phenomenon.
Drs Amici and Ciucci also tested what made an individual likely to trigger a contagious yawn. Intriguingly, holding positions of power within a pack did not matter. What did was how well-connected an animal was. The wolves most likely to get others yawning were the socialites of the pack—those who spent time with the widest variety of packmates—among both the purebreds and crossbreeds.
The strength of the relationship between yawner and yawn observer was also found to have no effect in triggering a follow-up yawn. That is surprising because in primates, such as chimpanzees and bonobos, the strength of a social bond, for example being close friends or family, is a crucial factor in determining whether one yawn follows another.
The loss of the contagious yawn in wild populations, as a result of interbreeding between dogs and wolves, may seem trifling. But, with her conservationist’s hat on, Dr Amici worries that it might end up having adverse consequences.
A range of other subtle behavioural changes associated with domestication, as yet unspotted by researchers, may well be migrating into wild wolf populations. This, in turn, could easily create a cascade of profound ecological repercussions. Indeed, if dog DNA ends up disrupting important elements of wolf biology—such as pack cohesion or co-ordination during hunts—it will ultimately impact the wolves’ ability to produce offspring which survive and reproduce themselves. Wolves are one of the most social species on the planet. It could prove fatal if they were to tire of one another’s company.

epub_92.title: Are some protein powders better than others?
epub_92.text:
Are some protein powders better than others?
Science & technology
| Well Informed
Are some protein powders better than others?
Pure whey is the way to go
Oct 29th 2026
ALCHEMISTS SOUGHT to turn base metals into gold. They failed. But for body builders, Eugene Schiff, a pharmacist from Detroit, managed the next best thing. In 1936 he turned whey, the liquid waste from cheesemaking, into a protein powder. Athletes and gym rats now pay top dollar for the stuff. And whey has been joined by powders made from its fellow dairy product, casein, and from leguminous plants, namely peas and soyabeans. Which is best?
A crucial ingredient to look for is leucine. This is about 12% of whey powder’s mass and one of the 20 amino acids from which proteins are composed. It is one of the nine dubbed “essential”, because humans cannot make them, so they must arrive in food. But leucine has many talents. It also activates a biochemical pathway, called the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR), that encourages protein synthesis.
After exercise, mTOR gets to work replenishing muscle fibres. Leucine thus helps provide not only the signal, but also the raw materials. Put another way, says Stuart Phillips, a kinesiologist at McMaster University, leucine is both brick and bricklayer. In younger, active adults, leucine’s muscle-building might goes only so far, says Brad Schoenfeld of Lehman College in New York: there is no additional benefit to taking more than that found in a standard 25g scoop of whey powder. Older people’s muscles are tougher to stimulate. For them, whey with extra leucine can be beneficial for building brawn, according to a study of 20 people in Nutrition Journal in 2014.
The other amino acids are important too. Writing in the Journal of Physiology, in 2012, Dr Phillips and his colleagues gave three groups of young men different combinations of whey, leucine and other amino acids immediately after a leg workout. Some took full whey, for example, whereas others had a quarter dose topped up with extra leucine. The researchers then took samples one, three and five hours later from the quadriceps above each participant’s knee. While leucine triggered the muscles’ response across the board, those who had received a full dose of whey enjoyed the most prolonged period of muscle synthesis.
How does whey compare to rival protein powders? Casein, the protein of the solid curds from which whey is separated during cheesemaking, is less leucine-heavy; it makes up 8% of the powder’s mass. That means it will not be as effective immediately after a workout, but it does contain a good balance of other essential amino acids. Pea and soya powders, in contrast, have less protein per serving overall.
Whey itself comes in refined varieties. There are isolates with less lactose for those wanting to avoid calories, and hydrolysates pre-digested with enzymes to make the powder easier on the gut. Such concoctions are often touted as offering greater benefits owing to their more refined nature. But a study published in Nutrition & Metabolism in 2021 found little evidence they boost muscle synthesis any more than pure whey. For gym buffs looking for a quick recovery after a workout, then, a full dose of unadulterated whey is the best bet.
A few ingredients are best avoided. Some powders are leavened with glycine and taurine, amino acids that can be synthesised cheaply. These inflate a product’s amino-acid count while doing little to stimulate muscle growth. Some makers bulk up their products with starches, gums and emulsifiers too. Buyers should remember: not all that glitters is muscle-building gold.

epub_94.title: Humans will never again create a project quite like Wikipedia
epub_94.text:
Humans will never again create a project quite like Wikipedia
Culture
| The last testament
Humans will never again create a project quite like Wikipedia
As it turns 25, one of the internet’s unlikeliest successes faces grave new threats
Oct 29th 2026
Written on nearly 23,000 rolls of manuscript, the Yongle encyclopedia, commissioned by a Ming emperor in the 15th century, was the largest reference work in history. It held that title for around 600 years—until
Wikipedia
, a startup run out of a chaotic office in Florida, overtook it after just six years in business. Today the collaborative online encyclopedia runs to 30bn words in more than 300 languages. Its Latin edition alone has more articles than the “Encyclopedia Britannica”.
As Wikipedia celebrates its 25th anniversary this year, it faces big problems. It is shedding both readers and volunteer editors. It is at the centre of an escalating culture war. And AI poses an
existential threat
. As Richard Cooke, an Australian journalist, observes in a thought-provoking new book, Wikipedia is the largest encyclopedia ever written by humans—and it is likely to hold that title for ever. (Any future rival is sure to be made with the help of AI.)
As the world’s go-to crowd-written reference source, Wikipedia serves as both an oracle and a mirror. Its story can be traced back to a childhood purchase. When Jimmy Wales was three years old his mother bought a copy of the “World Book Encyclopedia”, which the family updated each year using stickers sent by post. Decades later, Mr Wales was casting around for business ideas. An online encyclopedia never need go out of date, he reasoned. So with a colleague, Larry Sanger, he founded Nupedia in 2000. Its seven-step process of editing and fact-checking meant that after five months it had approved a single article (on “atonality” in music). So to speed things up, they changed tack, launching a crowd-sourced encyclopedia in 2001.
Wikipedia was dreadful—and this was the secret of its rapid early growth. “The average person seeing the young Wikipedia for the first time thought they could do better,” Mr Cooke writes. Later that year the site came into its own, as more than 100 articles about the
September 11th
terrorist attacks were added in less than a month.
Seeing its commercial potential, its bosses considered selling ads. Yet after defections from volunteer editors who didn’t want to work for “WikiPAIDia”, they backed down and ran it as a non-profit. Mr Wales has called it “either the smartest or the dumbest thing that I ever did”: he has not made much money out of the phenomenon he co-founded.
Mr Cooke’s book is an enjoyable rabbit hole of information, rather like its subject. It paints an affectionate portrait of the many oddballs and misfits who have made the site what it is. The second-largest language on Wikipedia is Cebuano, a minority tongue of the Philippines, which has 6m articles—mostly about insects—that have been uploaded by a bot made by a Swede who married a Filipina. A user called Giraffedata cannot bear the phrase “comprised of”, and has spent 15 years removing tens of thousands of occurrences. No one will be surprised to learn that most Wikipedia editors are men.
The make-up of Wikipedia editors is reflected in the site’s content. Its article about Scrappy Doo, a cartoon character, was at one stage 2,000 words longer than the one for
Poland
. And although editors wear their national dress on the first day of the annual Wikimania conference, in a multinational display of diversity, they are not an especially diverse bunch. For Wikipedia’s first ten years, half of all edits came from five countries; there were more editors in the Netherlands than in Africa.
But now Wikipedia faces even bigger challenges. One is the febrile political climate. Certain topics have always provoked “edit wars”: the most contested pages include
Israel
, Jesus and
Donald Trump
. There have long been problem contributors (the Church of Scientology was the first organisation to be banned from editing Wikipedia, in 2009). But recent arguments about misinformation and censorship have been harder to deal with. Mr Sanger, whose relationship with Mr Wales soured, has denounced Wikipedia’s “globalist, academic, secular and progressive” bias. Last year
Elon Musk
, a former fan of the site, announced Grokipedia, an alternative to what he called “Wokepedia”.
The charged political atmosphere has exacerbated a second problem: a lack of editors. Early Wikipedia welcomed newbie contributors. But after some sticky cases of defamation, it tightened up its rules, particularly regarding articles about living people. Since 2017 new editors have been banned from creating fresh entries. Trigger-happy editors even deleted an entry by Mr Wales—on Mzoli’s Meat, a South African barbecue restaurant—for failing the notability test. As Mr Cooke puts it, anyone can edit Wikipedia in the same way that anyone can, in theory, represent themselves in court. For amateurs it can be a complex, hostile experience. The number of active editors in English has fallen by a third since its peak in 2007.
The third, most
ominous threat is AI
. Wikipedia played a crucial role in training large language models (LLMs) with its vast, free, multilingual dataset. It is probably “the single most important training corpus in the history of artificial intelligence”, writes Mr Cooke. This has had the side-effect of immortalising the site’s many errors and hoaxes. Ask ChatGPT who invented the electric toaster, and it may still tell you it was Alan MacMasters, a Scottish prankster who once credited himself as its inventor on Wikipedia as a joke.
AI’s absorption of Wikipedia means that more people than ever are reading its content. Yet it also means that fewer people are visiting the site itself. When a Wikipedia link is suggested by a search engine, nearly a tenth of users click through. When Wikipedia is cited by an LLM, the clickthrough rate is only 0.33% (and not all credit their sources). Since 2022 Wikipedia has lost almost a quarter of its readership—and with it, opportunities to solicit donations and recruit new editors. Wikipedians are “a smaller club working harder to maintain something fewer people see”, laments one longtime contributor.
Wikipedia’s billions of words, written, edited and categorised by millions of human volunteers, helped create the conditions for AI. Now AI’s use of that material threatens to suffocate the very source that helped bring it to life.

epub_95.title: What the world’s most famous magician has to teach you
epub_95.text:
What the world’s most famous magician has to teach you
Culture
| Harry Houdini’s greatest trick
What the world’s most famous magician has to teach you
Hint: it does not involve handcuffs or a straitjacket
Oct 29th 2026
YOU COULD call it a re-appearing act. After he died on Halloween in 1926, Harry Houdini’s spirit supposedly returned. In Santa Monica his spectre was seen making a dramatic escape from handcuffs; in Chicago people saw the magician’s spirit swagger into a séance. His widow, Bess, dismissed such claims: if Houdini wanted to reach out from beyond the grave, he would use their secret code. Bess waited to hear from Houdini for ten years before declaring that “spirit communication in any form is impossible.”
This year fans are conjuring up Houdini again. On October 31st, to mark the centenary of his death, many will gather in dimly lit rooms to summon his spirit. In Europe and America
magic show
s
will recreate his most daring tricks. There are new exhibitions: “Houdini’s Library” at the Harry Ransom Centre in Austin, for example, shows he was a bibliophile as well as a showman. A new docuseries, “Houdini: Back from the Dead”, uses AI to render the magician and have him narrate his life. A council of magic enthusiasts has even planned HOUDINI100™, a four-day commemoration in Budapest that includes a lock-picking contest and a trip “to meet Houdini, the local celebrity rabbit”.
The fanfare is for good reason: Houdini is probably the most celebrated illusionist of all time. His name haunts dictionaries (the noun “houdini” is “a person or animal that is very good at escaping”) and pop songs (“catch me or I go Houdini,” trills
Dua Lipa
in one song). Houdini is famous in part because he was the “master of mystery”. But also because he was, as John Cox, a Houdini expert, puts it, “a master at understanding how to promote himself”. Just as you can study Houdini’s performances to understand magic, you can study his career to understand fame.
Houdini offers three lessons for anyone looking to sell something. First, work hard to polish your product. The magician trained like an athlete to ensure he could get out of tight spaces and straitjackets and learned how to hold his breath for minutes on end for underwater escapes. Houdini was also one of the first people “to take the scholarship of magic seriously”, notes Eric Colleary, curator of “Houdini’s Library”. He collected biographies of magicians and histories of sorcery; his research helped him refine his craft and invent new tricks, such as being buried alive or making an elephant disappear.
Second, learn the art of self-promotion. The “golden age” of magic in the 19th century was bolstered by mass media. Rather than buying an advert near the back of a newspaper, Houdini would pull off a stunt to get on the front page. “I’m not an advertiser, I’m news,” he once quipped. In every city he visited he dared police to lock him up so he could escape, and freed himself from straitjackets while hanging upside down from cranes. He was among the first magicians to use radio and movies to help promote his shows.
Houdini also understood corporate partnerships. “How Houdini Made Magic”, a new podcast, looks at his “brand deal” with Joshua Tetley & Son, a brewer, in 1911. Rather than escaping from a sealed milk can full of water, he was challenged to get out of one filled with beer. But the stunt went awry: Houdini, who didn’t drink beer, apparently passed out from the stench in the container and had to be rescued. But that made the episode only more headline-worthy.
Lastly, Houdini understood the importance of protecting his brand. Like the organisers of his centennial celebration in Budapest, Houdini tried to ™ lots of his tricks. It did not always work, in part because a patent spells out the secrets. So instead he launched attacks on his imitators, who called themselves things like Boudini, Hardini, Houdeen and Oudini. He challenged copycats to beat him on stage and threatened to expose the secrets of their tricks to the public. He also copyrighted illusions as “playlets”, that he performed to just one person, and then tried to sue anyone who copied him. If you can’t beat them, enjoin them.

epub_96.title: Why this is a golden age for conspiracy theories
epub_96.text:
Why this is a golden age for conspiracy theories
Culture
| The paranoid style
Why this is a golden age for conspiracy theories
They flourish during periods of social and political upheaval
Oct 29th 2026
John F. Kennedy junior died in a plane crash in 1999. Or did he? Some Americans insist he faked his death and is secretly working with Donald Trump to vanquish the “
deep state
”. In September heroic passengers and a wounded captain stopped a deranged co-pilot from flying a packed jet into Israel’s main airport. Or, online commentators suggest, they were all participants in a “false-flag operation” staged by Israel’s government.
Conspiracy theories are nothing new. Plenty of people have an uncle happy to argue after a few drinks that the moon landing was faked, or have walked past pamphleteers blaming some shadowy group for all the world’s ills. But never have so many spread so fast, so far and—with political leaders across the world eager to stoke conspiracy theories when it suits them—so high. To understand why, turn to three new books that show how
conspiracy theories
thrive at times of social upheaval.
Andrew McKenzie-McHarg, a historian, says two characteristics distinguish conspiracy theories from ordinary rumours or smears. First, they posit plots by the powerful. People spin conspiracy theories to explain secret forces shaping the world, not, say, why their dishwasher fails to clean between fork tines. And second, they refer “not just to a conspiracy but to a non-existent conspiracy”.
Watergate
and the Iran-contra affair, for instance, are infrequent subjects for theorising because they were actual conspiracies. (They were also exposed and punished.) By contrast, conspiracy theories focus on “hidden” plots.
The phrase “conspiracy theory” may have first appeared in the New York Times in 1863, in a letter rebutting the charge that Britain was “going out of her way to meddle with America” during the civil war. But the concept is much older. In the 14th century Jews were accused of spreading the
Black Death
by poisoning wells. Many Londoners said Catholics started the Great Fire of London in 1666. “The Protocols of the Elders of Zion”, first published in Russia in 1903, purported to reveal a Jewish plot for world domination. These theories emerged at times of social upheaval: wars, pandemics and the crumbling of the old imperial order. They provided simple explanations for complicated events—and a villain to blame.
Michael Taylor, another historian, explores the quintessential conspiracy theory of this type in his terrifically entertaining book, “Illuminati”. The Illuminati existed, but far from being an all-powerful group of string-pullers, they were a bunch of fissiparous nerds. The group was founded in Bavaria in 1776 to spread Enlightenment values. Were they a secret society? Yes, but secret societies flourished across Europe at that time. Did they want to reform and liberalise society? Yes, but there is nothing inherently sinister about that.
Bavaria’s authorities hounded the Illuminati out of existence after barely a decade, but the group lived on in the imagination. In 1797 a reactionary French priest called Augustin Barruel blamed thinkers including Voltaire and Denis Diderot for seeking to destroy Christianity with the help of
Freemasons
and the Illuminati. Revolutionary terror, he thundered, embodied “the black arts of Illuminism”. Like many conspiracy theorists, he spun a web of fantasy around a kernel of truth: the Illuminati really were a secret group opposed to religious repression. But that was a far cry from plotting to destroy Christianity.
In 1919, more than a century later, Nesta Webster revived Barruel’s theory. The English author wrote that the “diabolical methods employed by the Jacobins of France, indoctrinated by the Illuminati, have been repeated in Russia with terrible effect”. She added a nasty wrinkle: “a conspiracy of the Jewish race that began perhaps at Golgotha” had, in league with the Illuminati, inspired the French and Russian revolutions, the uprisings of 1848, the Paris Commune of 1871 and the rise of trade unionism. Nutty as that sounds, even
Winston Churchill
once called for “the schemes of the international Jews” to be exposed.
Even today, if you search “Illuminati” on any social-media platform, you will be faced with a deluge of lunacy, much of it
antisemitic
. In 2021 a poll of 25,000 people in 24 countries found that, on average, 37% believed “there is a single group of people who secretly control events and rule the world together”. Why do so many people buy such bunkum?
In “Conspiracy” Nicolas Guilhot, a French academic, writes that conspiracy theories “reflect a diffuse social malaise” and frustration with an “obsolescent variety of liberalism”. But disillusionment does not inevitably lead to delusion. Plenty of people agitate for political change by organising and voting, rather than posting about Democrats drinking children’s blood (the core of the
QAnon
conspiracy that raged during Mr Trump’s first term).
Mr Taylor suggests that people obsess over the Illuminati—or the Bilderberg Group, Freemasons, Jews or any other imagined conspirators often credited with superhuman powers of cunning and dominion—because they “have been unable or unwilling to accept that, sometimes, events are beyond the control of even the most competent actors”.
Revolutions, wars, pandemics and economic crises happen for complex reasons; many find it easier and more comforting to believe in a planned reality rather than one largely driven by chance and contingency. Small wonder that, as the post-war political order breaks down, people are again finding solace in conspiracy theories. Or maybe that’s just what the lizard people want you to think.

epub_97.title: John Green, a hit young-adult author, is now writing for adults
epub_97.text:
John Green, a hit young-adult author, is now writing for adults
Culture
| No longer green
John Green, a hit young-adult author, is now writing for adults
His latest novel explores social-media stardom; his own career has tracked it, too
Oct 29th 2026
John Green has many fans, among them
Taylor Swift
, who once called him “My. Favourite. Author.” He has sold over 50m copies of his young-adult books worldwide; more people have bought “The Fault in Our Stars”, a romance from 2012 about two young cancer patients, than “The Grapes of Wrath” or “
Catch-22
”. However, some have also found fault with the star writer. His first novel, “Looking for Alaska” (2005), has been the
most banned book
in American schools since PEN America, a free-speech group, began counting in 2021. (It contains swearing, drinking and an awkward sex scene censured as “pornographic”.)
Mr Green’s books offer earnest aphorisms that teenagers find profound, such as: “That’s the thing about pain, it demands to be felt.” He has written cringey musings (“my thoughts are stars I can’t fathom into constellations”) and musings on cringiness (“‘cringe’ is what people who can’t feel things call feelings”). Now Mr Green is back on top of the bestseller list. “Hollywood, Ending”, his first tale for adults, follows two actors in their 20s who become famous overnight.
“Hollywood, Ending” considers attention in the age of social media. Few authors understand the power of the internet quite like Mr Green: his career reveals how the relationship between writers and readers is changing in the digital age. In 2007, just two years after YouTube launched, Mr Green and his brother started a channel called Vlogbrothers, posting about their everyday lives. They were an unashamedly geeky pair: their fans were “nerdfighters” who came together “to do awesome things…and fight against world suck”.
The whole thing was terribly corny—but terribly popular. The Green brothers built a nerdy media empire—which includes educational videos about science and history—that has accumulated more than 6bn views on YouTube.
Mr Green’s online profile helped boost his book sales. He would read excerpts of his drafts for his fans on YouTube, or reveal he did not yet have a cover design (fans would then eagerly make and post hundreds of potential covers). He also promised to sign every pre-order, driving his books to the top of bestseller lists before they were published. He did this so often, in fact, that he was awarded a Guinness World Record in September for the most autograph pages ever signed by an author (see picture).
His fanbase also helped him understand who he was writing for. Authors of young-adult tales are often asked “When are you going to write a real book?” says Mr Green. He is “careful not to engage with that cliché because I think some of the most important novels of the last few decades have been written for teenagers”.
In the 2010s, when young-adult shelves were stuffed with fantasy romances such as “
Twilight
” or dystopian sagas like “
The Hunger Games
”, Mr Green instead published books about normal folk. He enjoyed interacting with his readers online and even based some of his characters on fans he met: Hazel Grace Lancaster, the protagonist of “The Fault in Our Stars”, was modelled in part on Esther Grace Earl, a “nerdfighter” who died of thyroid cancer in 2010. His books inspired other emotional, realistic books for teens, a trend some dubbed “GreenLit”.
Mr Green’s sincere, sentimental style just about worked in teen fiction. But does his book for adults hold up? “Hollywood, Ending” is more sophisticated than his earlier books. It muses on the entertainment industry, trauma and how well you can ever know someone. Yet some of the lines are less neat aphorisms than clunky tautologies: “The miracle of love is that yes, I am here and you are there, but the door is ajar…we break down the door with love.”
Fans will repost that sort of sappy line on their social-media feeds. Some may even notice that, as the author puts it, “we continue to come of age in different ways as we grow up.” John Green’s readers may have grown up—but they do not seem likely to outgrow him.

epub_98.title: How Lebanon’s civil war shaped America’s rivalry with Iran
epub_98.text:
How Lebanon’s civil war shaped America’s rivalry with Iran
Culture
| Death in Beirut
How Lebanon’s civil war shaped America’s rivalry with Iran
A new book argues a murder in 1984 can help you understand the Middle East today
Oct 29th 2026
FEW PLACES have fallen farther from their glory days. Beirut,
Lebanon
’s capital, was once a small corner of freedom in the Arab world, known for dance parties and louche living. Then in 1975 it descended into a vicious
sectarian conflict
. Israel and Syria occupied swathes of its territory. America sent marines to Beirut, and Iran cultivated Hizbullah, a Shia militia. By the end of the civil war in 1990 around 350,000 people, a tenth of the population, had been killed or wounded.
Into this carnage stepped Malcolm Kerr (pictured below), who became president of the American University of Beirut (AUB) in 1982. Kerr’s parents, who taught at AUB, had raised him on its leafy campus overlooking the Mediterranean from west Beirut. “I figure there’s a 50-50 chance that I’ll get bumped off,” Kerr confided to his daughter. But the university was a symbol of Lebanon’s cosmopolitanism, and he wanted to help keep it running. Less than two years later he was shot dead outside his office.
Kerr’s assassination is now little remembered. But Kim Ghattas, a journalist who grew up in wartime Beirut, puts it at the centre of her absorbing account of the war and its aftermath. Part murder mystery, part geopolitical history, “The Best Kind of American” uses the story of Kerr’s murder to explore how a small country’s conflict shaped America’s and Israel’s struggle against Iran.
For all its glamour, pre-war Lebanon was a powder keg. The government was weak; armed groups flourished. In 1970 it became the main base of Yasser Arafat’s
Palestine Liberation Organisation
(PLO), after it was expelled from Jordan. As the PLO’s conflict with Israel spread to Lebanon, tensions grew between the country’s religious sects. In 1975 the Wall Street Journal compared Beirut to Belfast: the city had become divided between the mostly Muslim west and the mostly Christian east.
AUB was “a microcosm of Lebanon”, writes Ms Ghattas. Students and faculty included right-wing Christians and downtrodden Shias. When Kerr arrived, there was cause for optimism. The PLO was leaving Lebanon for Tunisia, and America was preparing a peace plan. Those hopes would soon be dashed. In September 1982 Lebanon’s president-elect was assassinated, and Christian paramilitaries slaughtered Palestinians in refugee camps, with the tacit approval of Israeli troops.
Meanwhile the Iranian regime, which came to power in the Islamic revolution in 1979, spied an opportunity to use Lebanon in its struggle against Israel and America. Iranian operatives turned the Beqaa valley into a stronghold for their proxy Shia militias. In time these groups morphed into Hizbullah. In 1983 they bombed the American embassy and Marine barracks, killing hundreds. Kerr’s murder the following year was Hizbullah’s first high-profile political assassination and, Ms Ghattas suggests, part of a Shia takeover of west Beirut.
Many of these events read like a prelude to the present. Hizbullah’s creation was championed by
Ali Khamenei
, Iran’s president and later its supreme leader, who was killed on the first day of America’s and Israel’s war with Iran this year. Binyamin Netanyahu first appears as a suave young diplomat on American TV in 1982, defending Israel’s invasion of Lebanon. Today Israeli troops are there again; Mr Netanyahu went on to become Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. America’s failure in Lebanon was one of the superpower’s many botched efforts to fix the region.
This timely book has a few heroes, mostly the academics and activists who fought for peace. Like Kerr, many of them died prematurely. Those who wrecked the
Middle East
—in the region and beyond—would do well to learn from them.

epub_99.title: Once the heroes, ambitious outsiders have become TV villains
epub_99.text:
Once the heroes, ambitious outsiders have become TV villains
Culture
| Back Story
Once the heroes, ambitious outsiders have become TV villains
Call it the era of the talentless Mr Ripleys
Oct 29th 2026
He is a philandering tech baron; she is a preening actor. When they split up, how much of his fortune should she get? The answer to the big question in “War” is: who cares? As a dispatch from the front lines of duelling spouses and divorce lawyers, the glitzy new drama flops. It is, however, a telling snapshot of a different conflict—the class struggle—waged here by a revealing figure: the working-class villain.
Rags-to-riches fables are staples of fiction, from Charles Dickens to
“The Great Gatsby”
and beyond. Is it possible, these stories ask, to rise above disadvantage and vested interests, and what does it take to do so? The portrayal of the lower-class outsider as a baddie—in “War” and other recent tv shows—is a striking turn in an age-old narrative, which suggests a fatalistic social mood.
The high-powered solicitors in “War” spend lots of time striding portentously in and out of lifts and saying things that only fictional lawyers ever do, such as “See you in fucking court!” One of them, though, is not like the rest. Played by Archie Renaux (pictured), Johnny is a working-class boy who claws his way into a job at one of the swish, brawling
law firms
. He has also landed a posh, devoted girlfriend. You might expect the show’s verdict to be: good for Johnny!
Instead (spoiler alert) he is a liar and traitor, sneaked into his job by the firm’s hated rivals so he can spy for them. At risk of being rumbled, he incriminates a blameless colleague. When a snarling superior calls him a “jumped-up little twat”, it is hard to argue. He does the dirty on his girlfriend, too.
Speaking of girlfriends: “The Girlfriend”, a daft hit last year, has the same air of justified snootiness. Laura, a high-rolling mother, distrusts her son’s brassy new love interest. Laura thinks her name, Cherry, is déclassé. Cherry claims her dad was an architect (he was a builder) and to have attended a fancy school (she didn’t). She is disappointingly bad at tennis. Is Laura’s condescension out of order? Au contraire. She is entirely vindicated; Cherry is a malignant sociopath.
Meanwhile in “Sirens”, another recent hit, two hardscrabble sisters worm their way into a gazillionaire’s New England estate. Is the imperious matriarch secretly a murderer? No. Instead she is heartlessly usurped by one of the sisters; the other is a sex addict. Or consider “Industry”, a multi-series saga in which Harper, a young black woman from a troubled family, penetrates the citadel of high finance by forging her academic credentials. Before long she is insider trading and back-stabbing her friends. (Tom in
“Succession”
is an upscale version of these interlopers: a middle-class cynic who tramples to the top by betraying his wife.)
This is a departure. In recent, egalitarian decades, storytellers have generally sided with the underdog. So did many of their predecessors: even Victorian novels that satirise social-climbing—such as “Vanity Fair” and “The Way We Live Now”—tend to ridicule the snobs at least as much as the parvenus. “War” and other contemporary dramas are much harsher on their little guys. If “Slumdog Millionaire” were remade now, its hero might actually cheat to win the quiz jackpot; Rocky might take a fall for the mob in the fifth. Today’s upstart characters are heirs to Tom Ripley—
Patricia Highsmith
’s anti-hero, who prospers through lies, murder and impersonation—only mostly without his talent.
This newly jaundiced view of aspiration reflects a bleak reality of stalling dreams. Rates of social mobility in Britain and America have long trailed those in other rich countries. From a low base, they have on some measures declined in both places. Research across the rich world has found that, for people from modest backgrounds, going to university is a less reliable leg-up than it used to be.
So Johnny’s experience in “War”, as he struggles to capitalise on his education, is representative of his generation. Law is presented as a viperous profession, just as, in “Industry”, finance is a snakepit. In “Sirens” all the women are subject to a rich man’s whims. Life in all these stories is harsh and unfair; to join the wealthy, hustling outsiders first have to beat them. You could see all that as a frank reflection of prevailing conditions.
Except that the tone in “War” and “The Girlfriend”, say, often feels less sympathetic to these efforts than judgmental. It isn’t just that the odds are long; these working-class villains don’t deserve to overcome them. In a pessimistic commentary on a stratified era, they keep being told that they don’t belong—and, by and large, they don’t.

epub_103.title: Cecily Gemmell would do almost anything for Churchill
epub_103.text:
Cecily Gemmell would do almost anything for Churchill
Obituary
| Removing Winston’s socks
Cecily Gemmell would do almost anything for Churchill
His last personal secretary died on October 8th, aged 97
Oct 29th 2026
Heaven knows why the old man had painted her portrait. He didn’t do many; landscapes were more his style. Perhaps it was a reward for her washing his oil-caked paint brushes, a foul task that made her hands so rough and red. But she was the paints girl, who ordered his colours in for him because at the weekends she was at Chartwell, his country retreat, on duty. Perhaps that was why she looked sad, as well as rather too glamorised, and why she was holding her hands in her lap in that peculiar way.
She suspected that she had just been sitting around when he had the idea. But there certainly wasn’t much idling when one was employed by Mr Churchill. She did four years, covering most of his time as leader of the Opposition before, in 1951, he was prime minister again. She spent a good deal of it feeling utterly exhausted and trembling with fear, whenever she smelt that cigar smoke or heard that rumbling voice, that she was going to annoy the great man in some way. She spent much of the rest of it laughing.
When she first joined, in 1947 at the age of 18, she took months working 9 to 5 to sort his papers out. With not a jot of archive training and usually alone, she was faced with hundreds of black tin boxes and thousands of papers in no order, stowed in a perfectly stifling sub-basement right next to the furnace. The only window was under the front step, so she learned to identify famous visitors by their socks. Anthony Eden’s were pink.
Against anyone’s expectations, she laid the basis of the whole official archive. Her main task for the next three years, however, was “take-down”, typing up from dictation his speeches and the first draft of his war memoirs. Each evening after dinner she would hear that booming voice, like a dinner-gong, calling “Come!” She would leave the office, where the secretaries worked as a little team, take her book and climb the back stairs, to find the old man in the study or, sometimes, in his four-poster bed, which would be a total mess of newspapers, cigars, brandy, ashtrays and the occasional cat. He said: “Good evening. Put your paper in.”
The typewriter sat on a card table next to him. It was a brand-new model, electric, so clack-less, but the action was slow and hard and his flow of words was absolutely constant. He would speak and compose all at once, so driven that she didn’t dare ask him to stop. His speech impediment added to the nightmare. After her first session he came down the next morning and threw her pages on the ground, crying “You haven’t got one word in 50 right!” Worse was when she typed “Never in the field of human conflict” as “Never in the field of human conscience”, a mistake that stung him terribly because, as he tearfully reminded her, that was one of the greatest quotations in the world.
After the shouting, he would quickly start over again. That was what she found marvellous about him. But working with the old man was never exactly easy. When one was sitting ready at the table he might sit reading for an hour or so, often his own works. (“He’s very good, you know.”) Take-down sessions usually lasted til 2 or 3am, and long before that one’s eyes got so bleary that one would have to go downstairs and throw water on one’s face to stay awake. (“Don’t be long!” he would shout.) By that time she couldn’t safely get back to her room in Westerham, the nearest village, so she stayed in the Butler’s Cottage. That still entailed a fearful walk through the steep grounds in the dark, branches in her hair and burrs in her stockings, with the wind howling.
Yet she thought she had been picked for the job because she looked the toughest of the graduates from Mrs Hoster’s Secretarial College for “well-educated women”, where one learned to put three spaces after full stops and other essentials. She had been born in Bangalore, where her father was a map surveyor for the Indian army, and educated at Calcutta’s New School, aka “Harrow on the Hooghly”. Her nickname, “Chips”, came from an uncle killed in the Great War. The old man probably liked that background. At their first meeting, when again he was in bed, she felt bold enough to shake his hand. This, she was told, was not done.
After that, she was readier with her deferential thankyous. With the other girls in the office, though, she could go into fits about him. His awful striped siren suit was his “rompers”. His slow walk (shuffle, shuffle, in his monogrammed slippers) caused hilarity, as well as his voice, which she could imitate from shriek to growl. On one occasion they were so paralysed with giggles that the old man, who was painting in his studio, roared at his sergeant to take them out for a walk.
What did he make of her? Difficult to say. All the secretaries were just “Miss” to him. He would call “Miss!” to wait outside the bathroom door (loud sounds of splashing), so that she could take-down as soon as he came out. When in bed, he would stick his feet out sometimes for her to take off his socks. She was pleased to.
She left when Churchill became prime minister, feeling she would have to be so terribly responsible. For a while she worked as personal secretary to his wife Clementine, which mostly meant shopping for her and chasing up people for lunch. She left Downing Street in 1953 for New York, which she adored, secretarial work for Life and Time Inc and joyful partying in jazz clubs. She was now pretty good at late nights.
At their last meeting, on one of her rare returns, she sat beside Churchill at lunch at Chartwell. As he passed the mustard he scanned her face and asked, “Do I know you?” “Yes,” she replied; “I used to work for you.” “How long for?” “Four years.” “Oh,” came the comment. “What a long time.”
